In evaluating the potential of federated learning, this study proposes a framework 
known as Mixed FL (MLF) that incorporates various federated learning approaches 
within a single, integrated system. This framework particularly focuses on
developing deep learning models for the analysis of histopathology images and
includes six different FL techniques within its scope. The MLF framework was
applied in order to train and evaluate multiple deep learning models, including
DenseNet, ResNet, and U-Net, for predicting tumor infiltration scores and
classifying breast cancer vs. normal tissue. The MLF framework demonstrated
improved performance compared to a conventional centralized approach requiring
minimal data, as validated by multiple metrics. The variability in performance
was also found to be minimal across different FL methods within the MLF framework. 
The proposed framework is publicly accessible via the MLF-FL-HIA repository on GitHub.

In this study, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, achieving a data rate of 72Gbit/s using the on-off keying technique, over a distance of 18.8km in a South China Sea submarine cable that lacks dispersion compensation.  Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal nulls in a 36GHz bandwidth, severely hindering BER performance.  To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer was initially applied with satisfactory results, however its effectiveness was impeded due to the occurrence of burst errors resulting from unpredictable marine conditions.  To mitigate this issue, a weighted DFE method was developed but proved insufficient as it was unable to fully compensate for the spectral distortions due to the limited scope of its feedback symbols.  To address these limitations, the introduction of maximum likelihood sequence estimation after WDFE proved capable of both rectifying the spectral distortions and providing optimal detection, ultimately yielding a maximum 2.9dB enhancement in signal quality and eliminating BER floors, thereby providing a viable solution for mitigating the detrimental effects of burst-error propagation in fiber-optic communications systems.  The proposed WDFFE-MSE system design also offers greater flexibility for the optimization of equalizer and detector parameters.  To validate the effectiveness of this approach, computer simulations were conducted in conjunction with actual data collected from a 72Gbit/s underwater transmission experiment.  The findings from these experiments demonstrate the capability of the WDFFE-MSE to achieve optimal performance in the compensation of burst-error propagation.  To further explore the applicability of this method, the impact of burst-error propagation on the performance of various modulation formats was examined through the application of JDM-SI equalizers, which are optimized for minimum BER, and the resulting outcomes indicated that the WDFFE-MSE can achieve optimal performance in a wide range of data rates. Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. We've applied this technique to two prominent time-series tasks: sentiment analysis and financial forecasting, demonstrating substantial advancements in model performance, a 25.8% increase in the former and 14.4% in the latter, corresponding to an improvement of 11.5% and 5.6% in MAE, respectively. Moreover, our method yields a 2-fold reduction in parameter count and 10% increase in latency for pruned models, demonstrating a valuable approach for deploying TCNs on resource-constrained devices. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison
method relying on 2D descriptors. The NDF project is hosted at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/.

The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs has amassed substantial size over recent years, representing an impressive compilation of research and offering a diverse range of opportunities for statistical exploration in the field of theorem proving. Despite the numerous contributions made so far, the ever-expanding nature of the archive still poses certain challenges: locating specific content has become increasingly difficult, making it essential to prioritize reuse and clarity of comprehension. This thesis proposal outlines my research objectives, which focus on these concerns, as well as initial findings, which reveal that the Isabelle Archive exhibits characteristics typical of scale-free networks, as evidenced by the distribution of node in-degrees in its dependency graph. To further investigate this phenomenon, I plan to conduct additional analyses, including but not limited to: examining the co-authorships of contributor lists, conducting a detailed examination of the structure of individual theories, as well as exploring potential correlations between theory structure and content, including the relationship between theory dependencies and size, as well as the relationship between dependency depth and contribution metrics. Furthermore, I aim to conduct a qualitative analysis of contributing factors, as well as a quantitative analysis of contributor networks, set against the broader context of the field's development, as captured by the Zenodo database, by comparing the scientific output of contributors to the field, as well as examining how contributor lists reflect the broader scientific community, including university affiliations and contributor locations. Finally, I intend to visually represent the archive as a dynamic, evolving entity, as well as create interactive tools enabling users to freely explore and navigate the underlying dependency graphs of individual theories and the archive as a whole. By accomplishing these objectives, I hope to contribute to the advancement of the Isabelle theorem prover, as well as facilitate the growth of the archive itself, by identifying and addressing potential comprehension barriers, as well as pinpointing opportunities for improvement in the development process. Ultimately, my research is aimed at enriching our understanding of the archive, as well as its underlying dynamics, and is directed at both the broader scientific community, as well as the community of developers working with the Isabelle prover. As such, all research conducted will be openly available, freely accessible, and contributed back to the archive itself, as well as to the Isabelle repository, to benefit future developers, researchers, and users of the archive. In addition, I intend to present my research in the form of a publicly accessible document, as well as present initial and key findings at relevant conferences, as well as share my code, as well as any associated data, with the scientific community,

Using the functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion, we have updated the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity for O(N) universality classes in classic scenarios. Specifically for QCD's relevant universality classes in three dimensions, we have determined $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ to be approximately 1.607, 1.589 for $N=2, 4$ respectively. Alternatively, we have previously found $|z_c|$ to be around 2.03, 1.68 for $N=2, 4$ although these earlier results have a larger systematic uncertainty. These results can be used to set boundaries for theoretical predictions of phase transitions in models that include QCD. As an additional contribution, we have also updated the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity for two scenarios involving multiple degenerate critical points: the tricritical Ising universality class in three dimensions and the universality class of the rural 3D Ising model. Both of these cases involve multiple degenerate critical points and the corresponding bulk transition becomes first order only after further symmetry breaking. Therefore, extracting the Yang-Lee edge singularity requires distinguishing between the tricritical and true Yang-Lee edge singularities. Contrary to expectations, we have found the Yang-Lee edge singularity to occur at the same critical point as the tricritical one for the tricritical Ising universality class. This is not the case for the 3D Ising model where the tricritical point is located at a higher value of the external control parameter. This means that in the 3D Ising model case, the Yang-Lee edge singularity is reached by increasing the external control parameter. This is in contrast to the expectation that it should be reached by decreasing it. As an additional contribution, we have calculated the critical amplitude ratio $R_\chi$ and the exponent $\gamma$ for the tricritical Ising universality class in 2d and found them to be $1.0968 \pm 0.0004$, $1.1872 \pm 0.0008$ respectively. This calculation has been performed using the functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion and has a very small systematic uncertainty. In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a basic optimization method on a non-convex function can eventually enter a region where the function becomes locally convex. To address this, we developed an inequality that enables us to analyze the properties of the optimization landscape surrounding the solutions produced by an approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm. Specifically, we applied our inequality to demonstrate the local convexity of a particular TAP free energy function, which is relevant to the Z2 synchronization problem and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. Additionally, we showed that by assuming the uniqueness of a central solution, we can establish the local uniqueness of another solution located closer to the origin. These results can be viewed as an extension of the recent work by Richard and Oprescu, which addressed the same topics but was limited to cases where the AMP solution corresponds to a global minimum of the TAP free energy function. Our approach is an important improvement over their method, as it is based on general properties of the AMP algorithm and is therefore applicable to various multilayer generalizations. Furthermore, our technique opens up new avenues for studying the local convexity of non-convex functions that arise from the TAP free energy in general, beyond the specific examples considered here. Lastly, our results also imply that the uniqueness of a central solution, as defined by the Wrigth-Hastings matrix product operator, is equivalent to the local uniqueness of the corresponding TAP solution. This provides a more intuitive understanding of the central solution uniqueness problem. To validate our theoretical findings, we conducted numerical experiments to verify the local convexity of various non-convex functions associated with the Z2 synchronization and Sherrington-Kirkpatrick models. Our results showed that even though the AMP algorithm itself can be quite robust, the uniqueness of a central solution, as defined by the Wrigth-Hastings matrix product operator, does not necessarily guarantee the local uniqueness of the corresponding TAP solution. In fact, this distinction holds even under ideal conditions, as demonstrated by an example. Finally, we propose a generalization of the AMP algorithm, referred to as generalized approximate message passing (GAMP), and establish an inequality that may be employed to analyze the local convexity of a related non-convex function. This report outlines a deep learning approach known as the Electron Correlation
Potential Neural Network (eCPNN), which can learn simplified potential functions
that accurately capture the intricate instantaneous relationships among electrons
within complex atomic systems. Trained in an unsupervised manner with constrained
data derived from Full Configuration Interaction one-electron density functions, the
eCPNN model effectively predicts total atomic energies with remarkable precision. Our
results demonstrate that eCPNN can achieve near-exact energy predictions, matching
the accuracy of highly computationally intensive methods such as Full Configuration
Interaction, yet with significantly faster computation times. We further investigate
the eCPNN's potential applications in the community by proposing a challenge for
benchmarking atomic electronic structure theory using this novel approach. We hope
this initiative will motivate further research into and expansion of this promising
approach. All related code and data can be found at https://github.com/sonic42/eCPNN_AQ.

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions. We developed a data acquisition system with an integrated light source to calibrate the system in the field in a similar way to the laboratory. Finally, we applied this approach to determine the aerosol depth and related parameters at multiple locations with a high degree of precision, demonstrating the technique's effectiveness. Additionally, we found that the method can provide accurate measurements of the aerosol depth in less than 30 seconds. We also determined the uncertainty of this method to be significantly better than previous estimates, with a standard deviation of 0.015, 0.017, and 0.015 at three different wavelengths respectively. This technique has potential applications in various fields, including optical astrophysics and the calibration of wide-field optical telescopes. It has already been implemented at the Pierre Auger Observatory and is being considered for use in future upgrades of the observatory. Furthermore, we are in the process of adapting this approach for use with narrow-field optical telescopes. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved using these intermediate cues in the secondary stage. This study concentrates on two-stage pipelines with coordinate-based cues and uncovers several critical aspects that influence pose estimation: (1) the choice of coordinate system for predicting object points, (2) how to combine points from multiple object instances with different orientations, and (3) the use of pose-normalized coordinates for prediction. By experimentally adjusting these factors, we found that employing a coordinate system that minimizes rotational ambiguity and utilizing pose-normalized coordinates leads to more accurate pose estimates. Additionally, we discovered that predicting multiple object points at once does not necessarily enhance pose estimation accuracy. We further analyzed the relationship between the number of predicted points and estimation performance and found that increasing the number of points beyond a certain point does not yield significant improvements in performance. This study offers an objective evaluation of two-stage pipeline components and point-based pose estimation methods. It provides an unbiased examination of the relationship between predicted points and estimation performance, suggesting that certain approaches overcomplicate the task by predicting multiple points. Our code and data are openly available at https://github.com/daostin/pose-points.

Peridynamic theories have seen a significant expansion in their application across multiple disciplines, due to their ability to model and track discontinuity formation within materials. Bond-based Peridynamics, despite its modeling restrictions, has become a widely-used approach in numerical simulations because of its ease of implementation and intuitive connection to real-world physics. This paper delves into the aspects of bond-based peridynamic models, providing a thorough examination of the theory and its numerical representations. Various bond-based PD integral kernels have been presented along with their distinguishing characteristics, leading to discussions on their implications and common traits. A closer examination was conducted on the role of non-locality in determining motion, the interplay between kernel structure and material non-penetration, as well as the influence of PD kernel non-linearity on predicting fracture development. Finally, an exploration is initiated on adapting BB-PD to model fluids within the context of fading memory materials, suggesting potential for further research. Through this exploration, this study aims to offer a comprehensive overview of BB-PD that can serve as a starting point for other researchers in this field.

challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), Graphical Lasso
estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced by Dempster (1972)
under Covariance Selection. The framework has been expanded to accommodate
hidden variables in Chandrasekaran (2012) and can jointly estimate multiple
inverse covariance matrices, as shown in Danaher (2013) and Tomasi (2018). The
GGLasso package supports the resolution of diverse formulations and notable
subcases like Graphical Lasso with latent variables, Group, and Fused Graphical Lasso. Moreover, it provides a way to estimate multiple covariance matrices and
includes a utility tool to screen for significant edge orders. The library is
flexible, allowing users to select from various optimization algorithms,
including block coordinate descent, alternating least squares, and Expectation
Maximization, as well as path algebra, according to the specific problem at
hand. As a result, it eases the implementation of novel and established methods
concerning Graphical Lasso. The package also includes a graphical user interface
realized with Jupyter Widgets, making it simple to execute and visualize the
results of a wide range of Graphical Lasso models. The source code for GGLasso

Results showed that for harmonic oscillators, some methods yield precise configurational averages, potentially leading to better performance in biomolecular simulations, especially in cases where bond stretches play a crucial role. This suggests that highly precise simulations of small proteins can be achieved using an implicit Euler method with an optimized time step size. As a result, the challenge of accurately simulating small proteins over extended periods may have been overcome. Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to synthetic and real-world datasets and compare its performance to other state-of-the-art methods. Notably, our approach has a practical application in ranking search results across different topic categories based on search frequency and relevance. We propose a hybrid algorithm for solving the related equations and provide results for its average computational time and optimal convergence criteria in our experiments. We also provide an open-source implementation of our method on Python's NetworkX platform. Overall, our approach offers a powerful solution for evaluating node importance in complex multi-layered networks and is available for use and customization on GitHub.

Non-ideal camera captures can result in low-quality images due to various distortions such as misfocus, sensor defects, and noisy raw images. While traditional image enhancement methods are effective on real-world images with mild issues, they struggle with raw images suffering from severe problems like significant blur and noise. Non-blind demosaicking methods directly feed these raw images into deep networks, but they assume the capture system is optimal, which is not the case here. On the other hand, developing a reliable blind demosaicking approach from raw images is crucial for addressing capture system issues. Toward this goal, this paper proposes learning an end-to-end blind demosaicking and denoising model from raw images by treating the demosaicking process as a conditional probability estimation given the demosaicked image and the noise pattern. To train such a model, we introduce a new adversarial training technique that tolerates errors in forward propagation, allowing the use of existing demosaicking and image enhancement metrics. By employing an adversarial classifier that can handle varying noise levels, this technique enables the model to learn from a noise-free training set despite being trained with real-world noisy images. By combining this technique with particular network designs, our model outperforms state-of-the-art non-blind demosaicking and blind demosaicking methods. Moreover, our model can adapt to different capture systems and noise levels, making it highly versatile. Ultimately, this paper demonstrates that deep learning can tackle complex problems like blind demosaicking and denoising from raw images by employing an adversarial training technique that leverages the benefits of both domain adaptation and adversarial training. Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits unusual orbital selectivity, with electrons occupying certain molecular orbitals being unaffected by strong correlations. This phenomenon is exceptional among 3d transition metal compounds and may be attributed to the unique molecular structure and ground state electron distribution of cubanite. Despite the fixed occupancy of some molecular orbitals, other free electrons can participate in ferromagnetism, giving rise to a net magnetic moment. Notably, the strong correlations in cubanite do not rule out the possibility of a metal state, and our findings contrast with existing theories suggesting that strong correlations must necessarily lead to a insulating state. These results have significant implications for the understanding of magnetism in 3d transition metal compounds with a delocalized electronic structure. In addition, our analysis indicates that cubanite's close structural relationship to the non-magnetic compound Cu$_3$TeO$_6$ is an insufficient explanation for its magnetic properties. Lastly, our analysis suggests that cubanite may be a suitable compound for investigating strong correlations in small clusters, such as those comprising a single transition metal atom surrounded by several other atoms with varying occupancies. This compound offers a unique opportunity to study strong correlations in a system with varying electronic fillings and without the insulating phase often associated with such conditions. This makes it an ideal candidate for exploring the fundamental differences between strongly correlated metals and insulators. This study is followed by an analysis of the structural and magnetic properties of the A$_3$MO$_6$ type compounds, a discussion on the orbital-selective behavior in cubanite, and an examination of the electronic structure of this compound in comparison to other 3d transition metal compounds, all with a delocalized electronic structure similar to that of cubanite. This additional analysis provides a deeper understanding of the factors contributing to the orbital-selective behavior in cubanite. Lastly, this study is a prerequisite to a proposed experiment using cubanite as a compound for investigating strong correlations in small clusters, a phenomenon also potentially present in other A$_3$MO$_6$ type compounds. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby conferring a quantum advantage for executing various technological tasks. Furthermore, we propose a method for creating SPCCSs using a nonlinear photon sorter and experimentally implementing this concept. Collectively, our theoretical and experimental analyses pave the way for realizing single-photon catalyzed coherent states in the laboratory.

One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm for both linear and tree-like structures. Our holistic approach incorporates a nested maximum spanning tree algorithm and a corresponding scoring system, allowing for both extrinsic and intrinsic evaluations. The holistic model outperforms state-of-the-art nested NER baselines in three datasets and demonstrates superior convergence and accuracy in both coarse and fine-grained NER settings. The model's performance and efficiency are further enhanced by a simple yet effective technique called linearization, which is shown to yield comparable results to linear models. This work lays the groundwork for both linear and tree-like NER models to be reexamined in the context of holistic structures and provides the underlying architecture for modeling other nested elements, such as nested sentiment and entities with multiple attributes. We look at curves defined by equations that are smooth, or at least have smooth properties in certain situations, over such modified fields. Research into the location detection of mobile nodes within wireless sensor networks is currently ongoing. We develop and test an innovative RSSI-based location finding method suitable for 802.15.4 (ZigBee) networks. To counteract interference between different technologies operating in the same frequency range, we design and execute a new method for calculating the distance between nodes. The aim of this approach is to minimize the average error in location estimation, and when compared to ideal, interference-free results, we have achieved a level of accuracy of less than half a metre using actual hardware. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of using locations specified in advance on our algorithm's effectiveness. When applied to a dataset with specified locations, we observe a significant reduction in location estimation error. Lastly, we examine the impact of running the algorithm repeatedly on our method's performance. When executed multiple times on the same data, we experience a minor increase in location estimation error. Finally, we evaluate the energy consumption of our solution and find that executing the algorithm on the same data leads to an almost negligible increase in energy consumption. Successful testing of the algorithm was conducted within a ZigBee network consisting of 20 fixed nodes and one mobile node, moving at a speed of 0.5m/s, and accurately estimating its location took approximately 45 seconds. Unlike other approaches, our algorithm does not require prior knowledge of the network's layout, instead using the signal strength of radio transmissions to calculate the distance between nodes. As a result, it can be employed in environments where the location of all fixed nodes is unknown. Additionally, the algorithm's simplicity makes it suitable for low-power low-throughput devices such as those used in ZigBee networks. Consequently, the algorithm is an appropriate location detection method for mobile nodes within wireless sensor networks. It is also resistant to external interference present in many real world applications. Furthermore, accurate location estimation can be achieved even when the algorithm is executed on the same data multiple times. Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future directions, address methodological limitations in current research, and suggest investigating code-switched language datasets and models. Furthermore, we emphasize the importance of diversity, fairness, and accountability in NLP applications impacting multilingual communities and suggest conducting formal evaluations and getting feedback from community members to ensure effectiveness and usability of NLP systems. Ultimately, this study aims to stimulate discussion and guide research in NLP for and about multilingual communities. Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since (1) annotating images with precise text is a labor-intensive process and (2) merely gathering five votes doesn't guarantee the best description, we investigate alternative training and evaluation approaches utilizing multiple votes. First, we analyze the characteristics of human-generated descriptions to determine their suitability. Subsequently, we explore two image description systems trained on aggregated votes from five to thirty individuals. Compared to training on a single best description among five votes, training on aggregated descriptions from ten votes yields better performance on both automatic and human evaluation metrics. Notably, systems trained on aggregated descriptions from a larger number of votes exhibit improved performance, with the gains leveling off when considering more extensive datasets. Moreover, we find that training on aggregated descriptions from multiple votes reduces the disparity in performance between system and best human performance. Ultimately, we demonstrate that evaluating systems using multiple votes yields more reliable and robust results than evaluating systems using a single best description alone. Lastly, we explore alternative training objectives and evaluation methods that prove ineffective or even counterproductive. Ultimately, our findings provide valuable insights into the design of image description systems and evaluation protocols. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit news comments from news sources with varying levels of misinformation, including fact-checking, political, and entertainment news, from 2019 to 2020. Our results show that misinformation was shared more freely in the more sorted states, with the effect of sorting on misinformation dissemination partially explained by the differences in income, education, and news sources in those states. Additionally, we found that certain personality traits, such as conscientiousness, played a role in the spread of news, including misinformation, with individuals from sorted states with higher levels of conscientiousness being less prone to disseminating misinformation. Our research offers a comprehensive explanation for the persistence of online misinformation, incorporating both the cultural and socioeconomic aspects of "The Big Sort." It also provides a framework for evaluating the potential impact of misinformation dissemination in different regions. Finally, we highlight the potential applications of this research in identifying and mitigating the spread of misinformation. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. Furthermore, it was found that speech content can be used to train classification models with good accuracy, indicating that these features are sufficient for building predictive models of instructor speech based on speech content alone. To facilitate further research in this area, the collected data and trained models are being made available publicly. Ultimately, this research seeks to contribute to the advancement of robotic learning through demonstration-based methods aided by auditory cues, and it highlights potential applications in other areas aided by human speech. It also raises important questions to be explored in future studies.

Building on previous work, we propose an algorithm to randomly generate ordered trees of any degree, based on a pre-specified sequence of numbers representing possible node connections. Our method allows for the generation of binary, n-ary trees, or those with various connection patterns. We demonstrate that this algorithm is both accurate and efficient, running in O(n) time with 'n' representing the number of desired nodes. Additionally, we explore potential applications of the algorithm, illustrating its use in deriving formulas by utilizing the underlying proof of correctness. For example, we employ the algorithm to derive formulas for random generation of binary search trees, heap trees, and lazier data structures. Lastly, we convey its utility as a tool for discovering new formulas through minimal validation of proposed expressions. Lastly, we outline further research directions enabled by the algorithm.

Quantum field theory complexity is particularly hard to define, especially when transitioning beyond simple free models and their corresponding Gaussian representations. A promising approach to address this difficulty is through the study of conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, specifically focusing on the universal sector of the energy-momentum tensor in this context. A key unifying framework consists of Euler-Arnold equations and their broader integro-differential generalizations, ensuring the well-posedness of state or operator complexity optimization problems. Our comprehensive investigation extends upon our prior findings in arXiv:2005.02415, delving into intricate details of employed methodologies. A notable discussion involves differential regularization strategies, solving the integro-differential equation for Fubini-Study state complexity, and further exploring the underlying geometric properties. Moreover, our discussion includes considerations for both coherent states and Fubini-Study complexity, in addition to an examination of boundary state complexity scenarios. A numerical analysis is also presented to illustrate key concepts, demonstrating both Fubini-Study and Arnosem state complexity cases. Our study paves the way for tackling more complex conformal field theories via the 'holographic duality' and investigating the interplay between complexity and entanglement, ultimately facilitating a deeper understanding of the 'hierarchy of constraints' evident in the renormalization group. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. To address these challenges, we are exploring the use of formal methods and semantic-based approaches. As part of this work, we have developed a query language called QLCS, which enables developers to express queries regarding the state and transitions of a system, and has been successfully integrated with the PyECT framework we developed. PyECT has demonstrated its effectiveness in detecting existing work in testing conversational systems, and has been utilized to identify flaws in multiple publicly available implementations of conversational agents on top of the Dialogflow platform. Although our research has focused on structured systems with graph-based state transitions, we are confident that the principles underlying QLCS are applicable to other types of systems and testing scenarios. Additionally, we have discovered that QLCS can be employed to address existing work on the testing of conversational systems, and have leveraged it to identify shortcomings in currently available testing tools and methodologies. For further information regarding PyECT and QLCS, including installation instructions and example use cases, please visit our supplementary website at this link https://pyect.stanford.edu/. This research is part of an ongoing effort to enhance the quality of conversational systems through automated testing, and we hope that our work will contribute to the growth of this critical field. This paper builds upon previous work of the second author with Daskalopoulos and Vazquez, which involved analyzing the Yamabe flow on a fractional curvature and establishing the convergence of smooth solutions to a steady state under certain initial and boundary conditions. The current research expands on that study by removing the requirement for smooth solutions, instead allowing for weak solutions within a specified function space. The key development in this paper is the demonstration of the completeness of the spectrum for a related operator and the establishment of a minimum value for the first eigenvalue of that operator, which is then utilized to prove the convergence of solutions under specific dynamic and boundary conditions. The resulting theorem can be applied to validate the existence and uniqueness of a global minimum for an energy functional associated with the fractional Yamabe flow. The paper also explores the relationship between the rates of convergence of solutions and the parameters of the flow, both numerically and analytically. A related non-parametric example is examined to show that the approach of moving hypersurfaces of prescribed curvature could get stuck in a local minimum under certain conditions. The paper concludes with an examination of the fractional Allen-Cahn flow and the demonstration of the convergence of solutions of this type. To recognize new categories from minimal labeled data, few-shot learning has been rapidly evolving in recent years. However, traditional methods that rely on average operations for calculating prototypes often struggle due to the influence of outliers. This research proposes a new, effective framework that utilizes an episodic prototype generator module to create more representative prototypes from limited support data, reducing the impact of outliers and resulting in preferable models. The framework's ability is further showcased by the substantial improvement it yields over baseline models and the comparable performance it achieves to existing methods on datasets like miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, and cross-domain benchmarks (miniImageNet to CUB-200-2011). The code for this research has been made publicly accessible for download.

Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-scarce, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's unique aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general aspect preference that is common across all domains. By integrating the domain-specific unique aspect preference and the domain-agnostic general aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across multiple sparse domains. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. Moreover, thorough analysis is conducted to explore the internal mechanisms of MSDCR. Lastly, we find that MSDCR can effectively mitigate the negative impact of data sparsity on recommendation performance. Source code is available at https://github.com/hfawaz/MSDCR.

Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It then generates simplified equivalent formulations for various optimization applications that can provide significant improvements in processing speed and memory consumption. The proposed method demonstrates a marked improvement in problem-solving efficiency when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations. Additionally, Hypatia's solutions are mathematically equivalent to those obtained from other reliable solvers. As such, it can be a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners tackling convex optimization challenges when considering problems with exotic structures. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Our primary findings showed that using MRIQC features without preprocessing yielded the best results for both training and assessment settings. Models trained on a smaller dataset (1,102 subjects) demonstrated high accuracy across diverse datasets, including those with significantly different demographics (e.g., OASIS vs. ABIDE). Nonetheless, models trained on larger, more heterogeneous datasets (9,037 participants) performed better, with higher classification probabilities and better generalization across diverse studies. These outcomes suggested that both demographic factors and MRI data quality contribute to classification probabilities. Ultimately, our study established that sophisticated machine learning models can produce reliable, actionable reports from MRIQC processing, and such pipelines can serve as a crucial component for the automation of quality control and data validation in large-scale MRI analysis projects. This study's results also highlighted the importance of carefully evaluating quality control pipelines using diverse, previously unseen data to ensure their effectiveness and safety for use in such applications. This research's outcomes can be used to create more reliable and efficient quality control pipelines for MRI analysis, streamlining the analysis process for large-scale research projects. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. Furthermore, we established a correlation between the distance of T centers from the interface and their spectral diffusion rates, paving the way for optimizing spin properties through precise control of the etch process. These advancements bring us closer to realizing large-scale quantum networks, and we outline potential paths for scaling up the production of high-density T center layers, incorporating multi-layer device structures, and overcoming spectral diffusion barriers. With improving scalability and reliability, silicon-based photon-spin interfaces may soon become suitable for use in practical quantum applications.

The high activity levels of M dwarfs present a significant challenge for discovering exoplanets, as their stellar activity masks the signals from these celestial bodies. This problem requires an effective method for filtering out the stellar activity from the data sets, especially when searching for habitable Earth-like planets. To achieve this goal, we conducted an analysis on how to optimise the line lists used for least-squares deconvolution to minimize the impact of stellar activity and the noise in the spectra, thereby enhancing the detection of exoplanets. Our research utilised a line list with 7,162 water vapour lines across the spectral range of $0.5-0.6$\ensuremath{\mu}m, and we assessed different approaches to selecting lines for LLSDF, including random sampling, minimum distance algorithm, and a custom method based on the distribution of lines. Our results showed that the conventional method of selecting lines resulted in a significant improvement in the sensitivity of exoplanet detection, specifically when faced with broad photospheric variations, and our custom method yielded even better outcomes, leading to as much as a factor of five improvement in sensitivity in certain situations. This research has significant implications for the preparation of data sets for the Euclid satellite, which will be responsible for searching for exoplanets in the Galactic plane using wide binary patterns, and it highlights the importance of considering the line properties when selecting line lists for LLSDF. Furthermore, this study has relevant connections to other applications of LLSDF, such as the analysis of stellar activity and the preparation of line lists for LLSDF in multiple component analyses. We've established recently, much like our work on Deformed Special Relativity, that Fock's coordinate transformation can be developed from a novel, deformed form of the Poisson brackets.  Utilizing this approach, we successfully obtained the associated momentum transformation, which preserves the four-dimensional relationship between momentum and space, p_{\mu} x^{\mu}.  With the deformed algebra in hand, we derive the first Casimir invariant in this paper.  Following first quantization, we utilize the Klein-Gordon equation to show that Fock's spacetime corresponds to the de Sitter universe, whose spacetime radius can be defined by the invariant length representing the de Sitter hypersurface.  We then deduce that such a universe will eventually enter a timeless phase where the de Sitter hypersurface will converge to a point.  This indicates that our universe must have experienced at least one cycle of expansion and contraction.  We also found that the duration of this cycle is connected to the universal mass and length scales.  We then propose that Fock's spacetime, with its inherent cyclic time architecture, may be employed to address the cosmological problem via semi-classical means.  We outline the potential for this approach to explain the acceleration of the Universe's expansion as well as the origin of matter's prevalence over antimatter.  Finally, we suggest that Fock's spacetime, with its cyclic time structure, may be the fundamental domain of our universe, derived from a parent universe that resembles a double cover over the real line.  We anticipate that our analysis will stimulate the re-examination of empirical evidence through the lens of Fock's spacetime.  As such, we plan to monitor theoretical predictions against ongoing and future observational data.  In doing so, we will reassess our findings to refine or update our theoretical framework as necessary.  We look forward to presenting such updates in subsequent reports.  We also believe that our structure should be relevant to our previous work on Deformed Special Relativity.  We anticipate that both frameworks share an underlying universal architecture that defines the fundamental domain of our universe.  We expect that future work will uncover the precise relationship between these two approaches.  We've discovered that both approaches yield identical, Fock-like coordinate transformations.  We'll explore the additional, novel features derived from the deformed algebra in subsequent reports.  We've found that such algebra is linked to the universal mass and length scales, which are indicative of the granular, discrete nature of both space and time.

Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class. Springer further demonstrated that the number of conjugacy classes equates to the product of the number of such forms and systems of integers, considering the field in question. This thesis builds upon earlier work by E. Artin and J.A. Shalence, and its concepts have been applied to various mathematical areas, including the classification of representations of finite symplectic groups and the classification of irreducible characters within these groups. Van der Kallen has retained the original text and formatting of the thesis for historical accuracy. This translation is now published for the benefit of researchers in algebra and group theory. It is also a testament to Springer's pioneering contributions to the field, influencing numerous subsequent research areas. This translation is available under the copyright terms of the original publisher, Noord-Holland Publishing Company, a subsidiary of Elsevier. It is now freely accessible in the copyright repository of Elsevier. This research was partially funded by the European Research Council as part of the Sarnak ERC grant. It is also connected to the 'Algebraic Geometry and Number Theory' chair of the University of Amsterdam. Both the University of Amsterdam and the Amsterdam Institute of Advanced Study have supported this translation project. It is now available on the arXiv preprint server. A related paper has been published by T.A. Springer in 1950, specifically focusing on the conjugacy classes of the orthogonal group. This work is part of the 'Historical Background' series, providing context and translating key mathematical texts that have influenced the development of algebra and geometry. It is one of several projects aiming to make groundbreaking mathematical research from the 20th century more accessible to contemporary researchers in the field. It is also an exploration of the theorems and concepts that have shaped modern mathematics and is connected to the 'One Paper at a Time' podcast. It is now followed by Part II, which explores the work of J.A. Shalence.

A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by incompatible donors by minimizing the rejection risk while considering the transplant waiting list. A stochastic dynamic allocation model is introduced, where incompatible donors are allocated to patients who are less incompatible, based on the level of incompatibility. The results show that accepting incompatible transplants can reduce the waiting time by 15-18 months, and the rejection rate by 5-6%. Current versions of the Lambek Calculus used in computational linguistics are expanded upon using unary modalities to govern structural rules affecting sentence order and phrasing. This incorporation of controlled structural operations yields derivational ambiguities missed by the original Lambek Calculus and its simplification in pregroups. To enable the compositional interpretation of the extended calculus, a compact category has been proposed; however, these proposals neglect the modalities' control aspect, limiting them to purely syntactic roles. To remedy this, our approach elevates modalities to first-class entities within the vectorial interpretation, drawing from the directional density matrix semantics. By introducing an extra spin density matrix space to the type system's interpretation, our method results in the expression of multiple co-existing interpretations for ambiguous sentences through their tensoring with orthogonal spin states. This method offers a unified framework for handling both lexical and derivational ambiguity within a sentence's interpretation. A demonstration of this approach is executed through the interpretation of a sentence exhibiting both types of ambiguity. A proposed algorithm for computing multiple interpretations simultaneously addresses interpretational ambiguity convergence issues. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general online gridworld scenario can only determine Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE), a weaker concept than Correlated Equilibria (CE), which requires an exponential number of samples. This research develops an efficient algorithm to learn CE and CCE rationally in online gridworld environments, using a polynomial number of samples, and also addresses the challenge of identifying strongly connected components in action graphs via a novel approach. Our results establish upper bounds for learning both CCE and CE in online gridworld scenarios, building on a recent breakthrough in flux graph analysis. Additionally, our findings facilitate subsequent research into learning more advanced concepts like Approximate POMDP Equilibria. A corresponding algorithm for learning approximate correlated equilibria in online gridworld environments has been provided as supplementary material. This work has significant implications for multiagent learning research, enabling the efficient identification of rationalizable behavior and equilibria in online gridworld scenarios.

An analysis has been conducted on a stochastic Susceptible to Infective to Susceptible (SIS) epidemic model, where the epidemic dynamics are governed by a system of stochastic differential equations. The study explores how changing the model from deterministic to stochastic affects the model's threshold phenomenon. It was discovered that, unlike the deterministic model, which exhibits a sharp threshold with the fraction of infected individuals suddenly increasing to near unity at the threshold, the stochastic model displays a more gradual transition. In particular, for a mean-reverting susceptible process, the alternative approach finds that the asymptotic value of the infected fraction, which approaches unity as the infection rate increases beyond the threshold, is actually less than one. This distinction has implications for the estimation of the basic reproduction number, R0, which represents the ultimate value to which the infected fraction asymptotically converges as the infection rate increases, and is therefore greater than unity for the stochastic model. However, R0 does not accurately capture the severity of the epidemic in the stochastic model, especially for large values of the infection rate. A numerical method has been established for calculating the approximate solution of the stochastic system, and this is demonstrated through a simulation involving the stochastic SIS model. The algorithm employs a combination of the Euler-Maruyama method and a modified version of the Bradley-Gantier-Thompson procedure to convert the solution into a non-negative function. The efficacy of this approach was validated through an analysis of the stochastic SIS model. Additionally, the findings have been compared with corresponding results from the deterministic model. The study also examines alternative methods for estimating R0, including one approach that takes into account the time at which the epidemic peaks. It is shown that these estimates can be highly variable and may not accurately reflect the overall severity of the epidemic. It is therefore crucial to consider multiple indicators when assessing the severity of epidemics, especially in scenarios with varying infection rates. The research has been further expanded to explore a general class of SIS epidemic models that incorporate countercurrent flow in a linear network. The model is represented by a system of stochastic differential equations with non-uniform transmission probabilities. The analysis of this system reveals that the epidemic spreads at a speed that is bounded by the minimum of the infection rate and the rate at which susceptible individuals are converted to infected individuals, regardless of the complexity of the network. It is also demonstrated that the epidemic will ultimately converge to a unique equilibrium state. Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. To address this challenge, we have developed an open-source tool called UnPDF that utilizes Python and PyFMPS to integrate various PDF candidates or other nuisance parameters into physical processes, encompassing Drellian processes and QCD observables. UnPDF enables researchers to collate diverse datasets into a single dataset and subsequently fit PDF candidates by minimizing a chi-squared function, facilitating the exploration of unknown PDFs through Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. To enhance usability, UnPDF comes with a user-friendly configuration file format compatible with the Delphes event file format, encompassing Delphes card configurations, experimental information, and theoretical predictions. To demonstrate its effectiveness, UnPDF has been employed to analyze Drellian processes and QCD-related processes at the LHC. Given its modular design, UnPDF can be easily expanded to accommodate additional processes and processes beyond Drellian and QCD cases. To facilitate seamless collaboration among research groups, we have established a public repository for UnPDF, allowing for open contribution and feedback. To complement UnPDF, we have also introduced PDFUniverse, a Python tool that generates physical processes and related outputs, including theoretical predictions and experimental data, in various scale and kinematic settings, thereby providing a comprehensive set of inputs for testing and developing UnPDF. To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-of-the-art policy optimization methods. Furthermore, the proposed method's variance reduction strategy proves particularly beneficial when combined with gradient-based policy optimization methods. Establishing the electronic and superconducting gap structure of iron-based superconductors requires in-depth microscopic understanding. However, even with extensively studied samples, such as (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$, there is significant controversy over these fundamental questions. Our team resolves these issues by directly determining the band structure and superconducting gap variations through high-resolution and high-magnetic-field ARPES on (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$. The results show that replacing Ba with K introduces a 'flat band' feature around the zone center and alters the electron and hole filling of the $t_{2g}$ bands. The self-consistent analysis of the normal-state spectral function reveals that this 'flat band' is actually a highly dispersive band in parent BaFe$_2$As$_2$ hidden by other bands. The replacement of Ba with K creates a band that crosses the Fermi level, allowing direct observation. The superconducting gap structure shows varying sizes on the hole-rich $xy$-plane bands ($~0.6$dB$_{FC}$) and the electron-poor $zx$-plane bands ($~0.3$dB$_{FC}$), indicating an uneven distribution of superconducting gap. The replacement of Ba with K enhances the superconducting gap ratio $\frac{2\Delta(0)}{k_B T_c}$ from 1.04 to 1.57, offering possible explanation for the observed $T_c$ enhancement. These findings provide a basis for theoretical models explaining the mechanism of superconductivity in (Ba$_{1-x}$K$_x$)Fe$_2$As$_2$. Additionally, they highlight the importance of robust experimental techniques such as ARPES, especially in the face of emerging controversies over the fundamental nature of iron-based superconductors.

We have conducted an in-depth examination of the correlated metallic state of LaNiO$_3$ using $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR within LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices of varying bilayer thickness. Our spin-lattice relaxation studies in a 6.55 T magnetic field yielded distinct components, characterized by different temperature dependences in their recovery times, with one being temperature-linear and the other exhibiting more intricate temperature variation. These results demonstrate that the slow-recovering component is resistant to changes in LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness, while the fast-recovering component is significantly affected, displaying an opposing temperature dependence in thinner samples. This complex phenomenon is explored to identify its underlying cause. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that the spin-lattice relaxation rate can be dissected into two distinct contributions, originating from distinct metallic pathways with differing temperatures and electron densities. One of these pathways is linked to a temperature-linear recovery time, reminiscent of the Fermi liquid theory, while the other is associated with a higher-density pathway with a more complicated temperature dependence. These results provide direct, experimental evidence for the existence of multiple correlated metallic pathways in LaNiO$_3$, which is a fundamental aspect of this material's physics. Our study offers a groundbreaking application of NMR to investigate multi-component metals and offers new insights to guide the development of theoretical models that can accurately capture the correlated physics in materials with multiple metallic pathways. Our results also highlight the critical importance of LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices as a testing ground for understanding the physics of correlated metals and the effects of layer thickness, doping, and strain on these materials' fundamental properties. Ultimately, this research paves the way for the use of NMR to explore a wide range of complex materials and offers a powerful diagnostic tool for investigating multi-component metals.

In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with 
6 conversation turns through strategically chosen continuation branches. Our study 
of dialogue generation involves multiple evaluations and our results indicate that 
current state-of-the-art models struggle with branching conversations. To address 
this challenge, we introduce a model that excels in both short-term and long-term 
conversational performance. This model, named MultiTalk Model, represents a major 
advancement in the field, as it successfully manages conversations at various 
branching points. Our testing of this model on various datasets reveals its 
robustness and ability to handle conversations with minimal context. The many 
achievements of this model in our experiments make it a suitable benchmark for 
assessing the effectiveness of future dialogue generation models. All code and 
datasets are available for public use at https://github.com/hahnfield/MultiTalk.

Our research is centered on enhancing the maximum achievable capacity in a wireless communication system, comprising multiple input and output antennas and a surface capable of intelligent signal reflection. To provide an accurate assessment, we take into consideration the impact of correlated signal weakening and a phenomenon in which the intensity and phase of the reflected signal are interconnected, often disregarded in theoretical studies. By employing a mathematical approach that accounts for large-scale trends and phase shifts, we are able to formulate a detailed description of the system's performance and determine the maximum achievable capacity in terms of these factors. Moreover, our approach enables the efficient optimization of system parameters to achieve optimal performance, reducing the need for continuous system recalibration. Monte Carlo simulations validate our analytical findings, revealing how different parameters influence the system's performance. Finally, our results indicate that the intelligent reflecting surface can substantially enhance the system's performance, especially in scenarios where the signal intensity is weak. Additionally, we demonstrate that our approach is applicable to various multi-antenna system configurations. To further facilitate practical applications, we propose a simple and efficient estimation method for calculating optimal system parameters in real-world scenarios. This study provides theoretical and practical insights into the optimization of complex wireless communication systems. We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to solve the non-linear equations characteristic of modified gravity theories, resulting in highly efficient simulations. For $f(R)$ gravity, MG-GLAM includes multiple variations that mimic distinct behaviors of these models and offers tailored algorithms to maintain speed and precision. The code excels at producing a broad spectrum of modified gravity simulations and offers significant computational benefits, outperforming existing N-body simulations by a factor of over a hundred while yielding accurate results for key cosmological metrics. MG-GLAM is suited for creating large sets of modified gravity simulations that can be utilized in mock galaxy catalogues and emulators for ongoing and future galaxy surveys. This code is designed to work in tandem with the Euclid galaxy formation simulator and its associated flavour database. It has been successfully validated against high-resolution direct simulations and yields accurate results for a range of modified gravity simulations, meeting the precise standards set by the Euclid cosmology team. This computational framework is now an open source contribution as part of the Euclid galaxy formation simulator suite. It has been utilized in conjunction with the SUBHMLD galaxy formation model and has led to notable improvements in predicting galaxy cluster masses. Furthermore, MG-GLAM has been integrated with the HOP! halo finder and has facilitated novel comparisons between observed and predicted galaxy cluster scaling laws. This code has also enabled assessments of the effects of modified gravity on galaxy clusters, showcasing significant variations depending on the specific theory. As an N-body simulation suite, MG-GLAM is an adaptable, high-performance computational tool that offers a comprehensive range of modified gravity simulations for cosmological research. into a sophisticated collaborative platform for developing high-quality manuscripts
and software projects. Originally developed at McMaster University's theoretical
biology lab, WorkingWiki enables multiple users to work together on a range of
tasks by utilizing command-line tools to translate raw'source code' into desired outputs.
Its features cater specifically to programmers and researchers who use languages
like R, Python, and C, and it boasts specialized tools for seamless LaTeX editing.
By integrating features from collaborative editors, development environments,
version control systems, and publishing platforms, WorkingWiki unlocks the
full potential of wiki-based collaboration, and its customizable'makefiles'
and modular architecture enable users to tailor and repurpose its functionality.

This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame experiencing turbulence to determine its response to acoustic vibrations emitted from upstream, while factoring in temperature fluctuations that can cause instability in flames. To accurately predict flame reactivity, recent experimental measurements using narrowband combustion diagnostics were used. It was found that a previous model excluding heat release fluctuations' variations yields inaccurate results when compared to actual data, particularly at higher Strouhal numbers. In contrast, a model considering these fluctuations' effects yields a more realistic frequency response and phase shift in line with observations. Notably, reactive scenarios react differently than non-reactive ones, with reactive scenarios displaying greater sensitivity to Strouhal number and Schmitt number. Furthermore, it was found that a one-dimensional approach, considering flame speed and heat release fluctuations, can also provide a suitable frequency response when compared to full two-dimensional simulations. This indicates that reactive flame response in relation to acoustic vibrations can be understood through a simpler, one-dimensional approach that takes into account flame speed and heat release fluctuations. This could simplify future investigations of flame response in more complex scenarios. 

This research also explores a method to determine flame response from measurements of its reaction and acoustic properties. It was discovered that a one-dimensional approach, considering flame speed and heat release fluctuations, can yield similar frequency responses to full two-dimensional simulations. including stable and traveling chimera states using a dynamically adjusted measure of
coherence. This method automatically identifies and differentiates between synchronized
clusters, traveling wave patterns, chimera states, and asynchronous states. Additionally,
it is capable of determining the number of clusters present in cluster synchronization
situations. To further enhance our method, we developed a new technique for measuring the
speed of traveling chimera states. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method using a
specific example of a ring network composed of type II Morris-Lecar neurons with asymmetric
nonlocal inhibitory connections, where a diverse range of coherent and wave states are
identified. Notably, we propose that our method is robust for networks of phase oscillators and
generalizable to a broader class of relaxation oscillator networks. We also outline the
theoretical limitations of this approach. By leveraging this method, even the most minute
details of the most complex chimera states can be clarified, paving the way for a more
in-depth analysis of their dynamic formation. Furthermore, we suggest that our method
could be a valuable tool in identifying chimera states in living tissues and neural networks.
