Recently introduced is a special version of the Racah algebra, which is shown to be equivalent to the centralizer algebra of the embedding of the Lie algebra U(sl2) within a specific centralizer space. This study supplements our earlier research on WIMP-scattered nuclei, specifically examining how the incident velocity of these particles influences the scattering probability as they interact with target nuclei across various recoil angles and narrow energy ranges. Our simulation reveals that not only do the incident velocity characteristics of halo WIMPs play a crucial role, but so does the angle of the recoil itself, resulting in an irregular correlation of the two in specific energy ranges. Consequently, attempting to infer the 1-dimensional velocity distribution within these ranges directly from the overall WIMP halo velocities may not provide a complete or accurate understanding, which would further complicate attempts to derive these distributions through recoil probability measurements alone. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that even in cases where the incident velocity is tightly controlled (e.g., in experiments using pulsed lasers), the resulting recoil probabilities will vary significantly across specific angles and energy ranges, thereby necessitating a more nuanced consideration of these factors in future experiments. Ultimately, our simulation suggests that in order to make informed decisions about the design of these experiments, particularly in relation to the energy ranges they can effectively detect, it will be necessary to account for the complex relationships between these variables through detailed simulations, perhaps utilizing multiple Markov Chain Monte Carlo analyses to achieve this end. Our research includes a fully flexible code that can be used in conjunction with such simulations to determine the effective detection capabilities of these experiments. This code is also capable of handling a variety of WIMP mass ranges, as well as the complex velocity distributions that arise from varying recoil angles and narrow energy ranges. As such, it may be a valuable tool in informing the design of future direct detection experiments. We are suggesting the establishment of a state-of-the-art muon-proton and muon-nucleus collider that operates at the TeV level, capable of delivering highly accurate measurements in deep inelastic scattering in new areas, while also offering a comprehensive research agenda in particle and nuclear physics. Given its research capabilities and relatively low construction cost, we believe this concept has merit for funding by the US nuclear or particle physics programs or major global physics initiatives. Also, this concept could serve as a stepping stone for a future muon collider or lepton-nucleon colliders. Several expert opinions on this concept have been collected and are also shared in this report.

This research paper proposes a novel approach to developing safety-critical controllers for complex nonlinear control systems subject to input limitations. Specifically, it outlines the development of an Input Constrained Control Barrier Function, which pinpoints a secure subset of possible system states and designs a control mechanism to maintain those states. The devised controller can be optimized through an efficiently solvable quadratic program, enabling real-time application. Building upon earlier concepts of Higher Order Control Barrier Functions, ICCBFs demonstrate the ability to tackle a broader class of systems characterized by variable relative degrees. Finally, the paper showcases its efficacy through simulation examples in adaptive cruise control and spacecraft rendezvous. Additionally, it highlights the potential for seamless integration with learning-based control methods.

Graph neural networks have excelled in multiple applications by leveraging relational data. These models combine node features with the graph structure, creating flexible and effective models, but they can be challenging to interpret due to their implicit representation of node interactions and graph connectivity. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called Kedge, which involves explicitly reducing unnecessary graph edges by selectively removing neighboring nodes. By utilizing the Hard Kumaraswamy distribution for edge sparsification, Kedge enables a flexible integration with existing GNN models through gradient-based optimization. Experiments demonstrate that Kedge effectively prunes a substantial proportion of graph edges with minimal accuracy degradation. Notably, Kedge achieved a reduction of over 80% of edges on the PubMed dataset with only a 2% decrease in accuracy, indicating that node features have a more significant impact than graph connectivity. Furthermore, Kedge effectively mitigates the over-smoothing issue prevalent in deep GNNs by maintaining robust task performance even with multiple GNN layers. Source code is available at https://github.com/ghulghuleh/Kedge. Experimental findings have been incorporated into the GraphBurerNewton code repository at https://github.com/ghulghuleh/GraphBurerNewton for comparative analysis with existing edge sparsification methods.

A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more resilient estimator was proposed, which, albeit requiring quadratically more queries in proportion to the sketch size, significantly enhances the safety by a factor of k (with k being the number of key components) when compared to prior studies on CountSketch sketches. Additionally, this study introduces a new feedback-receiving sketch called FASter Sketch (FAS), which generalizes the classic CountSketch sketch and produces a more robust estimator with fewer queries, specifically in settings where the input vectors have distinct components and the sketch size is relatively small. The proposed FAS sketch can be viewed as a randomized linear transformation followed by a thresholding operation on the input vector, and its robust estimator can be acquired through an iterative learning process that utilizes the sketch itself. We demonstrate that the FAS sketch achieves a more robust estimator with safer query complexity of $\tilde{O}(k^2n)$ compared to $\tilde{O}(kn)$ for the standard CountSketch sketch. The FAS sketch can be applied to various applications, including finding the top elements of a sparse vector, identifying the largest entries of a sparse vector with non-negative entries, and determining the top elements of a low-dimensional non-sparse vector. We also present a practical implementation of the FAS sketch and its evaluation on multiple real-world datasets. The results indicate that the FAS sketch can effectively identify the top elements of vectors that are substantially longer than the sketch size, and its performance is comparable to that of the standard CountSketch sketch. Moreover, the FAS sketch outperforms the standard CountSketch sketch when the input vectors have distinct components and the sketch size is relatively small. Lastly, we demonstrate that the FAS sketch can be utilized to solve a system of linear equations and determine the top elements of a vector that is partially unknown. We also present a query-efficient sketch called Faster Sketch, which yields a robust estimator with safer query complexity of $\tilde{O}(k^3n)$, particularly effective at settings where the input vectors have distinct components and the sketch size is substantially smaller than the number of key components. Effective management of controllable loads relies on the strategic deployment of aggregators that can efficiently convey their flexible capabilities, referred to as aggregate flexibility, to system operators. Current approaches typically involve time-consuming estimates, with minimal research on real-time strategies that can make the most of real-time data through advanced algorithms. This paper introduces an innovative two-part solution for real-time management of controllable loads in power systems. First, a real-time aggregator-state estimator uses robust algorithms to handle sudden changes and outliers, providing accurate estimates for controllable loads. Next, a penalized predictive control method is employed to optimize the flexible capabilities of aggregators and controllable loads based on current and future electricity market prices, ensuring the best possible use of real-time data. Simulations using a test grid and actual data demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed system over traditional approaches, with the rapid estimator producing reliable results within one minute and the optimal controller achieving significant improvements over baseline strategies in various scenarios. Furthermore, the ability to operate in sync with the fast-paced nature of modern power markets is also highlighted. The robust estimator and penalized predictive controller have been implemented and are available for download on the author's website. The research offers a foundation for addressing complex energy management challenges in the modern power grid and paves the way for future studies on the integration of distributed energy resources and the direct interaction of aggregators with grid operators. One of the most intriguing phenomena in astrophysics is the common envelope (CE) phase of binary star evolution, where two stars are enveloped in the shedding material of one of them. This process triggers a shrinking of the orbit as the stars interact with the envelope. Ultimately, it can result in either mergers or further complex interactions, which can involve a mix of compact objects and stars. Certain CE scenarios, particularly those involving white dwarfs, can produce supernovae, while neutron star mergers can result in gamma-ray bursts, and all types of compact object mergers can produce gravitational waves. Predicting the end states of these CEs is challenging due to their diverse origins and the intricate processes involved, which are compounded by the need to consider many systems at once in population synthesis calculations. This difficulty often prompts the use of conservation principles such as angular momentum conservation to simplify complex scenarios, such as in the case of multiple star systems. This method allows for a simpler, more intuitive approach to understanding the behavior of these binary star systems, particularly in the study of higher order multiples which are increasingly being recognized as significant in the potential mergers of these stars. This particular work focuses specifically on the common envelope phase of binary stars, while an accompanying paper will explore the broader implications of this research for multiple star systems that undergo CE phases. This study employs a straightforward approach based on angular momentum conservation to model various CE scenarios, including those involving both first and second sequences of stars, as well as multiple stars, which are influenced by the decay of flat binaries and the mergers of smaller bodies. It also takes into account the diverse possible end states of these systems, which can include compact object mergers, supernovae, and a broad spectrum of binary star outcomes, to evaluate the potential for detection of these events in the era of multi-messenger astronomy. This approach allows for a more intuitive understanding of the potential for detection of these events, which are crucial for informing further research in this field. We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and hydrogel grains, at various speeds and depths. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Notably, the anisotropy increased more quickly in beds with low friction. Additionally, the drag experienced by the cylinder was found to be influenced more by its long axis than its ends. This phenomenon could be understood by studying the flow of sediment around the cylinder and estimating the drag experienced by its sides and flat ends. Estimates suggested that the drag experienced by the sides, which have a small diameter compared to the width of a granular bed, could be significant, even for long cylinders, where the flat ends may not contribute much to the drag. Lastly, our research revealed that the drag experienced by a cylinder in a granular bed can be understood using a simple model that takes into account the shear stresses and frictional forces acting on the sides and flat ends of the cylinder, in addition to forces related to the rupture of granular packs and the flow of sediment around the cylinder. This model allowed us to predict the drag experienced by a cylinder with different orientations, speeds, and depths, even in deeply packed beds, where the flow of sediment around the cylinder cannot be considered a steady-state flow. This was confirmed by comparing our model to our experimental data. This study could have implications for understanding how swimmers and intruders navigate through granular materials efficiently.

Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a significant correlation between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a relationship between outflow mass and gas usage times. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, the mass ejected through outflows actually exceeds the amount of gas converted into new stars, indicating a limit on how quickly gas can be turned into stars due to outflows. Our findings support the idea that outflows play a critical role in regulating the conversion of gas into stars, highlighting the need for further studies of outflows in galaxies across the universe. Additionally, we observed a relationship between outflow velocities and stellar mass, with more massive stars generating faster outflowing gas, which could be related to supernovae and the cooling of gas. Our analysis also revealed the presence of dust within outflows, with an estimated mass that is a significant fraction of the total dust mass within the galaxy, suggesting that outflows have the potential to shuttle dust between different regions of the galaxy, influencing how dust is distributed chemically. Furthermore, we detected various chemical elements, such as hydrogen, carbon, oxygen, and silicon, within outflows, which indicate an enrichment of elements within the galaxy due to outflows, supplying essential nutrients to new star formations in the galaxy's outer regions. Our research provides new insights into the cycle of matter within galaxies and how outflows affect both the galaxy's internal structure and its surrounding medium. Ultimately, our study highlights the significance of observing outflows in galaxies across the universe, which is critical for understanding how galaxies evolve over time. Our data are suitable for theoretical modeling and can be used to develop new codes that incorporate the effects of outflows in galaxies within the universe. Current auto-tuning frameworks for computer systems face challenges due to their large configuration spaces and the difficulties associated with evaluating their performance. Recently, researchers have made progress in this area using probabilistic models in Structured Bayesian Optimization, a technique that rapidly converges to optimal configurations by exploiting expert-provided context and the system's structure. However, building probabilistic models from scratch is a complex task, especially across different system structures. To address this issue, we introduce BoAnon, a novel approach that enables the transfer of expert knowledge from one system structure to another. By leveraging BoAnon, domain experts can share their knowledge with non-expert tuners, allowing them to successfully auto-tune new system structures. We evaluated BoAnon on multiple scenarios involving two different systems and showed that it can accurately identify the best configuration even when evaluated on unfamiliar system structures. Furthermore, BoAnon's effectiveness is demonstrated by its ability to discover the best configuration over expert-provided regions in systems the tuner has never seen before. We also compared BoAnon to other optimization strategies, including traditional Bayesian optimization and expert tuning. Results indicate that BoAnon outperforms these methods by a significant margin, achieving the best overall performance. We have made BoAnon available online for researchers to use. Additionally, we are collaborating with researchers from the HPC community to apply BoAnon in actual HPC benchmarking settings. We are open to collaborating with other domains as well, given that those domains' structures and performance metrics can be mapped to HPC's context. We have already begun exploring such collaborations with researchers from the database community. We have also started a community-based approach to address the scalability issue associated with evaluating computer system configurations by proposing a community-based evaluation approach. We are looking for like-minded researchers to join us in this endeavor. We plan to present our community-based evaluation approach at a future conference. We have also considered the issue of configuration validation, which is critical in computer system optimization, given the high evaluation costs associated with its components. We have explored the application of approximate validation techniques but require further research in this area. We are open to collaborations with researchers interested in this topic. We have identified several potential research directions for our community-based evaluation approach and are willing to collaborate with like-minded researchers. We have also acknowledged the limitations of our Structured Bayesian Optimization approach, specifically its reliance on expert-provided context and performance data. We have recognized the potential for incorporating machine learning into the optimization process and are open to exploring this further with researchers from the ML community

Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. These findings suggest the triangular flow of particles can be predicted using the same methods as elliptical flow, taking into account initial conditions and flow correlations. Upcoming EIC experiments may be able to measure triangular flow, providing valuable insights into the properties of partonic matter. Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has surged exponentially with more than 10,000 online datasets now available and formatted according to Linked Data standards, enabling seamless machine readability and interconnectivity.  While such datasets provide numerous opportunities, numerous applications remain hindered due to data of poor quality, significantly affecting tasks such as data integration, search, and interlinking.  Existing quality assessment techniques for Linked Data, although limited, suffer from decreased effectiveness with rising data sizes and become unmanageable for single machines.  To address these challenges, our proposed DistQualityAssessment is an open-source, cluster-enabled implementation designed for comprehensive quality evaluation of large-scale RDF datasets, leveraging the processing capabilities of Hadoop to distribute quality metrics computation.  This innovative, distributed in-memory approach allows for flexible metric extension and reduced data processing times by as much as fifty percent when compared to centralized implementations.  We have successfully applied DistQualityAssessment in evaluating more than seventy datasets with sizes ranging from a few hundred megabytes to over two gigabytes in size.  Our research has revealed notable time and precision gains, achieving precision levels of up to 0.95 in quality classification when compared to in-memory SPARQL queries.  Our proposed DistQualityAssessment is now available for public use on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license.  In addition to this, we have released all associated datasets and experiments for replication and further research.  Our proposed approach has the potential to contribute to advancements in the quality evaluation of large-scale RDF datasets.  As such, we invite feedback and suggestions for improvement through the project's GitHub repository. When working with data generated by random processes, an appropriate model is often employed for subsequent statistical analysis, but the standard method of maximum likelihood estimation is vulnerable to model imperfections and data contamination. As alternative methods without assumptions about a specific model typically lose efficiency, this paper introduces a robust procedure for estimating parameters in discrete data sets based on a well-known distance measure. Specifically, this method defines and evaluates minimum density power divergence estimators for independent increments and Markov processes, proving its consistency and providing distributional results in the context of dependent stochastic processes, ultimately showing the method's advantages in comparison to traditional maximum likelihood estimation for common processes like Poisson processes, Brownian motion and autoregressive models. 

This paper also explores the method's application to count processes and linear models, discussing potential future research directions. As a key step, the method requires an estimation of the underlying process's distribution by the minimum density power divergence estimator (MDPE), but a crucial aspect of this estimation is the specification of the number of observations, which can be challenging in practice. Therefore, as a practical solution, this paper proposes a data-driven approach for estimating processes that involves sequentially applying MDPEs to expanding data sets. 

The proposed method is evaluated in simulations and in relation to other popular time series estimation methods, such as maximum likelihood and autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA). The results show that this method can provide a robust estimate of the process parameters, often outperforming the standard methods in various processes and depending on the specific conditions, but the proposed method's performance can vary in certain situations. 

In addition to process estimation, this paper also discusses how to use MDPE for counting processes by adapting an existing approach and also considers a simple linear model, providing a robust estimate of the model's parameters. The paper's methods are implemented in R and the source code is available online. 

The paper's methods are validated through simulations and real-world data sets, and the estimated process or model is compared to the true process or the model that generated the data, as well as to standard estimation methods, such as maximum likelihood or ARIMA, which is a well-known approach for time series analysis. The results indicate that the proposed method can provide a robust estimate of the process or model parameters, often outperforming the standard methods under certain conditions.

This study presents temperature maps for electrons within one kiloparsec of three high-brightness Seyfert galaxies. The findings from Gemini's GMOS-IFU data, acquired at a spatial resolution of 110-280 parsecs, reveal temperature variations between 8000 to >30000 Kelvin. We discovered temperature ranges in these galaxies are significantly influenced by gas outflows producing shocks, particularly in Mrk 79 and Mrk 348, while photoionization processes fit the results for Mrk 607. The orientation of these shocks in Mrk 79 and Mrk 348 appears to be perpendicular to the axis of ionization, suggesting the potential for shock ionization to be observed more easily when obscured by a dusty torus. This implies that narrow ionization cones can coexist with wider shock patterns. Furthermore, we observed electron temperatures exceeding 10000 Kelvin at distances of 3-4 times the ionization widths, indicating the potential for shock persistence over several hundred parsecs. This study's results provide new insights, shedding light on the persistent challenges in modeling the spectra of Seyfert galaxies through gas dynamics. They also highlight the capability and utility of using optical emission lines to study electron temperatures in AGN, utilizing the capabilities of current generation integral field units. This methodology can be particularly effective in investigating shock ionization and gas dynamics in AGN, facilitating a deeper comprehension of the interplay between ionizing radiation, winds, shocks, and potential mergers in these sources. This approach may also help clarify the central engine's physics and the overall morphology and evolution of galaxies. Lastly, we highlight the potential for this study's results to guide and refine spectroscopic modeling of Mrk 79, Mrk 348, and Mrk 607 using 3D models. This includes optimizing ionization parameters, shock locations and orientations, temperatures, and abundances through comparison with data, all of which can be accomplished with current spectral synthesis codes such as TIGER and its variants. This approach may also facilitate a more detailed examination of electron temperatures in these galaxies, contributing to a richer understanding of the physics governing AGN. This study paves the way for a comprehensive comparison between electron temperatures derived from optical emission lines and those obtained from radio and millimeter-wavelength observations, allowing for a deeper comprehension of energy distributions and energy coupling in these sources. This study's results also highlight the necessity for multi-wavelength, spatially resolved spectroscopy to comprehensively comprehend the physics governing AGN and their host galaxies. As IoT systems shift towards Edge computing and less reliable infrastructure closer to users, the complex environments of IoT pose significant challenges for software developers when testing their applications. Although various testing tools are available for IoT, several issues persist, such as the absence of advanced features for logical dependencies, fault injection, and multi-platform testing. To address these shortcomings, we have developed Frisbee, a framework for the automated testing of IoT applications. By utilizing Kubernetes and virtual testbeds, Frisbee speeds up the testing process by streamlining the setup of distributed virtual environments and enabling complex 'what-if' scenario simulations. Furthermore, we have applied Frisbee to the development of an intelligent traffic system, and our results show that it can execute tests up to 4 times faster than manual methods. Additionally, we have incorporated a formal verification approach using Z3, allowing us to detect previously unnoticed bugs in several IoT applications. Our approach has been recognized through an award at the IoT Edge Challenge 2020 and an honorable mention at the 2020 Edge AI Challenge. Our research has also been cited in the 2020 Edge AI Challenge report. Our testing framework, Frisbee, is now available online.

The creation of realistic traffic scenarios through automation is the primary focus.
Currently used approaches insert virtual characters into the environment using predefined rules but struggle to capture the intricate nature of actual traffic conditions, ultimately resulting in a gap between artificially generated scenes and real ones. As a consequence, these simulation tools lack the required level of accuracy necessary to train self-driving vehicles. To mitigate this limitation, we propose SceneGen, a traffic scenario model that utilizes neural networks to bypass reliance on predefined rules. SceneGen is particularly adept at inserting a variety of virtual characters into the environment and accurately modeling their sizes, positions, and speeds. Through extensive testing on two large datasets, we demonstrate SceneGen's capacity to accurately mimic the distributions seen in real traffic environments. Furthermore, when combined with sensor simulation, SceneGen is shown to be an effective means of training perception models capable of performing well in real-world scenarios. Ultimately, our results indicate that SceneGen is a more robust and realistic approach to generating traffic scenarios. A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. Furthermore, this method is demonstrated through the numerical solution of a scalar advection equation, a system modelling a vibrating string, and the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations. Results show that the new iteration scheme preserves the structure of the Jacobian matrix, and significantly outperforms a fully iterative approach with explicit time-stepping methods. Importantly, this approach allows for large-scale nonlinear systems to be solved exactly at each time-step, while also enabling the flexible implementation of preservation techniques for complex applications. As such, it has the potential to enable innovative, accurate, and preserving numerical solutions of real-world problems. A group of integer sequences can be classified as jointly ergodic if for every ergodic system with a measure-preserving nature, their average values, determined by iteratively applying the sequences, converge on average to a specific, integrated product that aligns with the original values. We have derived flexible criteria that can not only verify ergodicity across most known sequence combinations, but also enable resolution for some outstanding issues. Notably, our reasoning employs a novel ergodic variant of a technique initially explored by Peluse and Prendiville in establishing quantitative versions of the finitary Szemer\'edi theorem's application. Additionally, our findings link ergodicity to new variants of a phenomenon known as uniform boundedness, as well as providing connections to the ergodic versions of Fourier sums and a related conjecture known as the Erdős-Wirton conjecture. Furthermore, we investigate the ergodic properties of a family of sequences classified as low-density, and show that under very strict criteria, sequence combinations with high density cannot be jointly ergodic. We also explore the ergodic properties of metric sequences, and are able to establish a critical density threshold below which non-trivial metric sequences can no longer be ergodic. We are also able to determine the exact ergodic properties of a family of highly structured sequences, and are able to demonstrate that certain sequence combinations, although individually ergodic, can nonetheless fail to achieve joint ergodicity. Our study also delves into the relationship between ergodic properties and the application of Furst's algorithm in homomorphism problems, and are able to provide a critical insight into the underlying reasoning behind the Polymath project's initial observation regarding the application of Gowers' correlation graph theorem. Lastly, our research offers a flexible framework that can be used to tackle more intricate problems defined by the definition of a set of jointly ergodic sequences. This framework already yields to new, previously unresolved consequences across both ergodic theory and combinatorial dynamics. Recently, lidar sensors have become the primary technology for obstacle detection in autonomous vehicles, allowing for the detection of objects at great distances. However, despite their effectiveness, lidar sensors have limitations when it comes to far-field object detection. This research addresses this challenge by developing a deep learning-based approach called SWE-FCN, an algorithm that uses a sweep transformer encoder featuring hierarchical structure and fence post convolutional networks for hierarchical feature extraction and refinement. By leveraging hierarchical encoders and fence post modules, SWE-FCN can effectively process long-range point clouds by dividing them into manageable sections and extracting meaningful features from each. This approach has shown significant improvements over existing methods such as T-ScanNet and RGCN, with an accuracy rate of 0.923 in evaluating scene understanding and a mean absolute error of 0.078 in bounding box estimation when tested on the KITTI dataset. This research demonstrates the capability of deep learning algorithms to tackle complex issues like lidar-based far-field object detection and encourages further innovation in this area. This paper's novel propagation of hierarchical encoders and fence post modules has the potential to be applied to other challenging point cloud processing tasks. Chemical reactions can be comprehensively understood through a primary analytical tool called the potential energy surface (PES) which maps the relationships between molecular nuclei and their energy levels. Nevertheless, this tool becomes impractically challenging to utilize because identifying a substantial number of ground states across the vast dimensions of PES requires an unreasonably large number of preparations. A recent study suggests utilizing a quantum machine learning algorithm as a more feasible approach. This model utilizes quantum data consisting of different nuclear coordinate-based ground state wavefunctions to prepare the desired states on the PES at will. A classical neural network transforms nuclear molecule coordinates into quantum variational circuit parameters and the fidelity loss function trains it to achieve optimal performance. Notably, this study found that, regardless of the complexity of molecules being studied such as hydrogen chains, water and beryllium hydride, just a small number of samples were enough to achieve high overlap rates with ground states in practice. A theoretical aspect also proves a limitation to these protocols suggesting it would be against the laws of physics if such efficient protocol could apply to regions where the ground and excited states exchange roles. In conclusion, this study proposes that quantum machine learning protocols have the potential to overcome the major challenge of working with PES and thus such an approach could revolutionize the field of molecular chemistry. Also, this study's findings could inspire other potential applications such as new molecules generation or decoding molecular processes. Finally, this study's theoretical aspects could guide the development of new learning algorithms by helping to identify potential issues of overfitting and explore the relationship between sample efficiency and the complexity of molecular systems. This study's findings could also contribute to a greater understanding of how quantum states are represented in the context of variational quantum circuits. Finally, this study's proposed approach could spark discussion on the role of chemistry knowledge in quantum machine learning protocols and also explore the possibility of replacing classical neural networks with quantum neural networks. Ultimately, this study paves the way for further investigation of whether such efficient learning could apply to excited states and also investigate the potential applications of such a model to other quantum systems. Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. The liver's featureless surface and varied image modality noises also pose significant challenges. We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset includes realistic biomechanical simulations of randomly generated organ models undergoing deformation. This allows it to efficiently apply to novel patient organs without retraining, also enabling robust performance against noisy intraoperative surface inputs. The trained network provides a discrete free-form deformation field at each point for mapping the preoperative volume to the intraoperative surface. A quadratic interpolation of the discrete field enables smooth field sampling for volume rendering. The results showed that the proposed method could produce accurate and detailed organ models of the liver, allowing for clear visualization of tumors and surgical tools during surgery. The method's efficiency allowed for multiple frames to be processed in real-time, demonstrating its potential for guiding laparoscopic surgery in real-time. The code has been made publicly available online for download. The proposed approach represents a significant advancement in registering preoperative CT volumes with partially reconstructed intraoperative surface data, offering a fast, efficient, and accurate way to render preoperative volumes onto real laparoscopic data. This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, applying the MIT bag model. Furthermore, we derived the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and subsequently, we examined the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars across varying temperatures and magnetic fields. Finite temperature and magnetic field effects were investigated in the phase diagram of spin-polarized strange quark stars, and a corresponding change in the first-order phase transition from the confined to the deconfined phase was observed. Additionally, we analyzed the impact of temperature and magnetic field on the cassini orbit of a spin-polarized quark star and compared this with the recently discovered X-ray binary candidate, 3A 0614+09. A maximum allowable temperature for this star was estimated and we found that the magnetic field influences the cassini orbit but not the maximum allowable temperature. Lastly, we calculated the thermal entropy of spin-polarized strange quark matter and identified how it varies with temperature, magnetic field, and baryon density. This research may contribute to a deeper comprehension of the behavior of quark matter under extreme conditions of high density and magnetic fields.

This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F) in cubic graphs. A more stringent condition, that of 2-factorability, requires that every pair of perfect matchings can be combined to create either a 2-factor consisting of two edges or a Hamiltonian cycle. Our work focuses on determining whether a graph has this 2-factor property and whether it can be determined by examining the graph's perfect matchings. Our results show that for graphs with which every perfect matching corresponds to a colour in a 3-edge-colouring, the E2F property can be determined by examining the graph's perfect matchings. Additionally, a finite cubic E2F graph was discovered, as well as the fact that a graph has the 2-factor property if and only if its complement graph does. These findings lead to the proof that determining whether a graph has the 2-factor property can be performed by examining the graph's perfect matchings, although a more efficient algorithm for this task remains an area for further research. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Lastly, we examine the effectiveness of Timeloops in preventing security breaches caused by system call misuse. This study examines the null controllability of a population model that includes an interior degenerate diffusion component. By first establishing a new Carleman estimate for the adjoint system in its entirety, and subsequently deriving a relevant observability inequality, we aim to demonstrate the existence of a localized control action capable of driving the population towards extinction within a finite time frame. Our approach builds upon earlier approaches to controllability in nonhomogeneous domains by exploiting the model's structural features, particularly its conservative nature, and leveraging dynamic degeneracy to concentrate control effort effectively. Numerical recovery of an approximate solution using a feedback linearization approach has also been observed, and this is illustrated through computational simulations. Notably, this work lays the groundwork for exploring optimal control strategies in this type of domain.

The dynamics of soccer games mean even small moments can greatly impact the outcome, making players, coaches, and scouts intensely curious about how to act effectively in pivotal situations. In such moments, teams may lose possession of the ball or score, leading to a desire for an optimal course of action. To address this need, we propose a novel way to describe the game's state and a batch reinforcement learning method to train a strategic policy network. By analyzing the contextual aspects of situations, the network can provide the best action to increase the team's chances of scoring, drawing on real soccer data from InStat. In a large-scale experiment with 104 European soccer matches, we found our optimized strategy consistently outperformed the standard policy, and it even mimicked the behavior observed in real games. Notably, we observed situations where action A was initially considered best, but after further analysis, action B was determined more effective, highlighting the complex nature of soccer. To facilitate future research, we are making our methodology and environment publicly available, incorporating real data from InStat to describe actions, game states, and rewards. By leveraging more advanced reinforcement learning techniques, we are also exploring ways to improve the team's scoring chances. Our study and resources can contribute to breakthroughs in soccer-related research, enabling applications in areas like player evaluation and skill training. High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. Formulations for WRI and ESI are developed within a Lagrangian-based mathematical framework, and both can be viewed as weighted versions of the classical FWI. Conjugate gradient methods are also explored to solve the normal equation for an efficient solution, and both time and frequency domain formulations of the wave equation solver are feasible. Despite these developments, the challenge of the large storage requirement for time-domain wavefields through iterations remains, and two possible workaround strategies for reducing this demand are proposed, including extracting sparse frequency-domain wavefields or utilizing time-domain data rather than wavefields. Ultimately, both WRI and ESI are tested on synthetic datasets to demonstrate their capabilities and both are shown to converge to satisfactory misfit values, with the added benefit of achieving this without the non-physical source approximation issue present in FWI. Additionally, the impact of both the weighting and relaxation parameters is examined through these numerical experiments. Lastly, the results in both the frequency and time domains are compared to each other as well as to the actual extended source used in the generation of the dataset. As the method is initially tried on 3D datasets before considering it for use on real-world data, the initial test case involves comparing frequency-domain extracted data with frequency-domain synthetic data generated from an extended source, and the analysis is then expanded to accommodate time-domain wavefields before concluding with discussions and potential directions for future improvement.

We've developed an all-optical technique for producing optical nonreciprocity on a microchip, achieved through the process of quantum squeezing a specific mode in coupled resonator systems. A key factor in this method involves applying classical coherent light in a one-way fashion to parametrically pump a nonlinear resonator. This selective pumping induces a chiral interaction between photons within the resonators, allowing us to build optical diodes and quasi-circulators. Notably, we've demonstrated the functionality of these nonreciprocal devices even with weak input, using a combination of squeezed and coherent light. We found that the squeezed light's influence is more significant than that of coherent light, with a 10.5 dB isolation ratio achievable with just 0.1 photons per mode. We also demonstrated the optical diode's ability to function at 100 MHz and with multiple resonator modes. This could lead to the development of fast and compact nonreciprocal optical devices.

To analyze the interplay of species competition and dispersal, an asymmetrical noisy voter model was developed for a regular lattice structure. The model allows one species to colonize nearest-neighbor sites, while another species can settle at any distance but is less successful in doing so. The model includes external noise, which can lead to random species swaps in the lattice. The combination of these dynamics results in various species competition outcomes, including the exclusion of one species, distinct population coexistence, or bistable coexistence dependent on the starting population ratio. The model shows that an abrupt transition occurs as immigration intensity surpasses a critical point, causing the irreversible decline of the species with shorter dispersal range due to a cusp catastrophe leading to half loop dynamics. The model also identifies that an increase in lattice size accelerates the irreversible transition, the abrupt transition is delayed by an increase in swap frequency under the limit of full substitution, and that the distinct stationary states merge into one under the limit of large immigration intensity, leading to the homogenization of species under intense global dispersal. The model further reveals that the variation of dispersal distance instead of intensity leads to a cusp catastrophe resulting in the exclusion of one species, and that the variation of swap frequency under full substitution or lattice size under regular substitution leads to bi-stable coexistence. The model also derives an effective mean-field model to describe the interplay of species competition and dispersal through the derivation of a piecewise smooth map, and the analysis of this map yields the same insights as the lattice model. The findings of the study have implications for understanding competitive species dynamics in spatially structured populations. The study also considers a scenario where the success rate of one species is affected by an external factor, leading to the exclusion of this species, and the investigation of the scenario where the success rate is affected by another species' abundance results in the capture of the dynamics of the harvested species through a approach of optimal adaptive harvest policy. The study ultimately explores the efficacy of this approach in preventing the decline of the competitively weak species. The results indicate that the model can reflect the dynamics of the system and the proposed harvesting policy can avoid the decline of the competitively weak species, although the success rate of the strong species is affected by the harvesting, and that the capacity to harvest the strong species can further improve the outcome by preventing the decline of the weak species. The study also finds that the optimal adaptive harvest policy can prevent the decline of the competitively weak species due to its ability to adjust to changes in the success rate

This research focuses on an integrated data and energy transmission network, which incorporates D2D communication. This hybrid network allows a central hub to transfer data to those in need and supply power to those who require it. This coexistence also allows D2D transmissions to use the same bandwidth. This integrated network is critical in addressing future energy and spectrum shortages. However, these D2D transmissions and wireless link losses could significantly impede the data transfer rate. In response to this challenge, we propose introducing an intelligent reflecting surface. We then develop an optimization algorithm to maximize the data transfer rate while ensuring that power is generated and D2D communication speeds are met. This is achieved through careful allocation of D2D transmissions, reflection patterns at the SRS, and power distribution between data and D2D transmissions. Ultimately, this results in an efficient solution for integrated data and energy transmissions. Interestingly, we discover that maximizing D2D communication speed is equivalent to solving a discrete minimum distance problem. Furthermore, we find that the reflection patterns and data transfer rates follow specific distributions. Despite the algorithm's complicity, we are able to derive a suboptimal yet simpler solution. This suboptimal solution is interesting as it is derived from an entirely different optimization approach. Through simulation and analytical analysis, we are able to show that this suboptimal solution is near optimal. This is particularly notable as the suboptimal solution is significantly easier to compute than the complex optimal solution. This is significant because the complex optimal solution requires an excessive number of computations, making it impractical for real-world use cases. This is in contrast to the suboptimal solution which is fast enough for real-world applications. This is demonstrated through a numerical example. This research opens up new areas of study such as examining the optimal size of the integrated network and exploring new transmission technologies. This could be particularly interesting as new technologies such as IRS and D2D communications continue to emerge and shape the future of integrated data and energy transmissions. This could also pave the way for the development of new algorithms and solutions that are tailored to these emerging technologies. This is especially important as these technologies are yet to be fully understood and their limitations are yet to be fully characterized. This is particularly true for IRS, a relatively new technology, is yet to be fully understood and its limitations are yet to be fully characterized. This is also the case for D2D communications and other emerging transmission technologies. This is the case even though these technologies hold significant promise and could be the key to addressing future energy and spectrum shortages.

The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate 
given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Through numerical analysis, 
we investigate the potential for a phase plate to attain down to 1 Angstrom 
resolution on an uncorrected TEM. By examining various design features 
(fill-factor, pixel pattern, symmetry), we identify how they influence the electron 
probe size and current density. Our proposed designs exhibit probe sizes ($d_{50}$) 
as low as 0.66 Angstrom, indicating that a programmable phase plate with 
electrostatic elements can successfully rectify spherical aberration well beyond the 
1 Angstrom threshold. Moreover, our results demonstrate that the optimal design 
features are relatively robust and not heavily dependent on the specific TEM 
configuration. Consequently, a programmable phase plate with achievable probe sizes 
of less than 1 Angstrom may be feasible for use in existing TEMs. To facilitate 
experimental implementation, we outline a strategy for designing and optimizing 
such phase plates. Furthermore, we outline the experimental protocol for obtaining 
the required probe size data. By adopting this approach, we believe that the 
achievable probe size can be as small as 1 Angstrom or less on an uncorrected TEM. 
Our proposed strategy may also be applied to other aberration-correcting devices

aberration correctors. To this end, we suggest that researchers collaborate to

The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on the quality of external knowledge gained during training. As external knowledge becomes more extensive, limiting its scope to only necessary information becomes increasingly crucial. Previous approaches to constraining the dialogue models' access to external knowledge were either too inflexible or ineffective. To address this issue, we introduce an alternative method called Knowledge Masking, which temporarily hides parts of the external knowledge from the model during inference. By fine-tuning the model to perform well under these hidden conditions, we can recover its original performance. Our experiments reveal that Knowledge Masking not only enhances the model's generalization to new data but also accelerates training and reduces memory consumption. Moreover, Knowledge Masking enables us to identify and rank the essential external knowledge for each utterance, which can be utilized in subsequent processing steps. Our analysis indicates that Knowledge Masking's effectiveness stems from its ability to enhance the model's semantic understanding and promote the utilization of previously learned information. Through various evaluations, we show that Knowledge Masking yields superior performance compared to alternative methods for constraining external knowledge. Moreover, Knowledge Masking is adaptable to multiple dialogue models and settings. Lastly, we highlight potential avenues for further research in this area. By introducing Knowledge Masking, we hope to stimulate the exploration of more innovative methods for modeling and exploiting external knowledge in dialogue systems and other machine learning applications. Our code and data have been made publicly available here: https://github.com/ghrua/Knowledge-Masking.

Streaming high-quality video, whether it's Video-On-Demand or live, demands transcoding to accommodate viewer devices. This requires significant computing power and, due to rising demand, streaming services now rely on cloud computing to ensure a seamless viewing experience. Cloud providers offer a range of Virtual Machines, each with varying capabilities and prices, which poses the challenge of optimizing cloud utilization for video transcoding. This study is the first to thoroughly assess how video transcoding performs across different cloud machines, which is essential for predicting processing times and developing effective scheduling methods. Based on this analysis and the cost variability of cloud machines, the paper proposes a new approach for dynamically estimating processing times and therefore determining the most cost-effective cloud machine for transcoding. This results in a dynamic threshold-based algorithm that can efficiently schedule video transcoding by considering both processing performance and price. The proposed approach was validated using real-world video content and demonstrated to yield superior performance over existing scheduling methods. The findings indicate that, contrary to common practice, a range of cloud machines can be more cost-effective for video transcoding than the highest-performance machines. The study also reveals that sorting cloud machines by price per performance can lead to better scheduling decisions. The introduced algorithm has the benefit of being simple, scalable, and suitable for dynamic cloud environments. The current approach has limitations, such as assuming that the same video content requires the same transcoding, which may not always hold true. Future work aims to address this shortcoming and integrate the algorithm with existing scheduling frameworks. The research is backed by thorough experimentation using Amazon Web Services and real-world streaming services. The proposed algorithm has the potential to reduce cloud costs by up to 30% for transcoding and outperforms existing scheduling methods by 10-20%. The associated data and algorithm are available for download at the specified website. The proposed approach addresses one of the most significant challenges in cloud-based video streaming services and can be applied to other compute-intensive applications. The introduced algorithm provides a practical solution for scheduling cloud machines and is ready for integration into production environments. The study's results have important implications for the efficient use of cloud computing resources in video streaming. The proposed algorithm is straightforward, scalable, and suitable for dynamic cloud environments. The research is the first to thoroughly examine the performance of cloud machines for video transcoding and explore the cost variability of these machines. The study's approach can be applied to other applications that involve processing different types of data and provide similar performance characteristics. Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. MaskedSpeech is a context-aware synthesis system addressing this limitation. By building upon a masking strategy, MaskedSpeech incorporates contextual acoustic features into each sentence, enabling a more detailed understanding of semantic relationships. Additionally, cross-sentence coarse-grained semantic features aid in the development of a natural prosody. Through augmenting masked acoustic features with contextual elements during training, MaskedSpeech outperformed baseline systems in expressiveness and naturalness. Results indicate that pre-training acoustic features on context on a large scale is not always necessary, with a smaller dataset yielding comparable performance. These strategies result in superior speech synthesis quality, particularly in terms of naturalness and prosody. Evaluations and comparisons reveal that MaskedSpeech surpasses not only text-to-speech systems but also direct speech synthesis approaches. Lastly, user assessments validated the system's performance, with preferred ratings exceeding baseline systems in both categories. Available at https://github.com/ghulgham/MaskedSpeech, the code allows for the generation of high-quality paragraphs. We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that includes a Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of the linearized equation's spectrum at the solitary wave state. Furthermore, we demonstrate that increasing the strength of anharmonic forces leads to a more stable solitary wave state. Additionally, we determine the conditions under which a solitary wave state with initial data close to it follows a similar trajectory in time. This condition is realized through a suitable choice of parameters in the model. We approximate the solitary wave state using a pseudo-spectral method and validate it against a finite difference numerical solution, revealing that our proposed method is capable of modeling the solitary wave state accurately. We also explore the impact of varying parameters in the model, such as anharmonic forces and external forces, on the solitary wave state. Our analysis and subsequent numerical experiments demonstrate the stability of the solitary wave state in both space and time. We also examine the scenario in which the solitary wave state collides with a different wave state, such as a soliton or a kink state, and observes that it maintains its structure and stability. Lastly, we discuss the implications of our findings to a related model, specifically the Klein-Gordon equation with an anharmonic force in a periodic domain. We anticipate that our methods and discoveries will be applicable to analyzing the stability of solitary waves in this model. However, this will necessitate an additional investigation due to the distinct characteristics of the periodic domain. We believe that our study will contribute to a better comprehension of the dynamics and stability of solitary waves in this model. We also propose future research directions, such as exploring other stability preservation techniques, conducting sensitivity analyses of our numerical methods, and investigating the dynamics of the model in a periodic domain. Q-ball studies have long been confined to scenarios where the global symmetry supports a single extremal Q-ball charge state. In situations where there are multiple extremal Q-ball states charged under the same symmetry, our findings show that an additional, intermediate-charge Q-ball forms, which can be both energetically stable and created in a particle accelerator, provided it has a higher mass than the extremal Q-ball counterparts and meets specific conditions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this intermediate Q-ball is actually a broken symmetry version of a more fundamental, core Q-ball, which reverts to its original symmetry form when surrounded by a field of "hedge" quarks. Suggested experimental searches could reveal evidence of this concept through the production of heavy quarks accompanied by light leptons and missing energy. Additionally, our theoretical framework suggests that very low-energy Q-balls might be able to escape detection as dark matter. For the case of Supersymmetry, our analysis identifies a possible range for the effective scale of the "flat" direction that falls within the range of 10^9 to 10^12 GeV. This new intermediate Q-ball is termed a "cored" Q-ball and its properties distinct from those of both the traditional and "hedgehog" Q-ball conditions. A theoretical framework has also been developed to determine the conditions under which a cored Q-ball can exist and be observed in experimental searches. 

This research is relevant to ongoing and future experiments at the Large Hadron Collider, considering that very low-energy, dark matter Q-balls may be accessible in upcoming direct detection experiments such as CAGS and XENONnT, while the production of heavy quarks accompanied by light leptons and missing energy could be observable in searches for vector-like top quarks at the LHC, specifically in searches for four top quark final states at 13 TeV, and possibly also in searches for vector-like bottom quarks and top quark pairs at 8 and 13 TeV, respectively.

migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, we utilize extended, high-speed lightsheet and two-photon imaging

patterns of multiple densely packed nuclei across the retina. By analyzing these migration tracks, we develop and test
a hypothesis that retinal IKNM is driven by a diffusive process fueled by the accumulation of new nuclei at the upper
retinal surface. Our results demonstrate how the tight packing of nuclei at the upper surface influences their movement
patterns, provide a reliable, quantifiable explanation for the uneven distribution of nuclei across the retina, and may
have implications for random cell fate selection within this system. Furthermore, we discovered that the rate of IKNM
proportional to the retina's rate of cell division. Through theoretical and experimental means, we found that the diffusion
of nuclei is sufficient to explain the observed distribution patterns across various zebrafish retina sizes and development stages. Moreover, our findings pinpoint IKNM as a crucial component in the random selection of cell fate locations within the developing retina. Lastly, our research reveals a direct connection between the rate of IKNM and cell division within the retina. In so doing, our study advances our comprehension of a unique and intricate cellular process involved in the early development of the central nervous system. Due to their accessibility and private data storage, these emails are vulnerable to cyber threats and can serve as lucrative targets. Our proposed approach aims to examine research institutions' internal communication networks for potential security breaches. We applied an SEIR complex network dynamics model to simulate and assess the vulnerability of these networks. surface's behavior near the (π,π) point mirrors that near (0,0) due to

The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be best measured through light curves as the phase shift accumulates over time in a quadratic manner. To study this effect in detail, researchers collected archived data and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro, before utilizing a light curve inversion method to match their shapes and rotation characteristics. By modeling the YORP effect and incorporating other relevant parameters into their analysis, scientists were able to detect the YORP acceleration in three asteroids and found that the YORP acceleration in all ten detected cases was positive, accelerating their rotations. Furthermore, incorporating solar precession into their algorithm revealed evidence of this phenomenon in the data obtained for Geographos, which may be a crucial feature that needs further explanation. Ultimately, researchers found that the YORP effect accelerates the rotations of these asteroids so quickly that solar precession cannot be ignored, which poses significant challenges in predicting their future rotational states due to the complex interplay between these effects. As a result, any detection of a YORP acceleration less than 10^-14 deg/day^2 in small asteroids may be distorted by solar precession over their lifetime. Therefore, scientists require even longer observation periods to validate such discoveries accurately. Lastly, by examining the YORP effect in these asteroids, researchers were able to provide predictions on their eventual rotational destinies, which range from entering a sidereal day-locking state to experiencing rotational disruption due to YORP acceleration over time. Consequently, continuous light curve observations of these asteroids are necessary to monitor their YORP effect and rotational states accurately, which can also lead to a deeper understanding of how solar radiation affects their surfaces in the long term. Moreover, incorporating YORP effect predictions into asteroid mission planning is highly advisable to avoid any unexpected changes in their rotational states during close approaches to these small asteroids. The youth are increasingly relying on Instagram as a source of information, with political figures leveraging the platform to disseminate opinions and agendas. We examined online discussions on Instagram in relation to politics from a network perspective, focusing on communities of co-commenters. Our analysis revealed salient co-interactions - instances of user engagement occurring more frequently than chance would suggest - to be crucial in driving online discussions and information dissemination. We based our study on 10 weeks of data surrounding key elections in Brazil and Italy, observing users who commented on posts from politicians and celebrities. We found communities centered on politics to be more active in discussions compared to other topics, and identified three distinct types of communities based on co-commenters' interaction graphs. These communities exhibited exponential and power-law distribution patterns. We further explored the dynamics of online discussions through temporal analysis, noticing that politics-related discussions tend to spike before elections, as well as exhibiting shorter durations compared to other topics. Furthermore, we discovered users with higher degrees of centrality to be more influential in shaping online discussions and agendas. Our results demonstrated users' actual voting behavior to align with their online interactions, with instances of voters defying their online comments indicating potential electoral fraud. We concluded that social media can serve as a reliable indicator of voters' intentions, as well as provide valuable insights into online communities centered on politics, offering potential tools for electoral monitoring and election campaigning strategy development. Moreover, our approach may be applied to analyze online discussions in relation to politics in various countries and cultures. We made all data and code publicly accessible to foster further research within this topic.

This is achieved by demonstrating that such a subgroup has a dense subgroup that acts in a highly transitive manner within the surface's boundary, whose topology is homeomorphic to that of the real line. Precise stellar characteristics are vital for both astrophysics and exoplanetary science, particularly when studying M-dwarfs. Researchers have developed numerous empirical relations that can utilize easily accessible observations to estimate stellar properties. However, these relations are often presented in a non-linear format, which is not suitable for Bayesian modeling. A novel Bayesian approach has been developed to consistently and simultaneously apply multiple empirical calibrations to accurately determine the mass, luminosity, size, and surface temperature of a typical M-dwarf. This new framework incorporates a mass-radius relation for M-dwarfs with a scatter of just 3.1% at fixed mass. The researchers also established the M-dwarf Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Sample (MUSS), and applied their method to obtain consistent stellar parameters for these low-mass stars. The MUSS targets are of interest primarily due to their potential to host exoplanets or serve as benchmarks for stellar activity across different wavelengths. Using the field MUSS stars, a mass range for low-mass stars in the solar neighborhood was defined through a process involving Gaussian Process regression. The resulting data show a distinct feature in the GP derivative at approximately 0.35 $M_{\odot}$. Below this point, M-dwarf stars are considered low-mass M-dwarfs, and above it, they are considered intermediate-mass M-dwarfs. The researchers also established that the Mu2d scheme, a color-based scheme for distinguishing between low and intermediate-mass M-dwarfs, is actually identifying the same threshold as the GP analysis. The developed framework and the MUSS initiative are now available for the scientific community to utilize and contribute with new targets, and can be accessed through the APOGEE 2 legacy library under the name MUSS Catalog. The MUSS Catalog contains a set of 30,000 targets with estimated stellar parameters, including those with low to intermediate masses, and can be used to study the structure and star formation history of the Milky Way. The MUSS targets also offer numerous opportunities to study stellar activity across different wavelengths and its related GP process can be applied to any spectroscopic dataset. The MUSS legacy is also expected to provide valuable constraints for the development of more accurate stellar models for M-dwarfs. Confining modes at the edge, known as line waves, can propagate on the boundary between two specially designed electromagnetic interfaces that maintain mirror symmetry properties.
Studies have previously analyzed line waves in theory and in practice, revealing their occurrence at both microwave and terahertz frequencies.
It has also been demonstrated that these waves can occur when there's a sudden change from a negative to a positive symmetric resistance and uniform surface reactance present.
Characteristics of line waves include highly confineable mode propagation, polarization dependent on direction, and unique localized field enhancements.
A new study proposes a graphene patch structure, showing that the line waves produced can operate in the optical range.
The design involves a graphene surface integrated with an epsilon near zero substrate, which considers the effects of both dual and uniform reactive impedances.
However, this work specifically focuses on utilizing line waves in dual impedance structures. 
A new type of mode is analyzed, a surface slope wave with distinct characteristics, including a varying local field and propagation direction.
It exhibits an unusual local field distribution and unique propagation properties.
It's shown that this mode can operate in the optical range and offers highly confineable propagation.
Additionally, the study demonstrates that this mode can be easily engineered by changing the unit cell size.
Both theoretical and experimental evidence confirm the existence of the surface slope wave. 
An optical range design is proposed, fabricated, and tested to show its capability for line wave operation. 
Theoretical and experimental results match closely, with a calculated effective wavelength of 9.8 um and an experimentally measured value of 9.9 um. 
The study concludes by discussing potential applications and future research directions for this newly identified mode. 
This work may pave the way for the realization of efficient, miniaturized devices utilizing the surface slope wave. 
It's also possible that this mode could be leveraged to improve the performance of metasurface antennas by substituting the design with a slope wave-based equivalent, resulting in enhanced gain and reduced size. 
Future research should focus on overcoming reflection loss limitations and exploring new operation frequencies and wavelengths. 
Ultimately, this study hopes to contribute to a deeper understanding of line waves and the development of new theories for analyzing and identifying similar confined modes in metamaterials and metasurfaces. 
It's also proposed that the surface slope wave be used as a benchmark for validating numerical simulation tools. 
Finally, it's suggested that future work consider investigating the topological properties of the surface slope wave to determine its potential as a viable candidate for topological mode applications.
