The ultimate goal of imitation learning is to develop efficient policies using nearly optimal expert examples. Nonetheless, getting numerous high-quality examples from human experts is very costly. On the other hand, getting vast amounts of low-quality or irrelevant paths in a task can be quite easy, but these paths aren't helpful for imitation. Nonetheless, these suboptimal paths still provide insight into the system dynamics and what actions are feasible within that environment. This study investigates whether these suboptimal paths can be utilized to enhance imitation learning performance using new objectives that learn a factored transition model. The learned model allows us to derive a latent action space, making downstream imitation learning much more efficient by reducing the necessity for extensive expert datasets. This is achieved by leveraging additional non-expert data. For practical applications, we suggest TRAIL, an algorithm that utilizes contrastive learning for energy-based models to derive the action space. The benefits of this approach were verified in experiments on navigation and locomotion tasks, yielding up to a 4x performance improvement compared to baseline imitation learning methods. The resulting systems exhibit better performance than both fully optimal and random trajectories in imitation learning settings, while also outperforming expert-only imitation learning by a significant margin. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on the union bound, which corresponds to a decoder that uses the logarithmic metric function after a fixed number of iterations. We have found that pac codes with this metric function have error-correction performance close to that of the best convolutional codes. The gap between the bound and the actual performance of these codes is relatively small, at around $2.5$ dB, which is a significant improvement over the $6.8$ dB gap of standard pac codes. This indicates that pac codes are essentially as good as conventional convolutional codes, which are widely used in practice, given their excellent performance and low computational requirements. As an example, we show that pac codes can be used to create reliable channels for the transmission of binary memoryless sources. Furthermore, we have found that convolutional pac codes outperform conventional convolutional codes in scenarios where the received sequence has a high signal-to-noise ratio, which is consistent with our findings on the performance of pac codes in other scenarios. 

As an additional contribution, we have derived an upper limit on the performance of pac codes, which is expressed in terms of the union bound after a fixed number of iterations. We have found that standard pac codes meet this upper limit, which provides an alternative explanation for their good performance. Moreover, we have found that conventional convolutional codes also approach this upper limit, which further supports the notion that these codes have similar good performance. 

Finally, we have investigated the impact of different metric functions on the performance of pac codes, which has led us to a novel upper limit on the performance of logarithmic metric functions, which is more stringent than the corresponding bound for conventional convolutional codes. This has enabled us to design a metric function that, while more complex to compute than the logarithmic function, achieves essentially the same performance, which is only $0.1$ dB worse than conventional convolutional codes. 

It is worth noting that, due to their high computational requirements, we have resorted to using a widely used standard decoder for pac codes, which is now widely available. It is also note that our findings are not limited to binary pac codes, as the theory is equally applicable to non-binary pac codes. Nonetheless, our analysis has focused exclusively on binary pac codes.

A rational number p/q represents the basis for a numbering system. Words composed of digits 0 through p-1 in base p/q correspond to unique rational numbers, which make up the set Np/q. While previous studies on base p/q systems focus on evaluating words that translate to nonnegative integers, our analysis examines subsets of (Np/q)d that are identifiable using finite automata in (Ap)d. Our initial contribution identifies the subsets defined by first-order logic similar to those defined by the Bachi-Bruyere Theorem in integer base systems. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that both natural order relation and modulo-q operator are not recognisable within base p/q systems. Nevertheless, our work also establishes that any recognisable subset in (Np/q)d can be expressed by a formula using the natural order relation and the addition operation, in contrast to base 10 systems where hybrid recognisability is possible. Our research also analyses the recognition properties in combination with Glassstone-Turing normal bases and highly composite base systems. Ultimately, our paper outlines a connection between base p/q systems and Sturmian sequences, which are highly self-repeating and self-similar in nature. Our study also introduces the concept of ultimately periodic base p/q systems, leading to the discovery that the subsets defined by first-order logic over (Np/q)d are equivalent to cross-cutting languages, which are known to be non-ambiguous and deterministic in nature. Our analysis also delves into the properties of recognition in base p/q systems, which we term as 'weak-proper' due to their ability to accurately identify strings without error, although they are not necessarily efficient in distinguishing strings. Our research also explores glassstone-turing normal bases with multiple digits, which enable the expression of all possible combinations of numbers using only two digits, specifically 0 and 1. Our study also examines recognition properties in combination with highly composite base systems that contain multiple distinct factors. Ultimately, our paper outlines multiple ways to determine whether a given base p/q system is weak-proper or not. Our research also highlights an instance of a base p/q system at 3/2 that is equivalent to a context-free language over nonnegative integers, which is known as the Fibonacci sequence. Our analysis also considers highly composite base systems that contain multiple distinct factors, which are key to the Rekayat system used in traditional Arabic mathematics. Our study also explores glassstone-turing normal bases with multiple digits, which are crucial to the FlexiBase system used in multi-base arithmetic.

In image recognition, distinct forms of visual cues, namely edges and textures, contribute uniquely to the overall understanding. While edges convey crucial information about a shape's form, textures reveal details about regional appearance. Current Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) applications often excel at extracting texture information but tend to produce vague boundary definitions. Expert medical analysts, for instance, primarily utilize organ edges when performing manual segmentations. Influenced by these observations, this study proposes Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), an easily integrable module that complements standard encoder-decoder networks, capable of processing edge and texture information simultaneously. By prioritizing edge extraction and incorporating an auxiliary supervision, the EG-CNN module refines its output and merges it with original network predictions. We validate the performance benefits of the EG-CNN module when integrated with mainstream CNNs across two public benchmark datasets, highlighting consistent improvements in semantic segmentation precision and overall robustness. Moreover, we include specific examples demonstrating the semantic meaning embedded in the learned edge codes. The open-source implementation of the proposed EG-CNN module is now publicly available on GitHub. With the ability to be seamlessly integrated into existing networks, the EG-CNN module serves as a versatile tool to enhance the boundary extraction capabilities of any CNN. We begin by positing that high-capacity models' ability to perform well on new tasks from minimal training data is largely an illusion when they are trained on vast amounts of existing data. This is because their initial training obscures their ability to form meaningful associations with new information. We test this hypothesis through the development of a task-efficient, few-shot continual learning task for models to truly showcase their capacity to learn from minimal data. 

Building on prior research in executive functions, we create a pre-trained model to replicate the ability to form associations from scratch. We implement this by introducing a simple memory-based model that mimics the few-shot learning process. This is done by training a series of linear transformers on individual tasks with limited examples. We then apply this model to the study of few-shot learning in the context of supercaps, a method that has been shown to achieve exceptional results in low-data settings.

We evaluate our approach through the use of a dataset consisting of 16,384 random tasks, derived from a combination of three existing datasets. Our findings indicate that models can achieve comparable performance to current state-of-the-art few-shot learning models, despite being trained on significantly less data. Furthermore, our observations suggest that even models with extensive training capacities can perform tasks with less than 0.1% error even without the aid of a memory-based model, provided they are trained on sufficient data. However, our results also show that the inclusion of a memory-based model leads to a substantial improvement in performance in low-data settings. 

Ultimately, our research indicates that models can benefit from a basic ability to form associations with new information, particularly in the context of few-shot continual learning. This has significant implications for the study of deep learning models and may facilitate breakthroughs in areas such as artificial general intelligence. The success of medical image analysis using machine learning largely relies on high-quality datasets.  However, when these datasets contain biases, the models can learn them, compromising their ability to produce unbiased results.  While research exists on developing unbiased models, the problem lies in identifying the source of the biases present in the data.  In an effort to address this issue, we first establish a metric to quantify data biases and develop a new framework that combines both bias and generalization metrics to guide the selection of unbiased datasets.  We validate the effectiveness of this approach using two publicly available datasets containing retinal and lung lesions, and observe significant improvements in the RANSAC model's performance when using the unbiased dataset.  Furthermore, we discovered that models trained on unbiased datasets show only a minor drop in accuracy when applied to real-world data, indicating a significant potential for this approach to be applied to other machine learning scenarios.  We have made our methodology and results openly available for the benefit of the medical image analysis community.  In the future, we anticipate this framework to play a key role in addressing the challenges posed by biased data in medical image analysis. Research on intricate systems from the human brain to social connections has uncovered a multitude of concealed layers hidden from direct observation.  Condensed matter physics too has numerous enigmas awaiting experimental confirmation. Both domains share a common challenge: without direct access, one must rely on theoretical models to fill the gap between experimental measurements and the underlying reality.  A particularly intriguing issue in condensed matter physics is geometric frustration, which arises when the arrangement of a system's connections impedes the alignment of any order.  A notable example is the triangular lattice of spins from the Heisenberg model, which has not been satisfactorily emulated using classical vectors.  Recent studies have proposed a different kind of reality - one where the true state lies between the measured layers - using proxy models that may reflect its structure.  In this work, we utilize a classical spin model on a triangular lattice to generate afrustrated order hidden from measurement.  Applications to other complex systems and a discussion on the proposed reality's relationship to its proxy models are also considered.  This work is further illustrated by a heisenberg model of a triangular lattice with two inequivalent magnetic sublattices and a novel multilayer hidden layer structure.  All theoretical models are supported by numerical simulations, with corresponding experimental suggestions for actual systems.  Ultimately, this research indicates that geometric frustration is not a necessary condition for the existence of hidden order and that a non-trivial, concealed state of matter is possible even in the absence of strong interactions.  This has significant implications for our understanding of condensed matter physics and may contribute to a fresh perspective on the study of intricate systems.  Together with ongoing experimental advancements, this provides a perfect opportunity to uncover more of the concealed worlds in both condensed matter and complex systems. Thanks to speech-emotion recognition technology, computers can engage with people on a more emotional level. Nonetheless, the accuracy of speech-emotion recognition in real-world situations remains an area of improvement. A major limitation of existing methods is their inability to adapt models to new domains without a significant amount of labeled data from those domains. In this study, we propose a technique called domain-invariant feature learning through adversarial training for speech-emotion recognition. Our method involves training two models: one that learns domain-invariant factors from speech samples, and another that uses those factors to predict emotions while ignoring the domain. The two models are connected through a cycle, allowing the speech-emotion recognition model to adapt to new domains with minimal labeled data. Our results show that this technique significantly improves the accuracy of speech-emotion recognition in real-world situations, surpassing state-of-the-art domain adaptation methods that require a large amount of labeled data from the target domain. In particular, our method achieves an accuracy of 53.14% in the IEMOCAP dataset and 45.69% in the CMU-MOSE dataset, which are two of the most challenging speech-emotion recognition datasets. Moreover, our method's ability to adapt to new domains with minimal labeled data is remarkable, requiring only 50 labeled samples from the target domain to achieve an accuracy of 53.14% in the IEMOCAP dataset. Our technique also enables the integration of multiple datasets, allowing us to create a unified dataset for speech-emotion recognition. We present an investigation of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO), a four-layer Aurivillius compound, under the influence of high hydrostatic pressure.  Our X-ray diffraction data does not exhibit a phase transition under pressure but lattice changes suggest a series of structural adaptations as the pressure increases.  Initially, BFTO displays a quasi-tetragonal symmetry but transforms into an orthorhombic structure beyond 8 GPa.  Our Raman spectroscopy analysis reveals local structure alterations at 5.5 GPa, contradicting crystallographic changes, and our Nuclear forward scattering measurements disclose the onset of magnetic order in BFTO above 5K under high pressure conditions, with enhanced magnetic order with increasing pressure.  Conversely, NFS at 6.4GPa and varying temperatures indicates magnetic loss at higher temperatures (20K), with the structural changes potentially influencing this magnetic phenomenon.  Additionally, our results demonstrate that high pressure can be utilized in manipulating the intricate relationships between structure, local chemistry and spin systems in this Aurivillius compound.  We propose that pressure may offer a means to discover new functional materials through an unexpected pathway.  This study is further backed by theoretical structure predictions using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP).  Our findings are shared, highlighting the value of combined experimental and theoretical approaches in understanding the complex phenomena observed in these materials.  Finally, we suggest that our findings from BFTO may be applicable to other materials exhibiting similar structural adaptability. Hybrid methods tackling continuous shortest path problems start by local optimization
of a discrete shortest path in a weighted graph. The convergence to the optimal
continuous path depends heavily on the graph from which it is derived. In high-density
graphs, small errors in discrete path selection can result in significant deviations
from optimality, making their use impractical for applications like flight planning.
In such cases, finding a suitable discrete subgraph with low density can be
challenging. We introduce an alternative approach based on super-source shortest
paths, where multiple subgraphs with low average densities contribute to a global
continuous path. The method determines a discrete subgraph for each source by
aggregating local shortest paths and selecting a subgraph with low average density.
Its effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to flight planning and
benchmark problems. Our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art continuous
shortest path methods in terms of precision and efficiency. In particular, it shows
substantial improvements for high-density graphs. The proposed method's simplicity
makes its implementation versatile and easily integrable into existing hybrid
algorithms. The code for the approach and experimental data are available at

As the index surpasses this threshold, pressure drops to zero at a finite distance from the origin, and in both scenarios, a spherical void forms. All matter becomes concentrated in a thin layer behind the shock wave's front. This layer's structure, however, changes depending on the index, especially where the inner edge meets a sudden and infinite density at approximately 1.4 in both models, even though the pressure at this edge remains consistently zero. If the index exceeds this threshold, further analysis becomes more complex due to the difficulty in determining inner edge conditions, and it's unclear whether a similar void and shock wave structure would continue in such situations. To overcome the coercivity issue inherent in the material structure, we employ two-scale convergence methods, while novel results are established for addressing the linear differential constraints via existence proofs for potentials and constraint-preserving extension operators. Ultimately, our investigation paves the way for tackling more complex nonlinear differential constraints. 

This research is a culmination of discussions and results derived from the following works: the non-periodic case studied with M. Rassias, the periodic case explored with G. Azzwell and A. Mihailescu, and the constraint-preserving extension operators analyzed with T. Rybka. 

In addition, our paper addresses an open problem posed by F. Smarowski and A. Szumata in asking us to investigate the $\Gamma$-convergence of the material energy when considering both the matrix and filling materials as doubly periodic structures. 

Our study offers an initial response to this query, while also examining the related case of a material composite where the filling material occupies a bounded region within the matrix structure.

A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic, a simple model allocates opportunities to maximize the long-term payoff of transferring wealth to future generations, considering both intra- and intergenerational dimensions. Analyzing the model, we find that even with perfect credit markets, there are limits to achieving infinite intergenerational mobility, and these limits are influenced by the level of education required to access better opportunities. These findings suggest that even with perfect credit markets, there are significant barriers to achieving full social mobility across generations. Moreover, these barriers can result in persistent income inequality. Finally, we demonstrate that even a slight imperfection in credit markets can completely eliminate intergenerational mobility. These concepts are further illustrated through numerical examples and policy simulations. These simulations show that increasing access to higher education can improve intergenerational mobility, especially for lower-income children, and that targeted policies, such as affirmative action, can accelerate this process. Overall, our study highlights the intricate relationship between social mobility and credit markets and underscores the importance of education in achieving greater intergenerational mobility. These results have implications for understanding and addressing inequality in societies with advanced education systems.

The combination of chirped pulse amplification and nonlinear optical systems has been the foundation for significant progress in numerous sectors, including semiconductors, communications, biology, defense, and national security. The absence of a unified software platform for CPA-NLO modeling restricts further development and potential implementation of these systems in data-driven approaches such as inverse design. The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset. Notably, our network's ability to adapt to low-quality and real-world videos surpasses existing methods. The code and dataset used in this research are available for public access at https://github.com/ghrua/MD-CSDNetwork.

Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable with only basic components such as linear optics, homodyne detection, and single photon detection, which poses a significant threat to the widely adopted vacuum+weak decoy state QKD system. Our findings suggest that randomizing the source phase to a limited degree may not be sufficient to safeguard phase-encoding QKD systems using weak coherent states. To mitigate this flaw, we propose a simple phase-ramping technique to pump the vacuum state, making the proposed attack strategy ineffective. In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building from this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though they lacked the full context of Menger's original thoughts. Now, with all prior work taken into consideration, we revisit and reframe the two problems, providing the necessary background and definitions to make them fully understandable. Additionally, we offer new solutions to both problems, which we then use as a starting point to explore further questions and possibilities. Lastly, we discuss the relationship between the defined angle functions and the underlying metric structures in these spaces. 

This research is in the form of an Exposition, which we hope will serve as a starting point for further discussions and the exchange of new ideas within the community of mathematicians and researchers. We welcome any feedback, counter-examples, or proofs that could enhance or clarify the presented concepts. 

With respect to the structure of the paper, we first provide the background and general definitions for the concept of angle function, before moving on to the focused discussion on problems 1 and 2. Problems 3 and 4 are then explored in the subsequent chapter, which is followed by conclusions and possible directions for further research. 

Throughout the paper, we use various notations and definitions from metric and semi-metric spaces, which are all defined at the beginning of the relevant sections to ensure clarity and understanding.

Leveraging the quantum duality of cluster algebras, we find that U_q(g) possesses a natural basis \bar{Θ} whose structural coefficients consist of non-negative integers in the variable set {q^(1/2), q^(-1/2)}. Notably, the basis \bar{Θ} contains the quantum minors \bar{θ}_w(q) as a subcollection, which forms a basis within the quantum torus U_q(T). In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD, yielding an improvement of up to $10\%$ in test accuracy over various data distributions. DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds by up to $20$, compared to traditional DSGD, while also ensuring fairness across decentralized devices. We have examined past methods of computing pressure for the hard-disk model, dating back to 1953, and contrasted these with results we obtained through a powerful simulation technique and a highly efficient algorithm that leverages many computer processors simultaneously. Like various simple scientific models, such as the Drosophila model, understanding the hard-disk model required significant effort. In our research, we argue that the difficulty of measuring the pressure has not been fully acknowledged in the long-standing debate regarding the hard-disk phase-transition scenario. Our paper provides the fundamental principles of the hard-disk model, defines the concept of pressure and presents new, unbiased methods of estimating it. Additionally, we explore different computational algorithms used for sampling and discuss critical factors that affect how quickly they reach equilibrium in the absence of theoretical guidance. Our findings, specifically pressure values calculated for up to one million disks, can serve as a benchmark for evaluating future simulation methods. Moreover, we make publicly accessible, in an open-source database, both pressure data and different variations of the used simulation methods and pressure estimation algorithms. This initiative is intended to benefit researchers and scientists working on the hard-disk model by allowing them to compare their own methods and algorithms for sampling equilibria without bias against our results. This approach has the added benefit of contributing to the ongoing discussion regarding the hard-disk model. This paper examines jet modifications within a medium using JEWEL and PYTHIA 6.4, emphasizing uncertainties associated with perturbative scales, nuclear PDFs, and temperature variations of the medium at onset and transition points. Jet spectrum and nuclear modification factor data from the LHC are used for comparison with simulated results. Additionally, the influence of nuclear PDFs and the medium on jet structure is investigated through Lund plane analysis, and the interaction between nuclear PDF choice and medium parameters is explored. Our findings suggest that despite variations in input parameters, jet modification traits persist, with medium effects prevailing over nuclear PDF influences for pT above 60 GeV. The study also reveals that medium temperature markings can simulate the behavior of JEWEL without medium effects, while comparison with EPJ HEP Volume 78, 83 (2018) reveals that uncertainties related to nuclear PDFs and medium parameters can be encoded into jet spectrum through scale choices, potentially allowing for medium insights through LHC data analysis. Lastly, within the considered scenario range, our simulations demonstrate that nuclear PDF choice has a minimal impact on jet spectrum shape. Lastly, we highlight the necessity of accurate nuclear PDFs for reliable jet data interpretation.

Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Furthermore, our results indicate that Forsage's development aligns with the emergence of cryptocurrency and crypto social media, with promoters primarily focusing on promoting the scheme through YouTube and other free advertising methods. In conclusion, our research into Forsage offers an original perspective on the inner workings of pyramid schemes and how they adapt to contemporary technology and platforms. Lastly, this research is a precursor to a more extensive study on the intersection of blockchain technology and deception. It is available online at https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.06248, and it will be presented at the 2022 IEEE Conference on Privacy, Security and Trust (PST).

A set of precise theoretical and experimental benchmarks at hadron colliders are based on color-singlet differential spectra, known as exclusive differential spectra. Our study provides a comprehensive effective-theory framework, using soft-collinear effective theory to account for the connections between quarks and gluons in differential cross-section calculations for these processes. This approach starts with leading-order perturbative calculations in quantum chromodynamics and incorporates the effects of threshold logarithms through the color-evolution of exclusive differential spectra. We implemented this framework in a code called DYCE, which can efficiently compute threshold-corrected cross sections for the Drell-Yan process and other exclusive differential spectra in hadron-collider collisions. We validate the code by comparing its results to existing studies of the Drell-Yan process at top- and bottom-threshold limits and at a 100 TeV pp collision, and also examine the effectiveness of DYCE in addressing phenomenological questions for future top-quark studies at LHC and a possible future 100 TeV hadron collider.

We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to converged first-principle simulations to validate our TB models' accuracy. The results indicate that the dipole-based model yields a more precise description than the velocity-based model. We attribute this to the imperfect compensation of diamagnetic and paramagnetic currents in the velocity-based model. To rectify this shortcoming, we formulated a sum rule that explicitly addresses the compensation issue, allowing the correction of velocity-based models to match dipole-based models and guarantee gauge invariance. We provide a straightforward pathway for converting velocity-based models to their equivalent dipole-based counterparts, facilitating the straightforward use of established light-matter simulation tools. These findings offer a crucial step in achieving reliable tight-binding simulations of light-matter interactions for the wide range of materials encompassed by the scope of this study. 

This study is part of a larger research effort aimed at developing a general-purpose tight-binding Hamiltonian formation method, capable of accurately modeling the electronic properties of any material by combining first-principle data, as illustrated by the application to h-BN. This application involves the creation of a robust TB model for this material, which has been validated through the calculation of optical responses under strong excitations, using a particle and hole field description for isolated and coupled systems. The calculated reflection spectra were compared to converged first-principle simulations, yielding an excellent agreement and demonstrating the capability of this approach to model h-BN's optical properties accurately. Moreover, we utilized this model to investigate the impact of h-BN's surface characteristics on its optical properties and examined the potential for this material to host strong light-matter modes via the simulation of interaction with a finite TB nitride monolayer and a nitride bilayer doped with Eu atoms. The results show that even a nitride monolayer can support strong light-matter modes and that doping a nitride bilayer may lead to the emergence of quasi-localized states and enable efficient light-matter interaction. Deep-learning techniques such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent
Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.
Compared to traditional approaches, they deliver superior results for various
predictive tasks. Our research expands on existing knowledge by testing five
different variants of deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks and
Multi-layer Perceptron with dropout, for predicting the characteristics and
occurrence time of subsequent process events. Uniquely, we assess these models
at multiple stages of a process, determined by event quantities and case
completion times, thereby providing valuable insights into their behavior under
different process conditions. Our experiments surprisingly reveal that the basic
Multi-layer Perceptron frequently surpasses more advanced deep learning models
in both prediction tasks. Consequently, when deploying predictive process models,
due caution is required as they perform differently across various process stages
and it's also advisable to establish results with strong baselines like simple
Multi-layer Perceptron. The underlying code for our analysis has been made
publicly available to facilitate future research. By combining deep learning
with process-mining, we aim to facilitate further improvement of process models
and enhance understanding of complex processes through the integration of data
and domain expertise. Additionally, to ensure reproducibility and usability of
our analysis, we will be openly sharing our code and findings with the research
community.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. This prediction model utilizes semi-empirical combinations of radiative electron beam flux spectra consisting of two electron beam models: a high-flux simulation with a high energy cutoff and a lower-flux simulation with a lower energy cutoff. This two-component approach effectively explains the Balmer line broadening, the optical color temperature, the Balmer jump strength, and the far-ultraviolet continuum in the peak phases of this flare. Additionally, a comparative analysis is conducted with solar flare data, including those from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph, which provide spatial resolution, combined with previous modeling of the SOL20140329T17:48 X1 solar flare, to demonstrate that the two-component electron beam model can be interpreted as the superposition of bright flare kernels and weaker ribbons in a larger area. This two-component electron beam model can be used to better comprehend the energy distribution of energy deposition in stellar flares, which has implications for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures. Moreover, it highlights the significance of obtaining actual spectroscopic data from white-light stellar flares, particularly in the near-ultraviolet range, to gain a deeper understanding of the energy distribution within these flares. Ultimately, such data will allow for more accurate assessments of the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. The newly developed formulae enable direct computation of matrix elements without needing to deconstruct the HFB wave functions, leading to an important increase in the feasibility of realistic applications of the Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov approach. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with notable improvements. As an example, our method achieves significant enhancement in validated accuracy when dealing with twisting transformation along the z-axis (within a 20-degree range) from 20.3% to 83.8%. All code and models are available for use at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a mathematical model is developed which takes into consideration various factors including how long microbial life forms can survive, the speed of stars dispersing, and how ejected material scatters across space, all to assess the likelihood of discovering evidence for interstellar panspermia. By examining statistical relationships between pairs of life-bearing planetary systems, a potential indicator of interstellar panspermia emerges under certain astrophysical conditions. Estimates for various environments suggest that clusters of open and globular stars represent the most suitable subjects for investigating the validity of interstellar panspermia. In order to validate or disprove the theory, a massive observational effort spanning a century would be required in conjunction with the development of sensitive techniques for detecting extraterrestrial life. Ultimately, answering this question will depend on a combination of astrophysical and biological developments. The proposed concept of induced spontaneous symmetry breaking is explored through a theoretical scenario. This scenario posits that spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs at the highest energy level, causing a cascade of symmetry violations at lower energy levels resulting from subtle mixings between them. A simple model has been devised to illustrate this idea using scalar portals, where the significant difference in energy scales, such as the Planck and electroweak scales, arises from the multiplication of several small factors related to the mixing coefficients. The formation of dark matter fields is also examined in this framework, where it is possible for these fields to emerge from matter fields located on one or more intermediate energy levels between the highest and lowest. Furthermore, the possibility of connecting the 125 GeV Higgs resonance to the dark matter field through the process of portal interconversion is also considered. This could occur either through the collapse of a scalar field on an intermediate energy level due to dark matter formation, or through the emergence of dark matter fields through the transition of the Higgs vacuum state as a consequence of the scalar self-interactions. This could provide a solution to the cosmological matter-antimatter asymmetry problem if the dark matter field is linked with the electroweak symmetry-breaking sector. Lastly, the implications of the Baryon Acoustic Oscillation feature rely on the existence of intermediate energy scales. The most suitable range for the dark matter particle mass, in relation to the Higgs resonance and the Baryon Acoustic Oscillation scale, is determined as between 10 and 100 GeV. The proposed concept and resulting theoretical outcomes offer various possibilities for investigating the existence of dark matter and the symmetry-breaking cascade in the universe through the study of particle physics. The theoretical framework presented also raises the question of whether the universe's highest energy scales hold the key to solving the cosmological matter-antimatter asymmetry problem. The findings from this study suggest that the universe's darkest substance and largest-scale structure patterns may be connected to a cascade of symmetry-breaking phenomena at its most fundamental energy levels. The proposed concept of induced spontaneous symmetry breaking, along with the related theoretical model, presents an innovative framework for exploring the universe's highest energy scales and the underlying physics driving the evolution and structure of the cosmos. Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at once.  This method results in enhanced precision when estimating population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters.  Notably, our study reveals that capture-recapture models alone can infer parameters for resource selection functions, enabling the exclusive use of capture data to investigate space usage, albeit with lower precision.  Nonetheless, using telemetry data yields superior precision.  We discovered that models employing standard encounter probability models can provide biased estimates of density when animals' spatial behavior correlates with environmental variables, which necessitates consideration of space usage in population density estimations through capture-recapture methods.  Nonetheless, no such bias arises with account-based models.  Our study suggests that capture-recapture models' ability to estimate encounter probabilities can leverage resource selection functions to enhance model fit and accuracy, which can be useful in scenarios where telemetry data is limited.  We also found that models incorporating telemetry data produce more precise estimates of resource selection probabilities than capture-recapture models alone.  Nonetheless, models excluding telemetry data produce similar results for density and capture-recapture model parameters.  We provide an R package called "SpaceR" for our proposed method and offer guidance on its usage through a provided tutorial. In designing minimum power networks, we are given an undirected graph $G = (V, E)$ along with associated edge costs. The objective is to select an edge subset $F \subseteq E$ satisfying a specific minimum power criterion. Specifically, for the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem, F must contain exactly k disjoint st-paths. Notably, a k-approximation algorithm has been previously developed for this problem; however, whether such an algorithm exists with an approximation ratio sublinear in k even under the scenario of unit costs had yet to be determined. We present a new $4\sqrt{2k}$-approximation algorithm applicable to general cost settings. Moreover, we establish a $2k$-approximation algorithm for the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem when costs are restricted to unit values. These findings address outstanding questions in graph theory and contribute novel results to the field of approximation algorithms.

This study proposes a technique for the autonomous planning of swarms of unmanned aerial vehicles within a predefined environment. When the swarm detects changes, such as the movement of a target, within a designated area, the command center recalculates and adjusts the swarm's flight path. Key algorithms employed in this research are A* pathfinding and Generalized Labeled Multi-Bernoulli for target tracking. Monte Carlo simulations were conducted to evaluate the performance of this approach under various conditions, including different target movements and densities of the swarm. Results demonstrating the effectiveness of this method in a dynamic environment are presented. Furthermore, a framework for real-time implementation using Linux clusters and Monte Carlo simulations to determine optimal planning parameters are also outlined. A preliminary demonstration of the system's capabilities is showcased through a real-world flight test.

Previous researchers developed methods for assessing football teams' defensive prowess by predicting the likelihood of gaining possession of the ball and being attacked, without considering the initial phase of a game. These existing approaches assume that possession of the ball is equally valuable, regardless of the phase of the game, but do not take into account the varying scoring expectations in different situations. Moreover, they fail to account for defensive actions that directly influence the probability of scoring, such as blocking shots or intercepting passes, by only considering possession of the ball. To address these limitations, we propose a framework for evaluating defensive game actions that incorporates the possibility of scoring from both personal and team perspectives. By applying this framework to NBA game data, we were able to determine the probabilities of certain game events, including the likelihood of being attacked, being scored upon, and being shot at, as well as the probabilities of certain scoring outcomes. One crucial step in the extraction process involves linking input text to predefined label fields. Our research offers an innovative, layout-agnostic method to identify pre-printed text, handwriting, and their relationships. Our technique excels in handling imperfect form images, unlike previous approaches designed for well-organized images. To test its effectiveness, we created a database of deteriorated forms from the late 1800s and early 1900s. Our model uses a neural network to identify both types of text, after which we classify their relationships through the analysis of the detected text features. Highly flexible recurrent state-space models can capture complex patterns in time series data, but typically assume a static and unchanging dynamic, a rare occurrence in real-world situations. To overcome this limitation, many systems exhibit patterns that are similar yet distinct, and can be described through a single underlying variable. To address this, we developed the Hidden Parameter Recurrent State Space Models (HiP-RSSMs), a novel framework that uses a compact set of latent factors to model interconnected dynamical systems. By implementing an efficient Gaussian graphical model, HiP-RSSMs can learn and conduct precise inference without resorting to approximations, such as variational inference. In our experiments, HiP-RSSMs consistently surpassed traditional state-space models and multi-task competitors on multiple demanding robotic tasks, in both real-world applications and simulations. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/algorithms/hip_rssm.

Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness in expectation is already known to result from this property. We've established an additional consequence: almost sure asymptotic freeness of type $B$ for unitarily invariant random matrices. This consequence leads to several secondary findings: the asymptotic cyclic monotonicity, and the derivation of asymptotic conditional freeness. Specifically, we demonstrate the empirical spectral distribution of randomly rotated matrices converges towards a conditionally free convolution. We've also identified new relationships between infinitesimal freeness, type $B$ freeness, conditional freeness, cyclic monotonicity, and monotone independence. Moreover, we show that the BBP phase transition in an additive rank-one perturbation of a GUE matrix is a consequence of asymptotic conditional freeness. This line of reasoning applies as well to an analysis of outlier eigenvalues in various unitarily invariant ensembles. Lastly, we discuss the applicability and implications of our discoveries to outstanding problems in random matrix theory.

Determining the extent of polarization within social systems is vital to studying its effects on political structures. While numerous methods are employed to analyze polarization in social networks through structural evaluation, our analysis revealed that eight commonly used methods yield elevated polarization scores even in artificially constructed networks that closely mirror real-world networks in density and distribution. Furthermore, some of these methods proved sensitive to specific characteristics of polarized groups, such as degree distribution and size. We proposed introducing a standard normalization to mitigate these issues, alongside a comprehensive set of criteria for effective measurement of structural polarization. By normalizing the scores, the classification performance increased by up to 220%, and notably, the choice of measurement method became significantly less crucial, with most methods surpassing the previous best performance following normalization. Our research lays the groundwork for a thorough evaluation and comparison of different structural polarization measurement methods. Additionally, we provide a suite of artificial networks that can be utilized as benchmarks, along with a comprehensive set of methods and guidelines on how to utilize them for future research studies. All benchmark datasets and method implementations are available for download at https://github.com/andersonryu/Polarization-Basline.

Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for renowned scientists such as G.B. Airy, J.C. Maxwell, and A. Einstein. This work identifies a widespread misconception among them, mistakenly using the Einstein operator and confusing it with the Cauchy operator and the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator. Determining the true compatibility operator, the Einstein operator becomes expressible in terms of the Bianchi operator, and the original discussion on this topic is revised. Furthermore, an intriguing connection between the Einstein operator and the Nijenhuis operator is discovered. The integration of formal verification and testing techniques aims to provide improvements in creating and testing dependable software, as well as its ongoing development. Our geometric testing theory is designed to be a blueprint for a testing environment that can be part of a toolchain used by software developers, including professionals and academics in computer science. This environment features a sophisticated automated tool that can identify mistakes found during testing and help fix them by visually presenting the underlying causes in a graphical format on a screen. This format can be easily navigated to pinpoint areas of the code that need adjustment to resolve the issue. Once modified, the code can be quickly retested to verify the effectiveness of the change. Our approach to testing also includes features such as automatic generation of test cases tailored to specific programming languages and the ability to perform multiple tests simultaneously. Furthermore, our approach enables software development to recover quickly from unexpected errors and allows for the efficient allocation of fixing tasks to team members with expertise in particular areas of the code. Our approach to testing has been put into practice through our JavaCheck program, which includes a range of advanced features such as the ability to check safety and performance properties in addition to error detection. Our approach has facilitated the creation of reliable software, including a media player, a web browser, and several games, and our research aims to contribute to the broader discussion on program verification and testing in the dependability chapter of the 2008 Symposium on Correctness Theory. We introduce HyperPrompt, an innovative architecture that utilizes HyperNetworks to create adaptable task-conditioning for self-attention in Transformers through prompt-based generation. In this setup, hyper-prompts can be optimized end-to-end by a HyperNetwork. By employing hyper-prompts as global task memories, HyperPrompt enables networks to learn task-specific features while facilitating flexible information sharing among multiple tasks. Notably, HyperPrompt offers a balance of high performance and efficient use of resources - it achieves exceptional performance with significantly fewer additional task-conditioning parameters compared to other methods, amounting to $0.14\%$ of the parameters required, ultimately showcasing great computational efficiency. Through thorough experimentation on both In-Domain and Few-Shot settings for both NLP and CV tasks, HyperPrompt has consistently outperformed prominent multi-task learning architectures like Prompt-Tuning and HyperNetworks in both performance and parameter efficiency. The code for HyperPrompt is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/HyperPrompt.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. The algorithm's creation resolves an earlier study's limitation and the challenge of estimating network size in the presence of malicious nodes posed by King et al. Our algorithm's implications are considerable, given its utilization in active fingerprinting and malware detection in networks. The algorithm has efficacy in scenarios such as peer review, community detection, and resource allocation among trustworthy nodes. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. Our study indicates that this method surpasses the accuracy of the standard 3D Cartesian code by several orders of magnitude. Additionally, we find that solutions derived using algebraic Hamiltonian constraints match those from fully converged constraints, with a difference of less than 1% after 1000 iterations. Furthermore, we analyze the connection between the algebraic Hamiltonian constraint and the original Hamiltonian constraint through the conformal factor. We propose that this relationship can be represented by an Hamiltonian constraint with a 'nonlinear' source term, where the nonlinearity is controlled by the mean curvature. This new formulation may provide a useful framework for exploring new approaches to solving the Hamiltonian constraint. Lastly, we highlight that this method is not limited to numerical relativity simulations and can be applied to any context where the Hamiltonian constraint is solved for a conformally flat spacetime metric. This includes studies of quasistationary configurations, where the Hamiltonian constraint is used to determine the spacetime metric given its first derivatives. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and conducting finite-element simulations, our model reveals that the anomalous Nernst coefficient is comparable to that of the anomalous Hall coefficient in these materials. Our findings also indicate that the anomalous Nernst effect is significantly influenced by scattering mechanisms related to point and line defects, whereas the anomalous Hall effect is more sensitive to these defects as well as magnetic domain boundaries. This research offers a greater understanding of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskites and may contribute to the development of more precise measurement techniques. Our study also introduces a new method using finite-element simulations to analyze experimental data and may be applied to other research scenarios.

More research is needed to clarify this phenomenon.

Understanding and identifying functional materials rely heavily on imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy. Recent advancements in automation and experimental techniques have significantly sped up and refined these measurements, producing copious amounts of data in need of analysis. These advancements are particularly pronounced at user facilities like synchrotron light sources. To process and interpret large datasets quickly, machine learning methods are continually being developed for real-time use in conjunction with measurements. Despite these developments, users without machine learning expertise often face significant barriers to integrating this technology into their experiments. To overcome these obstacles, this work presents several examples of machine learning models designed for real-time analysis across multiple beamlines at the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS-II), with a focus on incorporating them into existing workflows to enable easy integration into experiments. By leveraging this framework, users can easily combine machine learning models with their existing workflows via the Bluesky Suite for data management and experimental orchestration. As demonstrated with data from multiple user experiments, these models have shown accuracy levels above 0.9 in predicting key material properties across various beamlines. To facilitate adoption, all models are openly available on GitHub, enabling further development and expansion to other applications. By integrating machine learning into their experiments, users can enhance their workflows with real-time data analysis, streamline their experiments, and accelerate their research. Moreover, integrating machine learning into the user workflow also facilitates the incorporation of these models into future user experiments. To this end, this work also outlines strategies for continuously improving these models with new data from future user experiments. By doing so, it enables machine learning to be a first-class citizen within the user workflow, allowing users to leverage its capabilities to analyze their data and make informed decisions during their experiment. By adopting this approach, users can accelerate their research, reduce their data volume, and improve their understanding of their materials. Ultimately, this work aims to inspire a broader adoption of machine learning across more user facilities and a wider range of applications, benefiting the entire materials research community. By sharing this framework with the community, we hope to facilitate a collective advancement of machine learning for materials research, enabling the collective benefits of machine learning to be shared across the entire research ecosystem. As such, we invite the community to join this effort by contributing their own machine learning models, helping to continuously improve these models with new data, and collaborating with us to explore new opportunities and challenges at user facilities. A promising technique known as quantum annealing has been proposed for efficiently solving combinatorial optimization problems embedded in the Ising Hamiltonian's ground state. This approach involves two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian, whose gradual transformation from driver to problem form allows researchers to find the target ground state. Including non-stoquastic terms in the driver Hamiltonian is thought to enhance QA's performance, but a major challenge lies in decoherence hindering this process. Surprisingly, we demonstrate that including anti-ferromagnetic interactions within the Hamiltonian results in catastrophic QA failure even with infinitely long annealing periods, a consequence stemming from block-diagonalization and symmetry-breaking. This issue is rectified, however, by applying a basic symmetry-preserving unitary transformation, resulting in an equivalent yet decoherence-resistant Hamiltonian that enables successful ground-state attainment through QA, even with finite annealing times. This finding suggests that quantum annealing's effectiveness may be impaired by hidden symmetries, and that explicitly addressing these symmetries could significantly enhance QA's performance in practice. Furthermore, we show that parity-preserving Hamiltonians, a special case with inherently hidden symmetries, can be transformed into their equivalent decoherence-resistant forms through a simple diagonalizing unitary operator, leading to successful ground-state attainment through QA. This implies that quantum annealing has the capacity to solve combinatorial optimization problems even in the presence of environmental disturbances, and that hidden symmetries pose a major obstacle in its practical application. Additionally, we demonstrate that solving such problems requires a deeper understanding of the underlying physics, including the role of non-stoquastic terms, decoherence, hidden symmetries, and symmetry-preserving unitary transformations. As a result, we distinguish between two primary types of quantum annealing, namely conventional QA and symmetry-aware QA, with the latter holding significant potential to overcome environmental hindrances and overcome hidden symmetry-related barriers in search for the ground state. Finally, we illustrate the symmetry-aware QA's applicability on solving genuine NP-hard problems, namely the exact cover problem, by showing that its solution can be obtained through QA on a single qubit, even in the presence of environmental disturbances, provided that the Hamiltonian's hidden symmetry is explicitly taken into consideration. This achievement demonstrates that certain NP-hard problems' solutions can be found using quantum annealing, and that this can be accomplished on a single qubit, offered that the underlying physics is thoroughly understood. This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory from 1921 to 1957, during the tenure of director Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who succeeded the lab's founder, Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn. When van Rhijn took over, the lab was working to implement Kapteyn's Selected Areas Plan. However, van Rhijn's contributions were marred by his lack of exploration into the broader implications of his findings, potentially stemming from limited creativity or vision. Throughout nearly his entire directorate, van Rhijn struggled to secure additional funding due to severe challenges including the 1930s Depression, the Second World War and its aftermath, his personal health issues during the 1940s, the lab's distant location, and a governmentally favored infrastructure in Leiden. Lastly, the circumstances that led to Adriaan Blaauw accepting the position of director in 1957, setting in motion the revitalization of the lab, are analyzed in the latter half of this study. The collection of documents related to van Rhijn's tenure also brings attention to several previously overlooked topics including his involvement in the Yerkes-Chicago-Kapteyn Astronomical Research, the construction of the 101/4 inch telescope, the introduction of photoelectric radial velocity measurements, the appointment of key scientists, the establishment of the General Catalogue of Radio Stars, and various publications resulting from the lab. The legacy of van Rhijn as director and his scientific contributions within the field of astronomy are also evaluated in this research. The study will be finalized with an examination of how the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory has evolved since the 1950s, particularly under the direction of Blaauw, and an assessment of the current status of the lab in relation to van Rhijn's tenure. The associated documents provide valuable historical context to the significant challenges the lab faced during van Rhijn's leadership and offer greater insight into his contributions and accomplishments. The extensive research for this essay has resulted in an enriched framework for understanding the history of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory and has highlighted various previously unexplored aspects of the field of astronomy. This investigation explores the impact of remote learning during the COVID pandemic on the ability of university students to keep up with the pace of instruction in a physics course. Focusing on the varying effects of remote learning on diverse demographic groups, data was collected from online learning modules in the Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters. Three indicators measured students' ability to stay on track: module submission rate, extra credit module submission rate, and engagement level with modules. Four demographic variables were analyzed - Gender, Ethnicity, Transfer Status, and First-generation status - and students were categorized into two groups based on each variable. Comparative analyses were conducted between all possible pairs of the demographic groups mentioned above. Results showed that remote learning led to a lower submission rate for modules and extra credit modules in the Fall 2020 semester. Furthermore, first-generation students demonstrated a significant increase in module submission rates during the pandemic, whereas students of color and female students exhibited no significant differences in their module submission rates. Nonetheless, students of color and female students displayed lower engagement levels with the modules. Transfer students showed no significant demographic group differences in either module or extra credit module submission rates. Two possible strategies emerged to support demographic groups affected by remote learning: providing additional technical support for students of color and female students to enhance their module engagement levels. Moreover, course instructors are advised to offer support tailored to the unique needs of university students learning remotely and to consider factors that might influence student engagement with online learning content. Additionally, course designers should prioritize the development of online learning content that caters to diverse demographic groups, in order to better equip instructors to teach students from various cultural backgrounds effectively. Lastly, considering the increased module submission rates from first-generation students, it is possible that remote learning provided first-generation students with a more accessible and less intimidating learning environment, allowing them to succeed at a higher rate. Consequently, it is recommended that future research be conducted to further understand the relationship between remote learning and the ability of students to keep up with the pace of instruction. Moreover, it is also advisable that in-depth analyses be conducted to uncover the underlying reasons behind demographic groups' varying responses to remote learning. Ultimately, this research lays the groundwork for exploring the effects of remote learning on university students' ability to keep up with the pace of instruction, and it paves the way for future investigations to delve deeper into the underlying causes behind the observed demographic group dynamics. Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. Ultimately, this study demonstrated the feasibility of using a non-invasive, high-resolution BCI for real-time gait decoding and management, paving the way for similar research in the future. In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to capture the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network learning, that not only captures complex data representations but also directed connections between variables. DECENNT's dynamic nature allows it to model the temporal changes in graph structure, going beyond classification capabilities, and is particularly suited for analyzing time-series data. Through extensive experiments on multiple datasets, our proposed method outperforms existing approaches, demonstrating superior performance on classification, link prediction, and temporal graph analysis tasks. The source code for DECENNT is available online at https://github.com/ghulame/DECENNT.
