Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns. The developed algorithm has potential applications in enhancing video capture technology and animal research, in addition to its use in creating realistic animation of biological entities. A cell's behavior during spreading and movement is influenced by various interrelated events that are activated by external stimuli at different scales. Due to the cell's living nature and complex response mechanisms, it is not sufficient to apply traditional material mechanics principles to it. Rather, cells comprise constituents with repeatable reactions such as contractility in single fibers and actin networks but also exhibit non-deterministic reorganization upon external stimuli. With consideration of this complexity, our goal is to develop a multi-faceted framework for modeling cellular spreading and locomotion, taking into account the movement of proteins across lipid membranes. Due to its computationally expensive solution, we will rely on a method that involves separating the macroscopic and microscopic scales to achieve faster solution times. As a result, we will first derive a macroscopic approach using dynamic equations for mean velocities and diffusion coefficients, and subsequently validate our model microscopically through examination of protein membrane dynamics and comparison with existing models of contractile fibers and actin networks. Ultimately, we will utilize our approach to investigate the cellular spreading and locomotion patterns when contractility is unevenly distributed and when fibers and actin networks are subjected to different external forces. Overall, our approach provides a flexible framework that allows for examination of contractile cells spreading and moving under various conditions, and it paves the way for future studies of cells interacting with their surroundings at different scales. As an example, we show how an asymmetry in surface adhesion can cause a symmetrical cell to spread asymmetrically. Additionally, we illustrate how uneven contractility distribution can give rise to complex cell movement patterns. Finally, we also demonstrate that strongly polarized cells can spread and move more easily than those with weaker contractility patterns. Overall, our approach highlights the significance of considering multiple facets of cellular behavior when studying cell spreading and movement.

The unique combination of decentralization, redundancy, and pseudo-anonymity in public blockchain platforms has made them appealing for cryptocurrency adoption. However, these same features have enabled cybercriminals to exploit vulnerabilities in blockchain technology and deceive users through social engineering to execute malicious plans. Existing methods for identifying malicious actors typically rely on transaction history from specific wallet addresses, but often neglect the underlying money trails. In contrast, we propose an innovative approach centered on money trail analysis, incorporating new features to detect suspicious activities within cryptocurrency blockchains. Specifically, we investigate the cyclic behavior present in temporal transaction graphs within a blockchain, focusing on uncovering hidden patterns. By applying our methods to the Ethereum blockchain, we reveal distinct cyclic patterns indicative of malicious activities such as gambling, phishing, and money laundering, as well as identify two specific temporal cyclic transfers. Notably, our approach is versatile and adaptable to other cryptocurrency blockchains with suitable modifications tailored to the characteristics of the underlying cryptocurrency. By unveiling the underlying mechanisms driving malicious transactions, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in providing actionable insights to prevent the recurrence of these activities. Furthermore, we showcase the feasibility of our approach by applying it to the Ethereum, Bitcoin, and Litecoin blockchain platforms. In doing so, we highlight the advantages and limitations of our method, and suggest potential directions for future research in this area. Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models. Notably, we found that decoding skills learned in simulated environments can be transferred to actual physical setups, significantly improving performance compared to conventional maximum likelihood estimation in various scenarios. Furthermore, we found that decoding based on estimated noise models rather than actual decoded error patterns leads to even greater gains in efficiency. Finally, we explored the application of these techniques to the decoding of other topological codes, such as the stabilizer code, and found similar success. This work offers a novel approach to developing robust and adaptable decoding methods for continuous-time quantum error correction codes.

Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. The approach is shown to exceed the standard quantum precision limit, without needing highly complex quantum states and with greater scalability and practicality. The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011. These findings reveal that cold nuclear matter has negligible effects on $d$$+$Au collisions. A notable disparity exists in hadron production between Au$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions. Hadrons with high momentum fractions are suppressed in Au$+$Au, whereas those with lower momentum fractions show increased yields, exceeding $p$$+$$p$ collisions. This excess, observed at large angles and low hadron $p_T$, is more pronounced for hadrons linked to lower-momentum direct photons, indicating an increased response of the medium to deposited energy. The excess's magnitude suggests that a significant fraction of the energy emitted by the medium is carried by hadrons with lower momentum fractions. This result implies that the parton transport model needs an additional mechanism to accurately reproduce the observed hadron distributions. The excess may be attributed to hadronization involving multiple hard partons or interactions between partons and the medium's electromagnetic component. The excess's properties provide a key signature for studying the medium's response in heavy ion collisions and parton dynamics with direct photons as a probe. The excess's angle distribution is consistent with the Woods-Saxon distribution, with an $r^2$ scale that increases with the square of the direct photon's momentum. Over time, the trend of companies adopting remote working has been on the rise, leading many to adapt Agile methodologies such as Scrum to cope with distributed teams. However, the global shift to fully remote working brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic was a unprecedented phenomenon. This research involves a two-phase, multi-method approach. Initially, it investigates how working from home affected Scrum practitioners through a qualitative survey. Subsequently, it proposes and empirically tests a theoretical framework using PLS-SEM with data from a sample of 200 software engineers who collaborated on Scrum projects from home. Our results demonstrate the reliability of all key constructs and the validity of all hypotheses, while also highlighting the advantages of combining home working and Scrum practices through an IPMA analysis. Notably, supporting employees' inherent needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness is crucial in the remote working context. Our findings indicate that both home working and Scrum use contribute to project success, with Scrum playing a mediating role. Interestingly, our data show that home working can have a positive effect on project success when combined with certain Scrum practices, particularly Agile planning and review. These findings provide valuable insights for practitioners and researchers alike, addressing the current Scrum and home working paradigm shift. Our study also paves the way for further research into the dynamics of home working, Scrum, and project success. By doing so, it may contribute to improved methodologies and supportive environments that facilitate successful projects in a remote working context. This in turn could lead to better management of resources, risks, stakeholders, and technology, ultimately resulting in greater project success. This is particularly pertinent for companies that intend to continue adopting Scrum even after the pandemic, as it may help them navigate upcoming challenges. Our proposed theoretical framework is already being put into practice by companies like Infacta and Mobiplan in Brazil. This work utilizes the principles of power control optimization from information theory to investigate the extremal gain of power control under an average interference constraint in a multi-user, multi-access channel. We derive the extremal gain for any number of users, finding it to be $2^{2n}$, where $n$ is the number of users. We also determine that this gain cannot be achieved through uniform power distribution. Furthermore, we examine the effect of an average interference constraint on power control, determining that the extremal gain under this constraint is $2^{2n}$ as well. We establish that the optimal power control strategy distributes power non-uniformly among users, with some users transmitting at higher powers than others. We find that the optimal power control can be achieved through time division among users, even when the number of users exceeds the number of time slots available. We also determine that the extremal gain can be expressed as the product of the gain from optimizing power among users and the gain from optimizing power across time slots. We establish that the optimal power control can be expressed as a function of its own output distribution, further broadening its applicability. Finally, we explore upper bounds on the extremal gain through coding schemes, including an approach that achieves near-optimal performance under certain conditions. These findings provide a foundation for further investigation into the extremal gain in various information-theoretic channels.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained from traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Therefore, our multiple-time-step integration algorithm is an efficient and accurate solution for simulating complex particle flows. Additionally, our results suggest that artificially lengthening collision time steps may not be suitable for modeling the flexibility of particles. Our algorithm is highly versatile and can be applied to various particle collision models by modifying the sub-time steps for particle collisions. Furthermore, our algorithm facilitates the simulation of particle collisions with multiple time steps, and we suggest that future models should be developed with collision time steps that accurately reflect the actual collision time. Our algorithm has been made publicly available on a reputable open-source repository for the benefit of the computational fluid dynamics community. One proof draws upon number theory principles, specifically focusing on the properties of integers generated by the formula $f(x)=x^2+x+1$, their divisibility characteristics, and the implications of Dirichlet's Theorem. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. Ultimately, the robot attained its desired height within 10% of error in both cases. This study demonstrates the feasibility of precise force control for a one-legged robot jumping on a granular surface with rapidly changing ground reaction forces. This work has broader implications for the control of legged robots on other types of deformable terrain. It also highlights the importance of considering the interaction between the robot and its surroundings in the design of its movement patterns. This is critical for the safe and effective operation of robots in environments that are not carefully prepared. This research is an initial step towards addressing one of the most complex challenges in legged locomotion research and could be expanded to explore a wider range of robot movements on deformable terrain. This could ultimately enable the development of more practical and versatile robots for use in real-world applications. In this paper, the contact interaction model is applied to the study of meson elastic form factors. Quark and meson dressed masses are derived from gap and Bethe-Salpeter equations, with a specific focus on mesons comprised of distinct flavor quarks. An analysis of the generic $M\gamma \to M$ scattering process is performed. Furthermore, calculations for the charge radii of various meson types, including scalars, pseudoscalars, vectors, and axial-vectors, yield explicit elastic form factor values. These results demonstrate the capability of the contact interaction model to predict meson form factors with precision. A notable finding is the exact expression of a ratio of form factors for different meson types, leading to the derivation of a relationship that holds for all flavor combinations of mesons. This study provides a theoretical framework that can be utilized to examine the internal structure of mesons through the investigation of form factors in deep exclusive reactions. As an example, calculations are presented for the $J/\psi$ photon scattering, involving the calculation of a form factor for the $J/\psi \gamma$ system, which is crucial in explaining the observed width of the $J/\psi$ spectrum. Additionally, this study enables the investigation of how the internal structure of mesons is modified by temperature changes, as indicated by changes to the meson's root mean square size. Owing to the application of the Feshbach-Villars formalism, this study is also capable of examining the influence of the ground state and excited quark and meson configurations on the calculated form factors. It is shown that the contact interaction model can effectively replicate the outcomes of the DSE approach for the same set of quark and meson configurations. As an extension to previous studies, this work investigates the impact of distinct flavor quarks on the size of mesons, as well as the internal structure of mesons composed of heavy quarks. Although previous research has thoroughly analyzed the complex interactions of a liquid droplet under an electrical influence in air, the droplet's effects on the surrounding gas phase have been underrepresented. A notable phenomenon arises when the droplet undergoes significant oscillations, induced by the presence of a resonating electric field. The air circulation patterns that emerge as a result create localized aerodynamic forces that impede the droplet's ability to attract particulate matter in its vicinity, especially when the droplet is immersed in an aerosol cloud. The interplay between the droplet and its surroundings sparks curiosity in scientists, who see the potential for further discoveries in this two-phase system, encompassing both gas and liquid components, especially with regards to the transport of heat and mass. This study investigates how the droplet's oscillatory behavior affects its interaction with the surrounding air, including the circulation patterns that develop, the formation of aerosol particles on the droplet's surface, and the associated heat and mass transfer processes. The investigation employs a combination of numerical methods, specifically the Navier-Stokes equations for airflow and the Reynolds-Navier-Stokes equations for aerosol particle circulation, along with the Darcy equation for flow through the droplet's surface and the Nusselt-Hofmann equation for heat transfer. The study demonstrates that oscillatory airflow around the droplet contributes to enhanced surface tension-driven flow, elevates the Nusselt number, and accelerates the mass transfer coefficient in regions with recirculating airflow, ultimately facilitating the transfer of heat and mass, allowing the droplet to maintain its shape and position in the aerosol cloud. Notably, the findings indicate that the droplet's oscillatory behavior allows it to interact with the surrounding air in a way that facilitates its own survival, thereby granting the droplet a degree of autonomy in its environment. This study also explores multiple-frequency electrical stimulation of the droplet, revealing that the circulation patterns that develop in response can direct airborne particles to specific locations, thereby potentially enabling the control of particulate matter in the surrounding air. Ultimately, this study highlights the potential for the controlled oscillation of droplets in air to be used in the management of airborne particles, the directed transfer of heat and mass, and the targeted placement of particles in the surrounding environment. This could potentially enable novel methods for the controlled delivery of medications in aerosol form. Effective communication through language cannot be fully achieved without considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, even the best-performing model (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) managed only 42% accuracy according to our consistency metric, significantly lagging behind the 81% achieved by human evaluators. In a bid to fuel further NLP innovations, we publicly release our dataset, along with comprehensive evaluations involving fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot scenarios. Our research underscores the pressing need for NLP models that can accurately process negation and implicitly suggests that contemporary models have not fully grasped this fundamental language aspect. Consequently, our CONDAQA dataset is poised to drive significant advancements in models capable of effectively handling language's negation for improved communication. It is available at this link https://github.com/huggingface/datasets/tree/ea3d61c3e78f4d6d6c5b9c8f6f8f6f8f6f8f6f4#condaqa. It is also worth highlighting that the challenges posed by CONDAQA are not limited to NLP, but rather they reflect broader difficulties in artificial intelligence that need to be addressed to create models capable of emulating human-like reasoning and understanding of language. It is our hope that this dataset will serve as a catalyst for the community to participate in finding a solution to these challenges. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks at a near web-scale size, as evidenced by our experiments generating hierarchies for networks of up to 10 million documents, and specifically improving upon existing methods in terms of precision and performance in a range of tasks and datasets. Furthermore, we've integrated HDTM into a prototype application, InfraViewer, demonstrating the practical applications of this approach. InfraViewer enables users to explore and navigate the hierarchical structure of Wikipedia, revealing hidden patterns and connections within the data. This is accompanied by a detailed evaluation and user feedback on the effectiveness of the system in identifying key topics and relationships. The results of our experiments and user feedback have guided the ongoing development of HDTM and InfraViewer, and we invite users to contribute to the discovery of hidden knowledge within these networks by visiting our InfraViewer site at infraviewer.org. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a significant improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. Additionally, this study demonstrates that the same quench and annealing dynamics share a common steady-state regime in the deep asymptotic limit, despite their differing starting conditions and temporal development. This discovery highlights the robustness of quantum annealing and suggests that the underlying physics and dynamical patterns that govern the equilibrium and non-equilibrium phases of the Hamiltonian could provide valuable insights for improving the performance of quantum annealing algorithms.

Conformance checking focuses on comparing modeled process behavior to observed process behavior from actual event data. A recent technique, called alignments, identifies and measures deviations between process executions and predefined reference models, pinpointing the discrepancies in process traces. Notably, alignments require entire or initial segments of process runs from start to finish; this paper explores new methods to analyze partial process runs and assesses these methods with real-world event data. We also examine alternative measures of conformance and apply these methods to a notable case study. Our research reveals that using partial alignments and conformance measures offers more flexible and practical conformance checking tools. These findings have the potential to make conformance checking a more established process mining technique. We introduce an open-source implementation of these methods, called PaAl, and present an analysis of partial alignments, including new methods for assessing conformance and guiding the exploration of process runs. PaAl is compatible with the established conformance checking technique, called alignments, and is designed for use with process models and event data. We also present an evaluation of PaAl with process runs and conformance measures in relation to process models. Furthermore, PaAl is integrated with the established process mining technique, called Dynamic-Declarative Process Discovery, enabling the discovery of process models from process runs and the assessment of these models against actual process executions. Ultimately, PaAl and its integrated features have the potential to enhance the discovery and assessment of process models. We demonstrate the capabilities of PaAl with an prominent case study. We invite users to explore and apply PaAl in conjunction with process models and event data. We also invite feedback and suggestions for further development and application of PaAl. Finally, we invite users to participate in the evaluation and extension of PaAl with additional process runs and conformance measures. Ultimately, we believe that PaAl has the potential to contribute to the advancement and increased adoption of conformance checking as a process mining technique. Starting from a reliable two-dimensional model with two bands derived from
$d$ and $s$ orbital types for infinite layered nickelates, we investigate the
extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to a mixture of filled and weakly
coupled bands and results in a more complex, variably filled $d$-band and
electrons in the $s$-band now being localized by the more filled ones and
thus also becoming insulating. 
Interestingly, a simple one-band Hubbard model cannot capture these two cases
of the nickelates' physics. 
Additionally, a comparison with available experimental data shows that the
mildly screening case corresponds to synthesized thin films of the material,
while the strongly screening case represents bulk samples. 
A simple di-dimensional Hubbard model then emerges as an appropriate
simplification for this two different physics situations.

This paper examines the long-term behavior of the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation under weak collisions in an infinite space near a global equilibrium, specifically focusing on soft potentials. By analyzing initial conditions with sufficiently small magnitudes regardless of the collision rate, the study reveals various dynamic processes arising from the combination of the phase-mixing/dispersive effects of the transport operator and the singular collision operator. In regions where high-frequency fluctuations are prevalent, an accelerated decay phenomenon is observed, characterized by an exponential decrease in a time scale that inversely correlates with the collision rate and the frequency magnitude. In contrast, for regions where fluctuations are minimal, Taylor dispersion leads to an accelerated decay governed by the inverse of the frequency squared, multiplied by the collision rate. Moreover, this research proves the existence of almost uniform phase mixing estimates. Consequently, for observable quantities such as density, almost uniform bounds in terms of the collision rate are derived for decay rates, influenced by Landau damping and dispersive decay processes. Notably, this research implies improved regularity criteria for solutions to the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation under weak collisions. Additionally, the analysis reveals the existence of solutions exhibiting persistent oscillatory behavior over an infinite time period. Almost uniform estimates for the amplitude of fluctuations are provided, along with condition-dependent bounds on the decay time. Furthermore, this research identifies distinct dynamic processes arising from the interplay between the transport operator, the singular collision operator, and the initial data, resulting in accelerated decay phenomena driven by Landau damping, dispersive effects, phase mixing, Taylor dispersion, and stochastic separation processes. Consequently, this work establishes improved bounds on decay rates, influenced by the collision rate, and provides regularity criteria for solutions to the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation under weak collisions. This approach uses a large dataset of around 150 million observations, enabling the derivation of wind-speed dependent wave-slope probabilities up to high speeds. Our method validates previous research on wave-slope probability distributions and provides a more precise definition. Analyzing the dimensions of wave-slope probability distributions, we identify how parameters such as skewness, kurtosis, and correlation with wind speed behave in relation to other factors like wind intensity, current, and gravity. Our results show how wave-slope probability distributions evolve with wind speed, revealing how larger waves become more prominent at higher wind speeds. Additionally, our methodology allows for a more detailed examination of wave characteristics in different wind conditions, which can inform numerical model development. Furthermore, our study reveals how wave-slope probabilities are influenced by factors such as wind direction, being greatest at 180 degrees, and how long waves survive before breaking. Our approach also examines local extremes of the wave slope, which are highly scarce probability occurrences that are greatly affected by the presence of winds over mountains and by currents. Initially, the Lawrence-Doniach and interlayer tunneling models were the prominent theoretical concepts to describe cuprate superconductors by connecting CuO planes through Josephson coupling. Yet, the discovery of larger than predicted interlayer magnetic penetration depths in these materials raised issues with the tunneling model's validity. The emergence of planar stripes and charge domains enabled alternative Josephson coupling theories. Our study finds the average intralayer interaction to be greater than interlayer coupling and comparable to condensation energy, ultimately yielding long-range phase order-driven superconductivity. As an outcome, the relationship between the square of interlayer and intralayer penetration depths to the respective resistivity ratios exhibits proportionality near the superconducting transition, corroborated by multiple measurements. The proportionality is further analyzed to derive the ratio of the condensation energy to the Josephson coupling strength. This research indicates that planar stripe and charge domain physics hold significant potential to resolve long-standing puzzles in cuprate superconductors. The proposed theory is tested against established evidence, including the doping dependence of the superconducting gap, the shape of the superconducting dome, and the variation of superconducting properties with crystallographic orientation. Ultimately, this study suggests that the planar stripe and charge domain physics provide an avenue for resolving persistent issues in cuprate superconductors. The proposed theory is examined against established findings, including the doping dependence of the superconducting gap, the shape of the superconducting dome, and the variation of superconducting properties with crystallographic orientation. The findings from our Josephson coupling theory may have a broader impact on our understanding of other superconducting materials with multiple condensates and long-range phase order. The proposed model is also applied to describe the superconducting transition in La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$ and Bi$_{2}$CuO$_{4$ by considering planar stripe and charge domain physics. Ultimately, this research provides a theoretical framework for describing the superconducting transition in these materials through long-range phase order-driven Josephson coupling and is compatible with the existing evidence obtained from multiple measurements. The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index within neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars.  By simulating a smooth hadron-quark phase transition with different interface tension values, we found the expected sound velocity behavior may not be a unique signature of a phase transition, also occurring in a direct phase transition from neutron to quark matter which results in the sound velocity being only slightly affected. Conversely, the adiabatic index shows significant variation following a phase transition, demonstrating an identifiable characteristic that can distinguish between quark stars and neutron stars, and thus potentially facilitate the direct detection of quark stars through gravitational waves. This could be accomplished by detecting the gravitational wave signal with sufficient accuracy to determine the compact star's mass and radius, thereby identifying its equation of state. This research highlights the potential for gravitational waves to reveal the internal structure of compact stars, providing insights into the fundamental physics of dense matter. Additionally, we found that the characteristic sound velocity behavior may not be a unique indicator of a quark star, as it can also occur in stars with a neutron star core surrounded by a quark matter crust, which results in the sound velocity following a typical hadron quark phase transition relation at the interface but with an increased density at the star's surface. This specific type of star, with its core and crust, could also be identified through the characteristic sound velocity behavior. However, determining the maximum-weight Tai mapping between two unordered trees is a well-known NP-complete problem. We now introduce a contrasting concept - anti Tai mapping - as a binary relationship between two trees. An anti Tai mapping, defined as the subset $M$ of $V_1\times V_2$, excludes any node pairs $(x,y)$ and $(x',y')$ that would conflict with each other's ancestral hierarchy, given that $x<x'$ indicates $x$ is an ancestor of $x'$. Calculating the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping plays a significant role in solving the maximum-weight Tai mapping problem through integer programming by applying the cutting plane method. We provide an efficient algorithm for computing a maximum-weight anti Tai mapping when one tree is a path. Additionally, we show that by applying a restricted version of anti Tai mapping, where nodes sharing the same path as their ancestors must not correspond, we can obtain a polynomially computable lower bound for the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping between any two trees. We also present an efficient algorithm for solving this restricted version directly on unordered trees within $O(|V_1|^2|V_2|^2)$ time. This research addresses the challenge of protecting machine learning (ML) model outputs from an untrusted client and a semi-reliable server. The goal is for the client to obtain the inference output while the server learns nothing. Although initial studies by Lehmkuhl and Chandran have shown significant advancements, there remains a considerable gap between current solutions and practical implementations. To address this issue, our proposal SIMC 2.0 maintains the foundation of Chandran's work while improving the efficiency of linear and non-linear layers within the ML model. Key innovations include a customized coding technique for matrix and vector operations that reduces expensive rotation computations. Furthermore, SIMC 2.0 reduces the size of garbled circuits used for non-linear calculations and introduces an alternative lightweight protocol. As a result, our experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains for linear computations (up to 17.4 times faster), reduced computation and communication overhead in non-linear layers (by at least 1.3 times), and improved overall runtime by 2.3 to 4.3 times. Our evaluations using pre-trained ResNet-18 and Inception V3 models indicate SIMC 2.0 achieves comparable accuracy to Chandran's ChandranSIMC protocol while outperforming other secure ML solutions. In particular, our proposal surpasses the ChandranSIMC protocol by 1-10% in accuracy and outperforms other solutions by 1-20% in terms of runtime. Our implementation and evaluation are conducted using the ABY3 framework and the TensorFlow framework on a single GPU. In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging problem, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. 

This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues, especially in complex graph topologies. A random walk is used to visit different nodes, making local model updates at each stop, and the objective is to determine the optimal number of visits. A random walk learning algorithm is trained and tested on a cancer classification problem using the Mutag graph, and results show it outperforms a central server-based learning algorithm. A random walk learning algorithm can be viewed as a form of distributed learning, where each node makes a local update based on its own data and contributes to the global model through the random walk process. This method explicitly addresses issues of data imbalance and node isolation by visiting each node a certain number of times during random walks. 

A key contribution of this paper involves establishing a bound on the convergence rate of these random walk learning algorithms, taking into account various factors including the number of random walk steps, the mixing time of the walk, and the node degrees in the graph. This bound is expressed in terms of the spectral norm of a matrix that captures the connectivity and data imbalance characteristics of the graph. 

To determine the optimal number of random walk steps, an algorithm based on the exponential multi-armed bandit problem is proposed and shown to achieve a near-optimal regret bound, directly translating to near-optimal model performance when the true number of steps is known. 

Interestingly, even with suboptimal random walk step sizes, the algorithm can converge at a rate of $\Omega(1/\sqrt{T})$ in terms of regret, directly translating to a $\Omega(1/\sqrt{T})$ convergence rate for the model, given that the random walk step sizes are not too large. 

All theoretical results are accompanied by corresponding empirical studies, validating the analysis and providing further insights into the random walk learning algorithm. 

Finally, this paper closes with discussions on potential future directions and challenges in Federated Learning, including solving non-concave optimization problems and handling more complex data distributions.

A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed segmentations. This approach belongs to the category of adaptive data regularization techniques that reduce overfitting when working with highly confident labelled data. The method has several advantages over alternative techniques such as adversarial and generative models, primarily due to its minimal computational requirements. Evaluations using publicly available MRI datasets - specifically ACDC and MMWHS - demonstrate that this proposed technique outperforms existing semi-supervised models, with source code available on GitHub.

To gain a deeper understanding of the performance and lifespan of materials, 
it's crucial to assess their atomic disorder levels. To this end, we use a unique
approach that leverages graph neural networks to create an interpretable disorder 
metric, effectively capturing local atomic configuration variability across the
solid to liquid phase spectrum. This methodical approach is tested with three
models featuring different disorder levels, including interfaces between solid 
and liquid phases, multi-crystalline microstructures, and grain boundaries, 
using elemental aluminum as a prime example. Our study demonstrates how our 
approach tracks the space-time progression of interfaces and provides a precise 
definition of the boundary between order and disorder. Furthermore, we show 
how our disorder fields' physics-preserving gradients can be utilized to explain 
and predict the behavior and failure of materials. Overall, our framework serves 
as an accessible and universally applicable solution for analyzing the complex 
atomic structures within materials. 

Also, we have launched a public Python package named PyDisorderFields for this 
study, which is openly available at this link: https://github.com/fakhrilriza/PyDisorderFields. This package includes graph neural networks that can be used to create disorder fields from a variety of atomic structures, as well as other tools for processing and analyzing atomic data. It is possible to use this package for training models from scratch or for applying pre-trained models to various materials scenarios. For more information, please see the README file at this link: https://github.com/fakhrilriza/PyDisorderFields.

Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Omega$ and is independently distributed according to a mixing distribution $g(\theta)$. The Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimator (GMLE) is a method for estimating the mixing distribution $g(\cdot)$ based on a sample of $n$ independent observations of $Y_i, i=1,\ldots,n$ with a corresponding observation of the parameter $\theta_i$ for each $Y_i$. 

When the parameter $\theta$ has a specific range and is independent of $Y$, the GMLE can be obtained by maximizing the likelihood function $L(g;\mathbf{y},\boldsymbol{\theta})=\prod_{i=1}^{n}f(y_i|\theta_i)g(\theta_i)$ over the set $\Omega$. 

In this paper, we relax the condition that the data must be independent and instead consider a non-standard mixing model where the dependency between the variables is represented by a random graph $\Gamma_n$, specifically an Erdos-Renyi graph. 

For a finite and positive value of $p$, we establish an explicit formula for the GMLE of the mixing distribution $g(\cdot)$ and provide an alternate expression that is more suitable for simulation purposes. 

We establish the consistency of the GMLE by maximizing the likelihood function when the dependency between the variables follows a specific distribution, and we establish the same consistency result for a broader class of distribution. 

Finally, we provide a simulation to compare the performance of the estimated GMLE with the true GMLE. 

This research is relevant to a previous study discussed in Zhao and Kalisch (2016) which explored a similar mixing model but with a different estimation approach. 

The proposed method for estimation has several advantages, including the ability to handle complex dependencies between variables and providing better performance than the previous study's method for certain types of distribution. 

The new approach for estimating the mixing distribution can be applied to any distribution that belongs to the exponential family. 

The results from the simulation indicate that the proposed method yields better performance than the previous study's method for certain types of distribution, and the two methods perform equally well for other types of distribution. 

The code and data used in the simulation are available for replication purposes. 

The proposed method can be extended to accommodate time series data and the estimation of non-parametric mixing distributions.

Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation settings, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. We have publicly released PyKT and the associated research results at https://pykt.org/. We invite researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us and contribute to the advancement of deep learning knowledge tracing.

Ten years ago, at the inaugural PxTP workshop, veriT's proof format debuted,  
marking a significant milestone for the solver. Since then, veriT has evolved  
into a prominent SMT solver utilizing the format, with many other solvers  
gradually adopting it for various applications beyond SMT solving in its  
extended form. We review the development of veriT's proof format, highlighting  
its design principles, key advancements, and widespread adoption, as well as  
discuss its broader implications and the future prospects for the format in the  
field of formal verification and beyond. We also present an adaptable checking  
framework designed to accommodate various proof formats, including those for the  
PxTP benchmark, with the source code publicly available for further customization.

Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents and diacritical marks to make the transfer easier, and this strategy proved successful. Our best model, with only the alphabet modification, achieved a 12% reduction in word error rate (WER) compared to a baseline system trained from scratch on the same data, thereby demonstrating the potential for easier ASR deployments in language-specific domains. Additionally, we discovered that adapting the English model to Czech resulted in smaller model size without a decline in performance, indicating this approach may lead to other favorable outcomes. Furthermore, our results showed that the simplified alphabet transfer enabled the model to generalize to various Czech pronunciation variants, suggesting it could be a useful pre-processing technique for similar low-density character sets. We also found that WER continued to decrease with more-fine-grained pronunciation dictionaries, and that the method worked across multiple Czech dialects. Our study proposes that a previous observation made by Belle and BaBar of a complex spin state at around $1500$, which had been interpreted as a single entity or combination of multiple spin states, is now identified as the $\rho^0(1450)$ resonance reported by LHCb in recent times.  Employing a perturbative QCD approach, we calculate the di-kaon distribution amplitudes from LHCb data, specifically from quasi-two-body $B^{\pm} \to \pi^{\pm}K^+K^-$ decays containing the $\rho^0(1450)$ resonance.  The calculated distributions can be used to explain BaBar's measurements of the $B^+ \to K^+K^-K^-$ decay at an invariant mass $M(K^+K^-)\sim 1.5$ GeV, showing the contribution from $\rho^0(1450)$. Moreover, the observed structure around $1.5$ GeV in $B^+ \to K^+K_S K_S$ spectrum, where $\rho^0(1450)$ cannot contribute due to Bose-Einstein statistics, is accounted for by an $S$-wave contribution alone.  The theoretical estimates of branching fractions and/or direct $CP$ asymmetries for $B^{\pm} \to \pi^{\pm}K^+K^-$, $B^+ \to K^+K^-K^-$ and $B^0 \to K^0 K^- K^+$ decays are presented for verification with upcoming experiments at LHCb and Belle-II.  Therefore, we recommend experimental validation through a more precise analysis of relevant data by these research colleagues.  Additionally, the theoretical estimates of the observed structures in $B^+ \to K^+K_S K_S$ and $B^0 \to K^0 K_S K_S$ spectra will be useful in determining the residual $K^*K^*$ wave function, which has not been well-determined up to now. Recent research suggests combining the Swampland program with dark energy's scarcity could predict the presence of an additional dimension with a characteristic scale of a micron. We've investigated how this extra dimension affects the rate of Hawking radiation in black holes and found that their perception of it causes the radiation to slow down. We discuss how this affects the possibility that dark matter consists of primordial black holes and estimate a suitable mass range of 10^14 to 10^21 grams, which expands on the existing four-dimensional theory's scope by three orders of magnitude in the lower mass range. Furthermore, primordial black holes with a mass of approximately 10^12 grams may be responsible for the Galactic 511 keV gamma-ray line, assuming they make up a very small fraction of total dark matter. Conditions are also identified that would allow such black holes to survive for a significant fraction of the universe's age. Finally, we examine the effect on black hole formation in the early universe and find that primordial black holes with a mass of 10^12 grams require a rolling flat monopole problem to occur naturally. The extra dimension could also reduce the needed primordial density perturbations by a few orders of magnitude, making such black holes more feasible within the context of the effective four-dimensional theory. The presence of the extra dimension also raises the minimum spin-invariant density perturbation required to form primordial black holes by two orders of magnitude. We also explore the potential for primordial black holes to resolve the Hubble tension if they constitute a significant fraction of dark energy, independent of their relevance to the 511 keV line. We anticipate future quantum gravity experiments, specifically table-top labs and gravitational wave detectors, to provide crucial insights that could confirm or refute the feasibility of this model. The additional dimension's effects on gravitational waves could serve as a crucial signpost for such experiments to follow in their quest for a unified theory of gravity. The potential for the extra dimension to be explored through Hawking radiation in primordial black hole binaries is also highlighted. Ultimately, investigating the intersection of the Swampland program, dark energy's scarcity, and the properties of primordial black holes could yield fresh insights into our fundamental theoretical framework. The proposed model serves as an exemplar for this intersection, offering a range of predictions and hypotheses that can be tested by various experiments, either confirming or contradicting the presence of an additional dimension with a characteristic scale of a micron. A novel algorithm for precise force control in series elastic actuators is introduced in this paper, centered on a cutting-edge force estimation technique called the transmission force observer. This approach was developed to enhance the inaccurate force readings caused by the nonlinear elastic transmission and sensor measurement errors of the actuators' deformation sensors. The study first critiques conventional SEA force sensing methods, examining their stochastic properties that ultimately enable accurate force control through the proposed transmission force observer. A critical parameter derived from system analysis is key in optimizing the performance of the force-controlled system, guiding the achievement of the optimal outcome. This developed algorithm is successfully validated using actual SEA hardware setup for its effectiveness. The outcome shows that the estimated forces closely match the actual forces, achieving a notable reduction in mean error and overall system performance improvement. Moreover, it is demonstrated that the proposed approach outperforms conventional force sensing methods under varying operation conditions, indicating its suitability for SEAs across diverse applications and scenarios. Lastly, the developed algorithm is found to accelerate the achievement of desired forces in actual SEA experiments, indicating its potential to accelerate SEA system performance. Through thorough theoretical and experimental analysis, this study proves that the transmission force observer can accurately estimate forces in SEAs, offering a practical solution for precise force control in compliant mechanical systems. This breakthrough paves the way for the safe and reliable use of SEAs in collaborative and sensitive environments. Additionally, this development is expected to speed up the adoption of SEA technology in robotics and mechatronics. As a complementary aspect, the study also explores advanced algorithms for optimal SEA performance, highlighting the potential for future work in this area. As a byproduct of this study, high-fidelity force-sensing software for SEAs has been developed and made publicly available for the benefit of the robotics community. This software, named FSEN, is an open-source MATLAB tool that can be used to model, analyze, simulate, and estimate the forces within compliant mechanical systems, in addition to displaying the sensed forces. A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surface of support, we see that its breaking pattern changes constantly based on the rate at which we are stretching it. This effect is caused by the ongoing competition between two speed factors: the rate at which the particles reassemble, which is influenced by forces like viscosity and surface tension, and the rate at which neighboring particles move apart due to the expansion of the surrounding fluid. This balance of forces ultimately decides the length of clusters within the raft. A mathematical model that takes this competition into account predicts the breakdown patterns we see in experiments. Additionally, this model helps clarify the distinction between two previously confused terms in material science: "thermodynamic" and "dynamic" phase transitions. Due to its simplicity, our model can also be simulated on any computer and may be used to create more realistic visual effects in video games and other applications. This could involve stretching a particle raft to create crack patterns or allowing user input to control the movement of particles in a cluster. Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA: a new algorithm for offline policy evaluation.  Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in sparse methods and matches the accuracy of its precise equivalent while successfully being applied to underwater navigation.  Our approach also has a model-based variant known as SPGP-TD, and with minimal modifications, this variant is obtainable.  Our findings are backed by extensive simulations and actual underwater robot learning experiments.  Our code is available online at the designated link.  We also include a detailed analysis of the computational aspects of our algorithm. This paper explores the concept of sorting networks consisting of comparators with more than two input values. We focus on the interplay between three parameters: the comparator arity (k), the number of inputs (n), and the depth (d). Our model has significant relevance, as studying it helps us comprehend the inner workings of sorting networks and its connections to the construction of recursive and efficient circuits for sorting. In particular, we aim to identify the lowest required comparator arity (k) for sorting networks with limited depth. Through our research, we found lower bounds on the comparator arity (k) for sorting networks with constant depth. Specifically, we found the smallest k that allows a sorting network with depth d = 1, 2, 3, or 4. We found that k is equal to n for d = 1 and 2. We also discovered that k is equal to n/2 (rounded up) for d = 3. Interestingly, we found that k is equal to n^2/3 when d = 4, indicating that it grows sublinearly in n. Notably, we found this sublinear behavior occurs earlier in sorting networks than in majority circuits, which require d = 3 to achieve k = n^2/3. We believe our research will contribute to ongoing discussions regarding the capabilities of sorting networks and may shed light on additional theoretical questions related to k, n, and d. Additionally, our results on deep sorting networks may be of interest to researchers in machine learning and computational neuroscience. Lastly, our work lays the groundwork for further exploration of our found k values and may be used to improve existing lower-bound techniques. Our study offers concrete answers to open questions posed in prior studies and lays the foundation for additional research in this area. Our results are already leading to new questions that merit further investigation. We have a particular interest in understanding k values for d > 4 and the implications of our findings for comparative arithmetic and the broader field of boolean circuits. Galactic mergers significantly shape galaxy evolution, especially those involving massive galaxy combinations that significantly alter galaxy morphology. This study focuses on how magnetic fields affect major mergers involving abundant gas, using high-resolution simulations to examine the impact. Conducting this analysis within a realistic cosmic framework, this study employs advanced simulations to compare magnetic field effects on merging galaxies with and without magnetic field influence. Unlike previous non-realistic simulations, this study discovers that incorporating magnetic fields in simulations of massive galaxy mergers has a notable impact on how these galaxy combinations solidify. Although magnetic fields do not greatly alter general features, they have a notable effect on structural characteristics, forming extended discs and spiral patterns in simulations, whereas simulations without magnetic fields yield more compact, ring-like shapes. A separate investigation on resolution demonstrates that global features converge across various levels of resolution and physical modeling but reveals distinct differences in galaxy morphology at sufficient resolution, attributed to enhanced amplification of magnetic fields in high-resolution simulations, effectively impacting gas dynamics. This study further examines how the anisotropic thermal pressure of magnetic fields influences merging galaxies' evolution, leading to spiral structure formation. A thermal pressure map analysis discloses pressure anisotropy patterns across various regions, including disc, bulge, and shock-generated structures, contributing to the formation of distinct galaxy morphologies. Two regimes are identified: a magnetomechanical coupling regime, evident in simulations, and an electromagnetic coupling regime, apparent in simulations, where magnetic fields' influence on gas dynamics is enhanced due to insufficient mixing with shock-generated ions, leading to spiral structure formation. This study provides magnetic field effects on galaxy combinations, offering a realistic framework for further theoretical and observational studies of galaxy combinations. Observational studies of post-combination galaxies can be compared with simulation results to better comprehend how magnetic fields influence galaxy combinations. Moreover, this study sets the stage for investigating magnetic field effects on galaxy combinations involving supermassive black holes. Suggested future work includes using emulating realistic magnetic field effects to examine its impact on galaxy combinations involving black holes and how it may influence black hole growth. Additionally, this study raises questions about how magnetic fields influence black hole-driven outflows and combinations' overall evolution. Lastly, this study provides a method for generating realistic magnetic field effects in simulations of galaxy combinations, which can be applied to various resolution and physical scenarios, allowing for more accurate comparison with observations. This study also introduces a new approach for generating magnetic field effects in simulations of galaxy combinations using machine learning, referred to as EML-FE. Our solution to the 2nd COVID-19 Severity Detection Competition has been successfully presented, where our goal was to classify chest CT images into Mild, Moderate, Severe, and Critical COVID-19 grades. To achieve this, we proposed a cutting-edge infection-aware 3D classification network called the Contrastive Mixup Classification network. This innovative approach involved initially training two segmentation networks to identify lung regions and inner lesions. These lesion masks were used in conjunction with the original CT scans to generate additional useful information. To rectify data imbalance, we incorporated weighted cross-entropy loss into our improved Contrastive Mixup Classification network. Consequently, our approach earned top honors with a Macro F1 Score of 51.76%, outperforming the baseline by a substantial 11.46%. Notably, our technique demonstrated excellent scalability and flexibility, with the ability to accommodate various preprocessing techniques and modification of contrastive mixup hyperparameters without significant detrimental effects on performance. Ultimately, our approach successfully overcame the challenges of the competition and solidified our ranking on the leader board. The code for this project has been made available for public use at https://github.com/TrinhTrung/CSC2021_Code. In an effort to facilitate future research, we have released 2000 CT image samples used for training and testing at https://github.com/TrinhTrung/CSC2021_Data. Additionally, we have published 10 samples of lesion masks obtained from two segmentation networks at https://github.com/TrinhTrung/CSC2021_Lesion_Mask. These resources are intended to benefit the medical imaging community in the ongoing fight against COVID-19. In conclusion, our innovative Contrastive Mixup Classification network has been successfully applied to classify COVID-19 severity levels through the use of chest CT images, and we hope this to contribute to ongoing related research.

Recently, machine learning models have been successfully applied to Grammatical Error Correction (GEC). However, these models are typically trained on native speech and can fail when confronted with speech from domains they haven't been exposed to. This thesis addresses the challenge of adapting GEC models for few-shot domain adaptation, using speech data from new domains without retraining the model. We first investigate a method that fine-tunes a pre-trained GEC model on just a handful of sentences with correction labels, using a large amount of unlabelled data from the new domain as contextual information. This approach is then compared to a method that treats each new domain as a separate language, using a sequence-to-sequence alignment model to align the speech data with corresponding speech data from a source domain with similar language characteristics. We evaluate these approaches on data from read aloud speech in Hebrew, using speech data from new domains that weren't exposed to during training. We find that providing contextual information from a large amount of unlabelled data from the new domain significantly improves GEC performance, with results showing a 92% score on F-score. We also find that this approach performs better than the alignment model, which has a 79% F-score score. We conclude that a simple meta-learning approach is effective for adapting GEC models to new domains, and suggest that it may also be applicable to other NLP tasks. We also believe that this approach can be improved by incorporating more complex loss functions that take into account the variability in speech data from new domains. We hope that this thesis will inspire further research into meta-learning for few-shot domain adaptation in NLP. We have made our code and data available for download at: https://github.com/orellou/few-shot-domains-adaptation-gec. In our research, we diverge from the standard practice in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) of employing a direct one-to-one correlation ('mapping') between source and target domains. Instead, we utilize stochastic translations to account for the inherent ambiguities in domain transformations. This strategy enables us to achieve better results by generating various outputs based on a single source image, thereby utilizing both accurate translations and data augmentation to handle visual variations, producing reliable target labels through the averaging of source predictions across multiple transformed versions of a single target image, and training and aggregating diverse target networks by regulating the degree of stochasticity in translations. Notably, our findings demonstrate notable improvements over strong recent baselines, ultimately resulting in cutting-edge UDA performance on two challenging semantic segmentation evaluation sets. The code for our method has been made publicly available.

Researchers propose using paleo-detectors, an experimental technique, to detect dark matter. Unlike conventional detectors, which require massive and expensive set-ups, paleo-detectors utilize naturally occurring rocks with deep geological history that contain tiny damage tracks from dark matter interactions. Thanks to advancements in microscopy and the ability to study samples over billions of years, paleo-detectors can potentially offer more sensitive detection at significantly lower costs. This could significantly expand the range of sensitivity in dark matter research. Using updated analytical methods, scientists have simulated the capabilities of paleo-detectors under various conditions and found them robust against inaccuracies in age measurements and the composition of samples. Even with relatively high concentrations of radioactive contaminants, the sensitivity of paleo-detectors can surpass current limits, offering the possibility to detect dark matter interactions below existing detection thresholds, even when masses are less than ten GeV. Furthermore, paleo-detectors can potentially complement other experimental approaches by providing a more sensitive means of detecting dark photons and dark axions in the mass range of 10^-5 eV to 10^-2 eV. If demonstrated effective, a large-scale implementation of paleo-detectors could significantly impact the field of dark matter research. Although the first-generation of paleo-detectors is likely to be comparable to state-of-the-art underground dark matter detectors in terms of sensitivity, the unique advantages of paleo-detectors enable them to offer greater sensitivity at lower costs, allowing for a significantly longer integration time, greater density, and more robust operation. As such, paleo-detectors could serve as an innovative, ground-breaking technology capable of greatly expanding the sensitivity of dark matter detection. This new approach may also pave the way for a large-scale, multi-ton dark matter detection system that could be built at a fraction of the cost of conventional underground detectors. This could be accomplished by deploying paleo-detectors in multiple deep boreholes located in areas with suitable rock formations and minimal radioactive contamination, thereby potentially leading to a major breakthrough in the field of dark matter research. The extensive use of Machine Learning (ML) in high-security sectors necessitates a transparent understanding of its methodology. Nonetheless, research into decoding ML models like Random Forest is in its nascent stages. To bridge this knowledge gap, we employ rigorous mathematical techniques and logical reasoning to create a pioneering method for explaining the predictions made by Random Forest. Our approach revolves around Minimal Unsatisfiable Cores and furnishes an exhaustive analysis for feature importance, encompassing both localized and broad aspects, along with adversarial sample examination. Empirical results across multiple datasets showcase the precision of our feature importance assessments. Furthermore, our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art adversarial analysis technique and offers the ability to generate user-centric reports that can inform recommendations in real-world scenarios. Additionally, we demonstrate the versatility of our method by applying it to an actual security-sensitive scenario. Minimally invasive surgery has emerged as a highly effective treatment, allowing for non-invasive exploration of abdominal organs. Advances in medical technology, particularly high-definition cameras and sophisticated software, have enhanced its efficacy and paved the way for computer-assisted procedures. Although the process still faces technical challenges, we have investigated several popular deep learning approaches, including U-Net, FRUNet, and T sNet, among others, for automating tissue segmentation in laparoscopic surgery. Despite these efforts, there is a notable lack of studies focusing on using deep learning for predicting organ movement in real-time, a critical step for registering preoperative images with intraoperative data. To address this gap, we proposed LArGe Deformable Network (LARGeDN) a novel deep learning framework specifically designed for laparoscopic organ segmentation and movement prediction. Initially, we developed two parallel streams: a segmentation stream derived from UNet++ and a movement prediction stream based on AlleviNet. These streams were combined with a deformable transform block using discrete cosine transform and bilinear interpolation. We validated our approach with 1000 training samples and achieved impressive results, yielding a mean absolute error of 5.46 mm for prediction and a Dice similarity coefficient of 0.886 for segmentation. Notably, our framework has been designed with real-time capability in mind and has demonstrated excellent performance on multiple organs, including the stomach, small intestine, colon, and liver. Furthermore, we incorporated it into a registration system, leveraging its predictive capabilities to compensate for organ movement and obtain clear, noise-free images even during surgery. We also explored integrating this approach with multi-frame data, demonstrating potential for further improvement. As a result, we believe LArGeDN offers an innovative solution for addressing organ movement in laparoscopic surgery. Current public datasets for re-identifying individuals are limited due to the difficulties associated with labeling them. Despite the abundance of unlabeled surveillance footage that can be easily obtained, it's unclear how to effectively utilize this content to develop useful re-identification representations. Typically, existing methods focused on unsupervised and domain adaptation use publicly available datasets and then apply them to the target domain after removal of the labels, relying heavily on the relatively small size of the training data. This typically involves fine-tuning the method using the target domain's unlabeled training data in order to achieve good results. By building upon recent advancements in large-scale self-supervised image classification that utilize contrastive learning, we propose learning re-identification representations directly from large quantities of unlabeled surveillance video without relying on labels. By utilizing pre-trained pedestrian detection tools and applying contrastive loss at both the image and tracklet levels, we also integrate camera labels that are available free of charge for the principal component analysis step. Our large-scale evaluation of the method on an unlabeled dataset demonstrates significantly superior performance when compared to other methods that do not utilize training data from the target domain. Additionally, we observed a notable increase in accuracy with deeper network architectures, which is also confirmed by the bar chart provided. By conducting additional experiments, we found that the method is robust to various hyperparameter settings and is capable of producing representations that are effective in other re-identification tasks, which is evidenced by the reduced gap with the state of the art on the standard evaluation datasets after fine-tuning on just 1% of the data. The code and model for the method are available for download at https://github.com/zhubo1988/surveillance-self-supervised. The project also includes a publicly accessible dataset that is comprised of 50,000 unlabeled video clips spanning 1,976 hours, which is available at https://surse.net/.
