The new framework utilizes a non-linear model that takes into account the 'leverage effect' and models the connection between realized volatility and hidden volatility. A specific estimation method was adopted, a simulation test was performed to evaluate its effectiveness. Nevertheless, enhanced datasets are expected to yield statistically significant evidence in the future. This study endeavors to eliminate sampling bias in data analysis. By examining various configurations of nested samplers and traditional Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods, we aim to identify the time efficiency and consistency of these sampling techniques on pulsar timing array data. Despite producing consistent parameter results across methods, our research suggests the implementation of two robust sampling methods for cross-validation and realistic run times in future analyses. Nonetheless, neither time-to-convergence nor model likelihood preferences provided in this study reveal a clear preference between sampling techniques. Nonetheless, we anticipate that the comparison of sampling methods for validating results will prove valuable in ongoing and future searches for a nano-Hertz gravitational wave background signal in pulsar timing data.

The results show that participants generally want to reduce the gap in earnings, but are less motivated to do so and react differently to circumstances where luck has an impact on job success rather than overall income. These findings have implications for research aiming to model people's opinions on income inequality and the apparent disparity between laboratory research and real-world inequality trends in the US. We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework to examine its underlying principles and worst-case scenarios. This framework informs our proposal of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, a novel task aimed at recovering a real-world hypergraph from its graph projection using domain-specific knowledge. To achieve this, we develop a method that involves two components: first, a sampling strategy is employed to significantly reduce the large number of potential hyperedges; second, a hyperedge classifier with two optimized variants is designed to identify candidate hyperedges based on their structural properties in the graph projection. Our experiments validate the efficacy of our approach and its extensions, with impressive results that outperform baseline methods by a significant margin in accuracy, particularly on difficult datasets. Our implementation and data are freely available for download.

We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the degree of unidirectional light release, outperforming previous methods which struggle with variation. Secondly, we introduce a phenomenological angle for measuring emission directionality, but its practical application is limited to straightforward cases due to the inability to handle complex structures. Conversely, entropy based on semi-marginal probability in the Cartesian coordinate achieves comparable results and is also adaptable to emissions with complex structures. The validity of our proposals is verified through numerical simulation and comparison with an empirical formula. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between entropy and other factors including mode order and defect shape, revealing that entropy provides a clear and quantitative indication of emission directionality. Lastly, we experimentally demonstrate the ability of entropy to predict directional emission in ring resonators. Our research offers a theoretical and experimental framework for evaluating emission directionality in microcavity lasers through entropy calculation. Additionally, this research can be expanded to analyze emission complexity in other microcavity devices.

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. The intuitive design of the SIT framework makes it easy to integrate into existing offline learning algorithms. The code is available at: https://github.com/hjdw/SIT.git

We developed a novel approach for registering MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to align images, yet they fall short for low-quality megavoltage images and have limited capture ranges. To overcome these challenges, we employed a Convolutional Neural Network, resulting in a dataset-based comparison using 50 brain images, which demonstrated improved results relative to conventional methods. Experimental evaluations using three public datasets confirmed the effectiveness of our methodology. Interestingly, our 2D network performed better than the 3D network on the large skull base dataset, yet it underperformed compared to 3D networks on the smaller brain dataset. Additionally, we explored non-regularized and regularized 3D CNN results, discovering that T1-weighted images served as a suitable alternative to megavoltage images for input. Ultimately, our study demonstrated the feasibility of CNNs for registering megavoltage images and provided insights for further research. We also openly shared our 3D dataset and implementation of the non-regularized 3D CNN code. Despite achieving promising results, several challenges remain, including addressing batch normalization and incorporating internal structure information to enhance network performance. Still, our research offers a starting point for exploring CNNs in medical image-to-image translation and registration tasks. In the future, we intend to investigate methods for generating realistic capture ranges and addressing the inherent differences between megavoltage and other modalities, such as CT and MRI. Additionally, we aim to apply CNNs to register real megavoltage images, using only images taken during actual treatments. This would enable us to bypass the need for additional training datasets and utilize only the available data. Lastly, we look to combine CNNs with physical models that describe the interaction between radiation sources and the subject's anatomy, with the ultimate goal of generating realistic megavoltage images from CT scans. This would be particularly beneficial for external beam dosimetry. Nonetheless, this research faces significant challenges, including finding suitable datasets and developing techniques for handling dose information. Nonetheless, we believe that exploring CNNs for registering megavoltage images presents an opportunity to break new ground in this area.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that single-particle entanglement results in genuine non-local effects between distant locations, paving the way for its utilization in implementing truly non-local tasks. Moreover, our study reveals the relationship between single-particle entanglement and its capacity for non-local functionality in quantum mechanics. Furthermore, our findings imply that the instantaneous non-locality of single-particle entanglement enables the demonstration of quantum steering without the need for measurement-related correlations between parties. Consequently, this study offers a fresh perspective on the nature of single-particle entanglement and its capabilities in executing non-local tasks in quantum mechanics. Additionally, our study proposes a novel approach to defining the completeness of quantum mechanics, one that is grounded in the capability of single particles to exhibit non-locality in quantum mechanics. A discussion on the relevance of this study to Einstein's original concerns is also included. We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and determine the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in nuclear star clusters. We predict that a significant proportion, roughly 45%, of Population III binary remnants inhabiting these clusters will merge in massive black holes located at the centers of galaxies and that a substantial number, approximately 200,000 per year, will merge in nuclear star clusters located in massive galaxies at low redshift. Additionally, we find that the rate of Population III binary remnants contributing to stellar masses greater than $10^{3.5} M_{\odot}$ in nuclear star clusters and massive globular clusters is around 0.3-3 times the expected number based on detected Population III candidates and implied rates of formation of massive stellar clusters. Our results also indicate that a significant number of Population III binary remnants will merge in nuclear star clusters at redshift greater than 0, and that a considerable proportion of these mergers will produce detectable electromagnetic signatures, offering promising targets for future surveys such as LSST and SKA. Our study provides a comprehensive framework for exploring Population III binary remnants and their mergers and can be further developed with more detailed simulations of stellar clusters and nuclear star clusters. This, in turn, will allow for even more precise predictions of the detection capabilities of future surveys. This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA_p and its analogue VMOA_p. BMOA_p is a part of the family of F(p,q,s) spaces introduced by R. Zhao and serves as the M\"{o}bius invariant subspaces of the Dirichlet spaces D^p_{p-1}. Our focus lies in analyzing the maximal subspace of continuous operators, determining sufficient conditions for strong continuity, and obtaining estimates for the norm of $\mathcal{A}^s$ on VMOA_p when s belongs to (0,1]. Additionally, this investigation is complemented by a study of the spectral properties of a concrete generator on BMOA_1, and an exploration of the relationship between BMOA_p and the Dirichlet spaces D^p_{p-1}. These findings provide initial insights into the operator semigroups on these spaces. As a technical precursor, we establish the equivalence of BMOA_p and F(p,p,1), and demonstrate the connection between VMOA_p and the analytic Dirichlet spaces D^p_{p-1} via the $\mathcal{D}^s$ semigroup. As a result, our study resolves a problem proposed by A. Battaglia and M. A. Picone.

Humanity has continually sought knowledge, a pursuit amplified over the past century through the vast growth of scientific literature. However, despite employing metrics such as citation counts and impact factors, it remains unclear how a discipline's knowledge amount correlates with productivity, specifically how the value of new knowledge varies with each new advancement. To address this question, researchers compiled 185 million articles spanning 19 disciplines and analyzed the citation networks between authors, essentially mapping the evolution of scientific knowledge within each area. Using both structured and unstructured entropies to analyze the resulting data, they devised the Quantitative Index of Knowledge (KQI), which measures knowledge amount as a disorder difference created by increasing order within the scientific literature. Subsequently, they discovered that the growth of new literature accelerates the growth of new knowledge, but there is an evident slowdown before this threshold. Furthermore, at this point of accelerated growth, a discipline's productivity accelerates in tandem with knowledge amount, indicating a significant relationship between the two. Interestingly, if the discipline is narrow enough, new knowledge can arise from an existing body of work, enhancing our understanding of scientific progress and suggesting that both structures and cultural shifts within a community can influence productivity. Ultimately, by applying this framework to various scientific disciplines, it was shown that a slowdown in new knowledge occurs before a threshold of citation density, providing insight into the temporal and structural components of scientific progress. Additionally, the analysis indicates that the acceleration of productivity and new knowledge is linked to a specific slowdown in entropy growth, giving insight into the temporal components of scientific productivity. The proposed methodology can be applied to any temporal citation network, offering a unifying framework for analyzing the evolution of scientific disciplines and providing a tool for diagnosing the underlying structures of a research community. As such, it has the potential to be utilized for personalized paper recommendations, automated generation of discipline-specific reports, and pinpointing key contributors within a research area. By leveraging this framework for 19 compiled disciplines, featuring 185 million articles, researchers have integrated the results into an interactive web application, allowing for exploration of the underlying data and providing a foundation for future applications in scientific literature analysis. The full dataset, featuring 185 million literature entries, is also included with this research, providing a foundation for future investigations within scientific disciplines. In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use dual hop OFDM technology. To mitigate this issue, we analyze two main cases: one involving a single user with a single relay, and another with multiple users and relays. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. By utilizing high signal-to-noise ratio approximations and optimization techniques, we can develop effective power allocation methods that prioritize system security while minimizing interference from power consumption at transmitting nodes. Furthermore, a dual decomposition framework enables us to employ convex optimization to find efficient power loading solutions. We also investigate several suboptimal schemes for various configurations and present simulation results to validate the efficacy of these methods in real-world applications. Ultimately, this study provides a foundation for the development of secure next-generation wireless communication systems. To this end, we propose a coexistence framework that enables interoperability between secure and insecure systems, and demonstrate the security performance gains resulting from the application of this framework. In the complex context of an urban intersection with automated and human-driven vehicles, we explore an essential challenge: generating safe pathways for automated vehicles. Our research focuses on preventing rear-end collisions when a connected vehicle's human-driven leader approaches the yellow and red phases of the traffic light. We've developed a predictive control system that can instantly forecast the leader's braking timing and speed based on the connection's warning functionality, together with data from the surrounding environment and the leader's operations. In a simulated test with a large and diverse dataset, our approach outperformed a basic rule-based system and a machine learning alternative that doesn't utilize the connection's data. When the connection's data isn't utilized, our predictive control approach also outperformed a more advanced machine learning-based brake timing prediction method. We've validated our method's effectiveness in the absence of modeling errors and also explored its robustness to incorrect predictions of the leader's future actions. Our study provides a solution to a significant safety issue at traffic signals and also highlights the value of utilizing connected vehicle technology to enhance automated vehicle safety. Furthermore, our approach can be adapted to handle other safety threats from human drivers.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
Notably, we discovered that aggressive optimization techniques led to unexpected gains in testing efficiency of around 16 percent. 
Evaluations using both human and automated testing revealed that unoptimized models perform similarly on both methods, whereas there was a notable difference in results for low-count neural network models. 
Furthermore, we found that high-performance models undergo significant changes during their initial stages of training in response to the faster simulation rate, necessitating a reevaluation of their evaluation metrics. 
As a result, we propose new evaluation criteria that account for the unique testing environment of Express, which we believe will guide future research toward more effective solutions in this domain. 
The source code and models are now available for public access on both GitHub and PapersWithCode. 
In addition, we have launched the TextWorldExpress platform on the Unity Multi-Agent Learning platform, along with a leaderboard that encourages the community to participate in efficiency-based challenges. 
Ultimately, our research aims to accelerate the development of more complex text-based game challenges, enabling tests of relational knowledge, dialogue management, and other advanced capabilities that can drive substantial progress in the field of virtual agent research. 
We look forward to collaborating with the community to achieve this goal and welcome feedback on our work.

Significant advancements in NLP have been observed in the last decade thanks to neural models and substantial labeled datasets. However, NLP models are often hindered by a reliance on extensive data availability, hindering their application to resource-constrained settings and unique tasks necessitating large-scale labeling. As a means of enhancing NLP data efficiency, data augmentation techniques have been investigated in recent years. A systematic examination of data augmentation in NLP under low-labeled data settings has been lacking until now, resulting in difficulty in comprehending the efficacy of diverse methods in various contexts. This study provides a comprehensive survey of data augmentation in NLP under low-labeled data settings, encompassing an overview of methods such as token-level and sentence-level augmentations, along with experiments conducted on 11 datasets across topics/news classification, inference, paraphrasing, and single-sentence tasks. Our research enables the formulation of recommendations to guide practitioners in selecting suitable augmentations tailored to different settings and highlights the current limitations and potential future pathways for NLP under low-labeled data settings. As an additional contribution, we have developed a publicly accessible repository containing all experiments and data used in this study. This study is a crucial initial step towards unlocking NLP applications in low-resource settings and necessitates further research in data augmentation as well as other efficiency enhancement techniques. This proposed framework we present also opens up new lines of inquiry to be explored in the future. This work is also accompanied by a publicly accessible repository containing all experiments and data used within this study. This study represents a fundamental starting point on NLP under low-labeled data settings, and further research in data augmentation, as well as additional techniques, is required to achieve this goal.

To determine a pure quantum state from a series of measurement results, a common approach is to use a mixed-state simulation by assuming a specific form for the quantum state and estimating its corresponding variables. However, this approach is time-consuming due to the need for a random initial state and a lengthy convergence time for variational algorithms. We present an alternative protocol using the hybrid classical--quantum algorithm "classical diagonalization" to accurately determine a pure quantum state from multiple copies of a single copy of the state. This protocol involves using a small unitary operator that is efficiently simulated on a quantum computer and provides spin contamination-free information about the quantum state. The efficiency of this protocol is demonstrated through the simulation of a 2-D Heisenberg chain and a fermionic surface code, and it is shown that the required number of quantum operations is significantly lower than alternative classical--quantum algorithms. Notably, this protocol enables the simulation of quantum states with extrinsic noise and faulty quantum gates. Furthermore, it paves the way for the effective elimination of spin contamination in quantum state simulations. The proposed protocol is readily implementable using current quantum simulation hardware and could serve as a crucial tool for the development of fault-tolerant quantum algorithms. The protocol is also applicable to scenarios where only a single copy of the target quantum state is available, as indicated by an example simulation of a quantum state corresponding to a specific final state of a time-dependent Hamiltonian. Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system enabled by the Cassini spacecraft has facilitated a comprehensive study of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex through the application of infrared spectroscopy. By analyzing this phenomenon, researchers were able to identify the rates of formation and dissolution of these polar vortices in both hemispheres. The vortex in the north began forming in the late spring, but it took until the end of the summer for it to exhibit the temperature and chemical contrasts seen in the southern hemisphere. The vortex in the north was found to be surrounded by a strengthening temperature gradient at 78 degrees latitude and displayed a hexagonal shape. This indicates that a particular type of atmospheric wave, previously thought to influence temperatures deep in the planet's atmosphere, has the ability to impact temperatures as high as 300 km above the clouds. The formation of the vortex in the north was found to be slowed down by a persistent pattern of winds known as a "rostral nose" and was accelerated by a change in the direction of the winds at 75 degrees latitude. The vortex in the north was also discovered to be surrounded by a polar jet that rotates counterclockwise and is influenced by the movement of three-metre high mountains of air in the mid-latitudes. The formation of the vortex in the north was found to be influenced by the movement of air from the equator, which is driven by the differences in temperature created by the varying amounts of solar energy absorbed by the different latitudes of the planet. The rotation of the planet also plays a key role in the formation of the vortex, causing the slow movement of air towards the poles and resulting in the accumulation of warm air at the poles and the formation of the vortex. The study of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex provides a comprehensive understanding of the complex interactions of the atmospheric and internal forces that shape the polar atmosphere of Saturn. It also highlights the unique opportunities that the Cassini spacecraft has facilitated for the exploration of the Saturn system through the application of infrared spectroscopy. The discovery of the seasonal variation of the vortex in the north and the comparison with the vortex in the south pave the way for a broader study of the seasonal variations of the polar atmospheres of the outer planets. This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. A previously established approach, derived by Glassey through the concavity of variance, is not applicable in this context due to the appearance of boundary terms of undesirable sign in the second derivative of variance. Our primary argument introduces a new, modified variance measure, bounded from below and concave in a way that is relevant for solutions in this particular scenario. This approach allows us to establish the optimal blow-up criterion even in the presence of an obstacle, under conditions that are as broad as those which ensure the finite-time blow-up of solutions over an unbounded domain. A secondary argument extends this optimal blow-up criterion to all solutions, including those with positive or zero energy, through a approach that combines moving boundary estimates with an energy estimate that relies on energy decay. This method of estimation relies on an expression of solution energy concentration near the boundary, as well as the definition of an appropriate boundary blow-up criterion. Ultimately, this enables us to prove the optimal finite-time blow-up criterion for solutions over a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space, under conditions that are as broad as those which ensure the finite-time blow-up of solutions over an unbounded domain. A final observation addresses solutions that may develop boundary blow-up in the presence of an obstacle. This study was motivated by a conjecture presented at the NUS-CRM School on Mathematical Science.

A significant reorganization of spectral weight across the metal-insulator transition has also been observed, with an observable transfer of spectral weight across the entire energy scale from the high-binding energy regime to the low-binding energy regime, in contrast to our findings of unconserved total spectral weight across the metal-insulator transition, which indicates a failure in applying'sum rules of spectral weight',  a hallmark of systems with strong correlations.  Our data suggest that changes in hybridization, effective carrier density, lattice volume, and spin degrees of freedom, possibly all interlinked with the change in electron correlations across the metal-insulator transition, are responsible for such a shift in spectral weight.  Furthermore, our research demonstrates that in V$_2$O$_3$, the metal-insulator transition is fundamentally driven by correlation between electrons, with the effect of these interactions playing a pivotal role in determining the transition's occurrence.  Our studies also offer a greater insight into understanding the electronic structure of systems with strong correlations, underscoring the significance of factoring in surface-related effects while interpreting experimental data collected through surface-sensitive techniques such as resistivity measurement, as this has significant implications for comprehending physical characteristics. The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample's molecular, atomic, or nuclear components. Although scattered light conveys both amplitude and phase information, this phase information is frequently lost during standard intensity measurements, yet it is crucial for reconstructing essential details of a target, as evident from applications like coherent x-ray imaging. A new algorithm is introduced that allows for retrieving phase information from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra, a feature we demonstrate with x-ray scattering off M\"ossbauer nuclei using a synchrotron radiation source. The knowledge gained through phase information also leads to accurate reconstruction of energy spectra from experimental data, a level of precision that cannot be achieved with other methods. Our approach provides a powerful data analysis tool, capable of making full use of x-ray scattering information to investigate the electronic and nuclear properties of a target in various environments, including those involving strong interactions. Hypothesis evaluation is an essential component of scientific inquiry, yet many psychologists who conduct research in cognitive science appear to undervalue this critical step in the research process. Bayes factors can provide a useful solution to common problems associated with traditional statistical methods, such as point estimates and p-values. When applied to cognitive research, Bayes factors facilitate a more meaningful assessment of the relationship between variables and can inform theoretical development through an objective evaluation of competing hypotheses. However, applying Bayes factors to cognitive research requires careful consideration of several factors, including the choice of prior distributions, model parameters, and whether to employ nested or non-nested designs. This knowledge can be leveraged to inform theoretical development and shape future research directions. Through a simulated modular theory of mind task and a real-world study investigating the neural correlates of theory of mind, we demonstrate the practical applications of Bayes factors in cognitive research. Our results suggest that Bayes factors can provide a more accurate and meaningful assessment of the relationship between variables and facilitate a deeper understanding of the underlying cognitive processes at play. Consequently, we believe that Bayes factors offer a valuable tool for hypothesis evaluation in cognitive research and encourage other researchers to incorporate this approach into their own research. This approach can lead to a more rigorous and theoretically driven research practice in the field of cognitive science. 

Keywords: Bayes factors, hypothesis evaluation, cognitive research, statistical methods, psychology and neuroscience. 

Note: This work was inspired by the 2019 conference 'Changing the Research Paradigm in Cognitive Science' held at the University of Kiel, Germany. Our paper aims to provide an overview of the benefits and practical applications of Bayes factors in cognitive research, in addition to presenting two methodological studies. Due to the strict word limit imposed, our paper had to be divided into two parts, which are available at the cited URLs.

We investigate the properties of a negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond under high-temperature and vacuum conditions.  By combining optical detection of magnetic resonance (ODMR) and optical spectroscopy, we studied the spin resonances and radiative transitions at high temperatures.  Our findings indicate that increasing temperature leads to a reduction in the intensity of visible and infrared light emitted from the diamond, as well as a decrease in the frequencies of ODMR resonance and a shift in the emission line towards longer wavelengths.  By comparing our measured data to theoretical predictions, specifically from the Mott-Seitz model, we estimated that a significant nonradiative energy barrier has a height of approximately 0.24 electron volts.  Furthermore, by examining the temperature-dependent frequencies of the ODMR resonance and emission line, we determined that there is a very small vibrational frequency of the system on the order of 0.01 electron volts.  Our results also show that placing the diamond in a vacuum does not significantly affect its properties at high temperatures.  By numerically solving a rate equation, we found that the system's behavior under high temperatures can be described by a mixture of two-timescale dynamics.  Our study provides a thorough understanding of the properties of a nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond under high temperatures and vacuum conditions, which is crucial for optimizing sensing and quantum technology applications that rely on this center.  In particular, our findings can inform the development of methods for reducing the intensity of high-temperature emissions and improving the center's optical properties.  Additionally, this study sets the stage for a comprehensive investigation of the center's properties when subjected to a combination of high temperatures and mechanical stress.  Our research also examines the effectiveness of optical spectroscopy in detecting the Gruneisen parameter, which represents the change in frequency in response to mechanical strain and temperature, and raises the question of the feasibility of detecting the center's optical transition energy through optical detection of electrical spin resonance.  Finally, our study suggests that a more precise measurement of the center's optical transition energy may provide a more accurate determination of the Gruneisen parameter.  This could potentially enable the detection of mechanical stress in diamond based on the center's optical transition frequency, offering a non-invasive and optical-only approach to measuring stress in diamond.  This could have significant implications for various applications, such as the development of more accurate and robust methods for calibrating and controlling diamond-based sensors and quantum technology devices. The backpropagation algorithm, though effective for training neural networks, has a significant drawback: it mandates the sharing of weights. This presents an insurmountable challenge to modeling brain function accurately. A new algorithm developed for two-layer networks overcomes this hurdle by doing away with explicit error calculation and backpropagation altogether. This algorithm remarkably translates to a neural network that closely mimics the brain's connectivity pattern and learning processes, and experiments show it rivals the performance of backpropagation across various datasets. Moreover, the algorithm facilitates weight sharing, addressing a long-standing concern in neural network modeling. We also explore the possibility of its extension to neural networks of greater complexity. The source code for the proposed algorithm is available online.

A new implementation of the Hartree-Fock (HF) method has been developed to efficiently achieve robust convergence for well-behaved central potentials. The method converts HF equations into a generalized eigenvalue problem by using a B-spline basis in a finite-size box and incrementally increases the strength of electron-electron interactions. The accuracy and performance of this implementation were verified through a series of benchmark tests, involving calculations of atoms and ions with central Coulomb potentials, electron gas confined by harmonic and uniform potentials, and alkali-metal clusters modeled by the jellium model. The results were compared to established methods, showing good agreement in terms of convergence patterns and energies for atoms and ions, electron energy and density for harmonic confinement, and dipole polarizabilities for sodium clusters, aligning closely with theoretical and experimental expectations. The developed approach facilitates a straightforward implementation of robust HF theory for electron systems confined by central potentials. The code is also open to further expansion, such as adding spin polarization or experimental tools. The implementation details and the findings from the tests are shared with the electron system community as an open-source code called HfConverger, based on the FiniteBoxHF package written in Python, and the source is included for the examples presented here. The code can be obtained from the GitHub repository https://github.com/fernandoup/FiniteBoxHF and used for calculations of similar electron systems confined by central potentials. The guidelines for using the code are outlined in the GitHub repository documentation. The findings from this study have been published in multiple sources. The results for alkali-metal clusters have been used to guide the design of an experimental study on sodium clusters, as reported in Ref. [25]. The findings on the HF energy and density for harmonic confinement have been compared to data from quantum Monte Carlo simulations, as described in Ref. [26]. The findings on the HF polarizability of sodium clusters have been used to guide the development of an experimental study, as outlined in Ref. [27]. The implementation of robust HF theory for electron systems confined by central potentials is the subject of an ongoing research thread, as described in Ref. [28]. Let $q\ge 3$ be an integer, with $\chi$ denoting a Dirichlet character modulo $q$ and $L(s,\chi)$ being the associated Dirichlet L-functions. This paper will present specific function series, along with novel identities linking the L-functions with Gauss sums, particularly focusing on identities related to $L(2,\chi)$. Additional discussions will surround the application of these identities to nonvanishing values of L-functions and related topics. Furthermore, this paper proves that $L(2,1)$ does not equal $2$, a statement previously proven by Conrey and Ono but here derived from a more general identity. This paper also establishes that $L(2,\chi)$ is linked to sums of reciprocals of powers of integers, a relationship initially explored by Gremer and von Pippich but now confirmed for all Dirichlet characters $\chi$ for even $k\ge 4$. Lastly, this paper presents a method to determine the nonvanishing nature of $L(1/2,\chi)$, a problem particularly significant in random matrix theory. This approach specifically utilizes the work of Diaconis and Shahshahani but offers a more direct computation of the relevant field norms. This computation can also be applied to compute the relevant field norms for $L(s,\chi)$ for any $s$ and $\chi$. This paper's findings provide a more general framework for understanding the nonvanishing values of L-functions and related quantities, indicating that this framework has a potential connection to random matrix theory. This connection is then confirmed for the specific case of $L(1/2,\chi)$. This paper will also present one related open question for further investigation. This question revolves around the application of these identities to further compute the minima of L-functions and related quantities. This computation is particularly important in random matrix theory but also has a potential connection to the distribution of L-functions over the set of Dirichlet characters. This distribution is then represented by an ensemble of random matrix known as unitary orthogonal invariant ensembles but its analysis is currently not well understood. This analysis is instead handled by computing the relevant characters sums or L-functions sums over a specific set of Dirichlet characters, a computation generally achieved by applying the circle method. This method generally computes the relevant sums as an asymptotic formula but can also provide information on the local behavior of these sums, a behavior generally represented by an identity related to the Fourier transform of the Dirichlet L-functions.

High-energy particles with masses beyond the TeV range are difficult to access experimentally. Current constraints from Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis already set a strict limit on their lifespan, at under 0.1 seconds. Next-generation gravitational wave detectors have the potential to drastically improve these limits to the point where their lifespan could be constrained to as short as 10^-16 seconds. This could be possible if these particles once controlled the universe's energy density and led to a transition to a matter-dominated period before decaying in time for our cosmos to form as we know it. As a result, such particles would produce distinctive signatures in gravitational waves emitted during the Big-Bang, including oscillations in the primordial black hole spectrum and spectral shifts in the cosmic microwave background. Furthermore, we find that in order for such particles to influence the early universe in this way, they would have to be long-lived enough to shape the universe's early structure, making them relevant to the search for their direct or indirect signatures in future experiments such as LISA. As a result, we can anticipate groundbreaking constraints from gravitational wave experiments on the properties of these high-energy particles. Additionally, we anticipate that LISA will be able to set lower limits on these particles' masses, potentially below 10 TeV, and place upper bounds on their lifetimes, potentially below 10^-11 seconds. Furthermore, we anticipate that LISA will be able to set long-lived neutrino mass lower limits below 10^-8 eV and upper bounds below 10^-7 eV, and that it will be able to set lower limits on the mass of sterile neutrinos below 10^-5 eV. Our experiments examine how the geometric structure of force-free rigid swimmers interacts with different fluid properties: Newtonian and viscoelastic (specifically Boger fluids).  By changing the swimmer body and its helical tail dimensions, our findings reveal that viscoelastic properties' influence is largely dependent on the swimmer design, potentially amplifying its speed by as much as five times, or instead, diminish its velocity by a similar amount, or leave its locomotion mostly unaffected. Analysis and corresponding theoretical modeling suggest that viscoelastic forces on these swimmers are dictated by a similar'snowman effect' found with linear swimmers, in which asymmetry in the swimmer causes an elasticity-related force that may aid or impede propulsion. Notably, even in cases where viscoelastic forces don't appear to impact swimming by seeming unchanged, close examination reveals that the fluid's properties are still having an underlying substantial influence, affecting the swimmer's trajectory and overall efficiency. Ultimately, our study shows that viscoelastic forces must be considered when analyzing swimming mechanisms, as the swimmer and its surrounding fluid are inseparable, and that swimmer design should take advantage of viscoelastic effects to optimize propulsion in various non-Newtonian fluids. We employed co-evolutionary genetic algorithms in a range of Cournot models to replicate players' learning behavior and assess their capacity for convergence to a Nash Equilibrium. Introducing "social-learning" variations of two algorithms led to successful attainment of Nash Equilibrium, unlike "individual learning" counterparts which consistently failed to converge to the desired outcome. Utilizing simulation outcomes with a specific approach and a particular Nash Equilibrium in focus, as well as a comprehensive statistical analysis of multiple settings, we confirmed that "social" learning variants resulted in higher probability of achieving the specified Nash Equilibrium compared to "individual learning" counterparts. Furthermore, we discovered that two "social-learning" algorithms exhibit distinct preferences in terms of exploration-exploitation trade-off and that some of these preferences result in higher likelihood of achieving the specified Nash Equilibrium. Additionally, we found that some of the "social-learning" variants outperformed the "individual learning" counterparts in terms of average payoff, ultimately achieving the highest average payoff in scenarios where the "individual learning" counterparts failed to converge to the desired Nash Equilibrium. This study provides initial insights into the implications of learning behavior in dynamic Cournot models and sets the ground for future research in this area.

Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. Despite some recent efforts to quantify uncertainty within NNs, no overarching framework effectively addresses uncertainty quantification, even for a single uncertainty source. Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Real-world deployments of these systems require ensuring the reliability of their underlying hardware, shielding them against faulty memory caused by hardware errors. Following the successful use of activation clipping, we have developed a prototype to demonstrate that range control can serve as a trustworthy error detection and prevention method for classifier CNNs, specifically against common memory malfunctions in a binary floating point system. We also explore non-uniform data restriction techniques that efficiently minimize silent errors and hardware-induced data corruptions. The efficacy of our approach is shown through a vehicle classification test, using the ResNet-50 architecture and the MIOVision traffic dataset. The results provided can serve as a foundation for further research and more intricate CNN reliability cases. The source code is available online.

By incorporating blockchain technology, we propose a novel nomenclature and corresponding data models that can capture the essence of netted transactions. Furthermore, our model can accommodate various data formats commonly used in financial transactions. Additionally, we examine how netting can be employed in a decentralized environment, using a sample use case involving a nation's economy. Our investigation involves an evaluation of graph, document, and relational database management systems to determine their effectiveness in storing netted transaction data. A comparative assessment of the performance of these systems in data storage is also presented. Lastly, we provide recommendations on the choice of database management system for netting applications. Our research is relevant to any economy that relies on centralized clearing systems and is considering the adoption of decentralized systems. Our work is a foundational stepping stone for further research and development of decentralized clearing systems. We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level attributes, and linguistic patterns, which can be leveraged from knowledge bases available for over a thousand languages. We employ a novel cluster-consistent neural network to construct this unified vocabulary space by synchronizing words and their clusters. Our results show substantial gains in intrinsic evaluations of monolingual and multilingual semantic tasks, surpassing the performance of current multilingual embedding techniques. Moreover, an extrinsic evaluation using a case study on low-resource language name tagging demonstrates a remarkable 24.5% improvement in F-score compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods. All code and data are freely accessible for download at https://github.com/ghulamei/MultilingualSemanticSpace.git. This repository also includes a pre-trained model for 1040 languages, along with detailed instructions for replicating our experiments.

The MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset has significantly accelerated the study of dialogue state tracking, yet contains considerable annotation errors that significantly impede the robust training of models. The recent releases of refined datasets, MultiWOZ 2.1 to 2.4, are not entirely noise-free, especially in the training subset, rectifying them proves costly. Instead of addressing the issues of annotation quality in the current datasets, we develop a versatile framework named ASSIST, aiming to train dialogue state tracking models with high reliability even from inherently noisy datasets. This framework first trains a baseline model on the original dataset and employs both self-supervision and supervision from correct labels to refine the model. Specifically, ASSIST incorporates both dataset cleaning and correct data selection methods to enhance its performance. When testing the framework with four popular datasets, it is evident that ASSIST delivers highly robust models capable of executing precise dialogue state tracking even from noisy datasets, with multiple evaluation metrics yielding superior results when compared to training from clean datasets. Notably, ASSIST is capable of producing reliable models even when trained on extremely noisy datasets containing as much as 43.4% annotation errors, with a trained model on the refined MultiWOZ 2.0 achieving a high DSTC5 score of 80.3%. The code and model have been made publicly available to facilitate future research in dialogue state tracking. The ASSIST framework serves as a crucial breakthrough in dialogue state tracking research, addressing fundamental challenges of annotation quality, data noise, and scalability. It is hoped that this framework will inspire future research to further improve dialogue state tracking models with high reliability even from noisy datasets, thus paving the way for real-world applications.

In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. A alternative approach, inspired by the theory of gravitating objects, was tested to assess its suitability in modeling Santiago's riots. This new model revealed results comparable to those of the epidemiological model but has a simpler structure. Further analysis was conducted to investigate the impact of modifying certain metropolitan characteristics, such as commuting patterns and neighborhood demographics, on the spread of riots. A crucial finding indicated that both types of models can replicate the distinct peak days of unrest observed in Santiago. Nevertheless, neither model was able to accurately forecast the city's rioting activity in areas not yet affected by the disturbances. Consequently, there is still a significant gap to be bridged in developing a credible theoretical framework that effectively captures the dynamics of urban unrest. Given the limited and often biased nature of available data, further research is required to validate these findings and explore alternative methods before applying them to study riots in other contexts. The new approach suggested that the distribution of riots is shaped by a metropolis's underlying structure rather than a result of a gradual diffusion process. Consequently, there is a need to reevaluate traditional methods for analyzing the spread of infectious urban phenomena. Moreover, it is proposed that a more productive avenue for inquiry involves examining how commuter flows between evenly populated districts contribute to the emergence of hotspots of disorder, in place of attempting to model the temporal progression of riots. A potential pathway for researchers to contribute to this field is outlined. Despite using different types of templates, all predictions accurately estimate Br$ eta$ based on other observable properties, but underestimate its strength by about 0.5{\ox}0.1 dex when using a specific set of templates. This discrepancy does not significant affect our analysis of SFR predictions, but may impact other analyses in the future. We also find that using observed templates results in more precise predictions of Br$ eta$ compared to using predicted templates, which is due in part to differences in the ultraviolet continuum in these templates. Additionally, we find that using a particular line strength threshold for detecting hydrogen recombinations in galaxies is an ineffective method for minimizing contamination by non-galactic sources. Finally, we demonstrate that using a specific machine learning algorithm allows for more accurate predictions of Br$ eta$ line strength when using a set of related spectral energy distribution features, which can be particularly useful in certain data limited scenarios.

We examine the effects of each set on the possible deviation of neutrino behavior from expected unitarity. We also provide a clearer understanding of predictions related to flux and cross-sections, taking into consideration any contamination from new physics affecting hadronic measurements. u$ experiment to show that certain neutrino experiments have sensitivity to this issue. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this algorithm acknowledges the extended features and character sets in its calculations, bypassing the necessity to translate to automata equivalents and utilizing instead a symbolic rewriting system to solve inequality problems with regular expressions. We introduce a new approach to determining containment using a combination of Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives and Antimirov's rewriting strategy, along with an expansion of Brzozowski's derivative operator that accommodates (potentially infinite) sets of recognizable characters. Additionally, this study proves the complexity of determining containment with infinitely vast character sets to be NP-complete. As a further contribution, it is shown that adding either the ability to compose regular expressions or infinite character sets to Brzozowski's basic patterns elevates the containment problem to PSPACE-complete. As a practical application, this research is illustrated by its ability to address real-world challenges in the development of XML dialects. Lastly, existing first-order queries over XML can be reinterpreted as containing issues with infinitely vast character sets, allowing for an expanded view of the containment theory for XML. Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These models, in particular the deep learning-based VIO ones, offer the potential to provide pose information without the need to craft custom algorithms. Presently, the majority of VIO models using learning techniques, often rely on recurrent models that fuse multimodal information and process signals, although they have difficulty training and efficiency limitations. This paper proposes an external memory attention learning-based VIO framework, capable of efficiently combining the data from both the camera and inertial sensors for state estimation, and we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this model by accurately estimating the pose in various challenging scenarios, surpassing even the traditional and current state-of-the-art VIO baselines in various scenes. Moreover, this model exhibits online inference capability with only a fraction of the computational cost required by the other models. Moreover, this model's ability to be trained from scratch on a relatively small dataset, shows that it has low requirement for data, thus making it more suitable for use on mobile agents. This model's excellent performance and efficient design make it suitable for use on mobile agents, and it has the potential to be used in real-world applications. This paper introduces a new robust federated learning approach called Federated
Selective Aggregation (FedSA) that allows the creation of a diverse range of
datasets for model training. The FedSA algorithm generates an initial model and
then creates a series of sub-models on different datasets through robust
federated learning processes. The algorithm's goal is to find a subset of clients
whose training data enables the most accurate model. The proposed method
incorporates both FedAVG and FedMA types of robust federated learning approaches.
The paper demonstrates that the FedSA algorithm's output leads to superior model
performance compared to traditional federated learning methods, specifically that
the error rate decreases with an increase in the number of selected clients. The
FedSA approach is further shown to result in models that are both more accurate
and interpretable. The paper provides the implementation details for the FedSA
algorithm and its components, including the robust federated learning sub-modules
that can be easily integrated into other algorithm frameworks. The paper also
includes the results of several robustness and generalizability tests, showing
that the FedSA algorithm effectively prevents degradation and improves model
performance even when faced with new data sets and client distributions. The
paper also includes comparative studies to the other federated learning
algorithms, specifically that the FedSA algorithm outperforms the FedAVG and
FedMA types with a 6% and 5% increase in accuracy respectively. The paper
also introduces a novel problem known as the selective aggregation problem and
provides the FedSA algorithm as one possible solution to address this issue. The
paper also includes code availability statement and the data can be found in

Approximately a decade ago, the existence of grid cells within the medial entorhinal cortex of rats was first identified. Researchers initially hypothesized that grid cells' unique firing patterns, linked to periodic locations within the environment, might serve as a spatial metric. Subsequent studies have since revealed significant new insights into grid cells' properties and the neural networks surrounding the parahippocampal-hippocampal region. As a result, existing models of grid cells require revision and refinement. This survey seeks to present an extensive summary of grid cell research conducted over the past decade, covering key aspects including grid cells' functionality and responsiveness to external stimuli as well as their underlying neural foundations. Furthermore, we explore and discuss various conceptual and computational models of grid cells, discussing their underlying principles, proposed mechanisms for grid cell operation, and the predicted behavioral outcomes. Finally, we examine potential pathways for future grid cell research, considering both experimental and theoretical studies. As one of the fundamental components of the spatial navigation system, understanding grid cells is crucial, and it is only through continued multidisciplinary research that their intrinsic roles and mechanisms can be effectively revealed.

Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified various differential rotation patterns, characterized by the Rossby number. Specifically, anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by rapid polar rotation and slow equatorial rotation, can occur in high-Rossby-number, slowly rotating stars. If this regime emerges during the main sequence and persists in slow rotators, it may impact the generation of magnetic fields through the dynamo process. Considering the possibility of magnetic cycles in these stars, we explore how they may be affected by their rotation rates.

Our research reveals that kinematic dynamos can generate magnetic cycles and global polarity reversals for both rotational regimes, provided the $\alpha$-effect is localized to the tachocline. However, when the $\alpha$-effect is distributed across the convection zone, solar-type cases exhibit cycles and polarity reversals, while anti-solar cases do not. The presence of magnetic cycles in slowly rotating anti-solar cases is hindered by the accumulation of magnetic flux in the tachocline.

We propose that the presence of magnetic cycles can be used to identify anti-solar differential rotation in slowly rotating stars, and that this may be detectable through the inspection of Zodi pictures from Solar Digital Spectropolarimeter (SDP) or the upcoming Solar Spectrographic Survey (S4). If found, this could provide valuable insights into the global dynamics of slowly rotating solar-type stars. Furthermore, it may also shed light on how the presence of magnetic cycles is linked to the formation of anti-solar differential rotation itself. Ultimately, a possible connection between the two could have implications for how we study and model the internal dynamics of slowly rotating solar-type stars. 

Keywords: Turbulent dynamo, solar-type stars, differential rotation, magnetic cycles, polarity reversals.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. Decentralized carrier concentrations were found to correlate with flux noise in the same resonators, highlighting the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. Decentralized carrier concentrations were found to be reduced by heat treatment, flushing the device with nitrogen, and replacing the silicon substrate with hydrogenated silicon, all of which resulted in significant decreases in flux noise. We also discovered that decentralized carrier concentrations flare out over several micrometers from the etched edge, directly impacting quantum device design standards. We propose adjusting the shape of the isolated area to match the extent of carrier flaring to minimize its influence, demonstrating a crucial role of near-field terahertz investigations in optimizing quantum device performance. Furthermore, we demonstrate the ability to detect persistent currents using terahertz radiation, offering a potential alternative to microwave measurement methods. This research showcases the capabilities of terahertz near-field optical microscopy in providing critical insights into the operation of quantum devices and offers a powerful tool for optimizing their performance.

This study employs a motivic perspective to examine twisted algebraic $K$-theory.
For a variety over a zero-characteristic field and an Azumaya algebra over that
variety, we develop the $\mathcal{A}$-twisted motivic spectral sequence.
By determining the motivic twisted algebraic $K$-theory spectrum as a twisted form
of motivic cohomology, our work expands upon earlier results by Kahn-Levine where the
algebra is derived from a base field.
Our methods utilize a combination of slice filtration and birational geometry to achieve this,
resulting in a representability theorem that expresses twisted $K$-theory space as
an extension of twisted Grassmannian by the twisted integers sheaf.
These results in turn enable proof of cdh descent and Milnor excision for twisted
homotopy $K$-theory. Lastly, this study includes computations of twisted homotopy $K$-theory
for smooth projective varieties over perfect fields and fields of positive characteristic.

This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future. Ultimately, this research aims to position Venus compared to other terrestrial planets and Earth's sister planet, Mars, in the context of the solar system's formation and evolution.

Investigating the chemistry occurring on charged droplets offers valuable insights into enhancing industrial chemical production methods, a phenomenon common in nature. To address this, researchers have developed a novel method using reaction nanoscopy on charged propanediol nanodroplets. By leveraging ultrashort laser pulses, they have established the capability to monitor the droplet's average size, charge distribution, and surrounding near-field. Furthermore, they have demonstrated the sensitivity of reaction nanoscopy by comparing two types of propanediol isomers, revealing that certain conditions produce a significantly increased yield of methyl ions. Simulation results indicate that this increase results from an optimal molecular alignment on the droplet's surface in one isomer, paving the way for the observation of charge dynamics and chemical reactions within droplets. Ultimately, this work positions reaction nanoscopy as a powerful tool for the in-depth study of droplet chemistry.

The success of cancer diagnosis, treatment planning, and patient outcomes depends heavily on the properties and spatial organization of cells within tissues. Therefore, computer-assisted cancer care relies heavily on accurate representations of tissues that can capture key histological details. Building upon existing cell-graphs that encode cell characteristics and spatial relationships, researchers have been using machine learning to establish correlations between tissue structure and function. However, a unified ontology for describing tissues has yet to be established, likely due in part to the absence of a standardized compositional framework for histological entities. In response, we propose a hierarchical scheme consisting of 13 tissue components at the atomic level, combining existing knowledge to define their characteristic features, arrangements, and relationships. By constructing tissues from these basic components and using them as nodes in a graph, we demonstrate improved classification performance using machine learning compared to traditional approaches. The proposed method also facilitates the efficient creation of large cell databases from smaller training sets. Additionally, we observe that focusing on key tissue components aids in generalizing across different imaging modalities. Our results indicate that identifying and modeling the composite nature of tissues enhances cancer classification accuracy and can be an effective tool for cancer diagnosis and research. This work has the potential to be expanded to other diseases and applications. It also provides a foundation for addressing additional challenges, such as modeling cell dynamics and responding to therapeutic interventions, all of which could be beneficial for cancer care. Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters, online messages, or neuronal activity, are used extensively in various fields. A key point process model that depends on the past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model relationships, both excitatory and inhibitory, between events of different types. We have investigated a nonparametric Bayesian approach to estimating the nonlinear Hawkes process parameters, obtaining results on the concentration rates of the posterior distribution. Additionally, this has implications for the convergence rates of Bayesian estimators. Another significant aspect in the study of event-data involves uncovering the graph that represents the connections and interactions between events, or the Granger connectivity graph. We have established the consistency of Bayesian methods in estimating this graph, particularly showing that the posterior distribution converges to the correct adjacency matrix, as does a Bayesian estimator based on a suitable loss function. This research has significant implications for the analysis of event-data, providing a way to estimate the parameters and Granger connectivity graph of the underlying process through Bayesian methods. This is especially important for capturing short-term relationships, as opposed to other methods that can become stuck in local minima. As an example, we apply our methods to study the dynamics of a Mexican earthquake network. Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which remain flawless when accurately integrated, maintaining machine-precise levels of total mass, energy, and linear/angular momentum conservation. Notably, this property holds significant value in computational astrophysics for processes such as binary interactions and compact object mergers. Although the inclusion of gravity in such applications leads to excessive computation in pairwise interactions, a Fast Multipole Method variant addresses this by substituting interactions between distant particle clusters, which however introduces inaccuracies in angular momentum conservation. Our modification of this algorithm eradicates spurious torques, guaranteeing angular momentum conservation without substantial computational overhead compared to standard FMM. This conservation enhancement is computationally minimalistic, totaling $O(N)$ operations per time step, making it an ideal utility for demanding simulations. Our conservation-intensive FMM library for spherical particles is an open-source, multi-threaded, and highly efficient C++ implementation, compatible with any SPH code via easy-to-integrate scripting. This library is particularly suited for binary interactions involving compact objects and may be downloaded from https://github.com/WilliamH1/FMMSPHConservationIntensifed. Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) techniques have potential in decreasing this burden, but they are hindered when datasets are small and have few labeled images. Future experiments to study the Cosmic Microwave Background will be able to measure a crucial parameter $r$ with high precision, however a significant challenge lies ahead. Delensing, the process to extract a primordial signal buried under another signal caused by gravitational lensing, is key. To improve this process beyond traditional quadratic estimators which may not be sufficient, the next generation experiments could potentially benefit from more sophisticated methods such as a maximum a posteriori estimator or even a machine learning approach, the neural network, that was previously shown to have superior lensing reconstruction performance when compared to the quadratic estimator in certain scenarios. We take this further by applying this estimator to a realistic scenario in line with the S4 experiment's design, and find that even when using a very simple model for the delensing process, the neural network estimator's performance is on par with the quadratic estimator when the noise levels are low, however when the noise levels increase, the neural network estimator takes advantage of its ability to handle complex priors, resulting in a significant improvement over the quadratic estimator of around 8 $\sigma$ for a 1% confidence level for $r \approx 0.1$. These findings demonstrate that neural networks have considerable potential to contribute to delensing in the future. We have also made our Python code publicly available to facilitate the comparison of different delensing methods in future research. We anticipate that as research in this area continues to evolve, the challenge posed by delensing will be an important driver in the development of new signal processing algorithms. In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson established a local and combinatorial approach to calculating Pontrjagin classes for differentiable manifolds. We delve into the specifics of their method and examine the underlying principles of their groundbreaking concept of combinatorial differentiable manifolds. Furthermore, we delve into the role of Gelfand and MacPherson's approach in their subsequent work on linearizing maps of differentiable manifolds, a theme that holds significant interest for us. Lastly, we outline how their methods have influenced current research in the field.

We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 3 up to day 434 after its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a notably faint absolute peak magnitude compared to other similar supernovae. Observations during the plateau phase revealed characteristic H-alpha absorption similar to other SNe~II. Furthermore, SN~2020jfo exhibited a prominent [Ni~II] line in its nebular-phase spectra, often observed in low-luminosity SNe~II. Using nebular-line flux ratios and spectral features, we categorized SN~2020jfo as group-B based on its spectral characteristics. Progenitor detection from pre-explosion images revealed that SN~2020jfo originated from a massive star with an initial mass between 18-25 times the solar mass, likely exploding within 0.5 parsecs of massive star-forming regions. SN~2020jfo's spectral and photometric patterns suggest a low-luminosity, short-plateau SNe~II with similar characteristics to SNe~2008cn and ~2011aw, indicating that this subtype may include explosions from massive stars with low initial masses, potentially in the range of 12-16 times the solar mass, over areas with moderate to high extinction. This finding would help clarify the diversity within the SNe~II category. Notably, SN~2020jfo's progenitor, observed in mid-infrared images, had a significantly larger radius compared to other directly imaged SNe~II progenitors, with an estimated initial radius greater than 10 days, indicating a possible connection to small red supergiant donors. This could imply that hydrogen-rich SNe~II with slow declines may come from red supergiant donors, with explosion masses around critical velocity for unearthing the star's outer layers, resulting in weaker nebular lines and [Ni~II] features in their spectra. This new perspective would help identify potential Type~II supernovae exploding from red supergiant donors. Lastly, SN~2020jfo's light curves and spectral sequences showed a marked similarity to SN~2008cn and ~2011aw, all of which shared a common ancestor with the SNe~10Be progenitor, suggesting a possible link between radiative SNe~10Be and certain low-luminosity, short-plateau SNe~
