To investigate the structure of dark matter, a deep learning framework was implemented and used to explore the impact of velocity and density information on the formation of halos through $N$-body cosmological simulations. A Convolutional Neural Network was trained on an initial snapshot of a dark matter simulation, with the goal of predicting halo masses at a given point in time, in a specific range of masses. However, when testing the inclusion of velocity information with the standard model of cosmology, negligible improvements were found. By increasing the amplitude of initial scalar perturbations in the simulation, a significant improvement was observed in the halo mass prediction when adding velocity field information. Ultimately, when the simulation parameters were modified further, models trained on density information alone failed to predict halo masses accurately, demonstrating the importance of velocity field effects on the halo collapse, particularly in certain mass scales. Additionally, when testing the inclusion of an external gravitational potential and tidal tensor on the simulation, it was found that deep learning models can distinguish between different components of the potential and learn about the halo's shape and its surroundings. Therefore, this study showcases the capability of deep learning to investigate the physics of dark matter halo formation and sheds light on the environment and shape of halos through the mass accretion history of the cosmos. It also highlights the potential of this to contribute to fundamental cosmological research.

We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of solving the equation of state directly to determine pressure and density. 

This method's key benefit is its universality, applicable to any equation of state without limitations, making it an ideal choice for future three-dimensional stellar evolution simulations that will tackle supermassive black hole surrounds and star-forming environments. 

We have successfully validated our method against the conventional approach for an isolated, rotating star and also considered scenarios where the star interacts with its surroundings and experiences external forces. 

This new method has been implemented within the {\tt StarEOS} module of the PHANTOM code. 
Our approach allows for any equation of state, including that of weakly interacting fluids, and it has been used to calculate rotating stellar models encasing massive scalar boson condensates. 
These models exhibit equilibrium configurations over a wide range of rotation rates and values of the Hertzsprung-Garloon mass and radius. 
Furthermore, this approach has enabled us to carry out simulations of evolving stars, matter, and massive scalar fields, even when the star experiences external influences, such as supernova explosions and gravitational waves, in scenarios such as star-planet interactions and binary stellar mergers. 
These simulations hold significant potential for advancing our understanding of rotating stars and their surroundings in complex astrophysical environments. 
These new numerical methods and associated rotating stellar references, including models compatible with the Effective One Body formalism, will be made publicly available through the {\tt Einstein Toolkit}. 
These developments will provide a foundation for conducting three-dimensional simulations of rotating stars in dynamic contexts, also enabling future simulations of star-forming environments surrounding supermassive black holes and involving weak interactions with massive scalar fields.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy. Additionally, our approach has been compared to other labeling strategies in a controlled setting, with results indicating that selective labeling can reduce costs by up to 7 times, without a notable impact on accuracy. The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their post-merger remnants. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves requires the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this within the strict timeframes mandated by gravitational wave observatories' real-time analysis policies. We introduce an innovative use of quantum circuit learning, specifically T-count variational circuit training for binary neutron star black hole waveforms, which exhibits rapid training speeds on quantum simulators and experimental quantum devices. Leveraging this approach, we developed a quantum neural network that can learn neutron star binary waveform templates in approximately 0.5 seconds to 1 second on a simulator, enabling potential application in real-time electromagnetic follow-up of neutron star waveforms. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these learned templates can distinguish neutron star waveforms from black hole waveforms, highlighting the potential for this approach to be explored in other gravitational wave physics topics. Given its training speeds on quantum devices, this approach may help bridge the gap between theoretical waveform models and real-world gravitational wave data. We have made the code publicly accessible to facilitate future research and potential use in real-time electromagnetic follow-up of neutron star waves. We intend to explore the capabilities of this approach in identifying post-merger neutron star remnants and anticipate it may be applicable in scenarios where waveform templates are not perfectly known. We encourage open discussion with the community on this topic.

The adverse effects of social determinants of health on the quality of care and healthcare disparities have long been acknowledged. However, many social determinants remain unstructured and un-coded within electronic health records, often only present in the free-text notes made by healthcare professionals. As a result, there is a pressing need for an automated method to extract this valuable information from clinical notes. Our research centers on the development of an innovative multi-stage system combining techniques like named entity recognition, relation classification, and text classification to identify and extract relevant social determinants of health information from clinical notes with minimal human intervention.

We utilized the N2C2 Shared Task data consisting of 4480 annotated sections on twelve different social determinants of health sourced from MIMIC-III and University of Washington Harborview Medical Centers to test our proposed system. Given the challenge posed by entities that overlap with each other, our team designed a unique marker-based model, which we incorporated into the multi-stage system. 

In our experiments, our proposed system consistently demonstrated exceptional performance by achieving better overall Micro-F1 score and outshining existing state-of-the-art models when handling the critical issue of overlapping entities.

Ultimately, our study successfully validated the potential of the proposed system to effectively identify and extract vital social determinants of health information from clinical notes, a crucial development with the potential to enhance clinical care and monitoring. However, there are concerns regarding error propagation, necessitating future research to further optimize entity extraction, particularly when encountering entities with complex meaning and a scarcity of available data.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about long-term economic and innovative declines. To explore these effects, this study uses a vast dataset that integrates technological tracking of individuals' physical encounters, financial transaction records, and innovative activity data for four major US cities from 2019 to 2020. By analyzing the pre-pandemic conditions, the data reveals a strong correlation between physical encounters and social interactions at lower population diversity levels and shows that encounters influence social interactions through both supply and demand mechanisms. Following the onset of COVID-19, reduced social interactions led to decreased economic productivity and innovative activity, with cities experiencing higher population diversity experiencing greater declines in productivity and innovative activity due in part to their greater reliance on local consumption. Notably, the data indicates that reduced physical encounters, rather than reduced technology use, primarily drove the decline in innovative activity. Long-term projections indicate that if cities fail to regain their pre-pandemic levels of physical encounters, they may experience persistent declines in economic productivity and innovative activity, prompting the need for targeted policy interventions to boost urban encounters and drive innovation and productivity growth. Furthermore, lower population diversity levels can exacerbate urban decline in the long term, making it essential for cities to diversify their populations through fair and inclusive economic and social policies to maintain their innovative and economic prowess. The methodology employed in this research can be used to monitor the impact of public health policies and urban conditions on social interactions and economic productivity, providing policymakers with a valuable tool to evaluate the effectiveness of these policies. Ultimately, this study underscores the significance of physical encounters as a key urban growth driver and highlights the need for targeted policies that promote equitable diversity and community resilience in cities. Such an approach is crucial for the long-term innovative and economic prosperity of cities in the face of public health challenges and demographic changes. While previous studies have analyzed the short-term impacts, there is a pressing need to explore the long-term consequences in depth. The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose an innovative method that leverages transformer-based language models to counter one of their inherent drawbacks, allowing our CMTR-BERT framework to combine diverse text representations, mitigate the sequential constraints inherent to the underlying architecture, and integrate contextual information effectively. Experimental evaluations using two disparate, publicly available datasets showcase our method's capability to achieve superior performance benchmarks, highlighting the benefits of both utilizing automatic text summarization and incorporating contextual information for enhanced performance. Furthermore, in-depth analysis of our results reveals the reliance of our method on text representations and contextual information for both accuracy and efficiency. Ultimately, our findings suggest that transformer-based models can serve as a viable alternative to linear baselines for the proxy task of binary text classification. The code for this study has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ArashAnazi/Contrastive-Binary-Text-Classification.

Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. Following an introductory section on BERT, EMO20Q data, and annotation tasks, we detail a method to fine-tune BERT, which entails assessing annotated labels by examining the classification of utterances with the same annotation as mutual paraphrases. We demonstrate this approach to be a reliable means of evaluating and revising the annotations of intricate textual data sets containing complex semantic labels. Specifically, we show that dialog system responses generated from these labels by text-to-text BERT models exhibit similar semantic meanings to their corresponding original dialog transcripts. Moreover, we observe that human annotators revise the labels based on the classification results from the BERT model and that these revised labels reduce the classification errors compared to the initial annotations. Ultimately, we conclude that BERT can be utilized as an expert in the annotation process, helping human annotators to evaluate and refine their labels by providing a more accurate semantic classification of the data. As a result, we are able to create a more reliable and robust EMO20Q dataset, which in turn facilitates the development of more effective dialog understanding systems. We will detail the implementation of two reduction methods and then apply them to a common test case, with a focus on a monolithic approach, solving both fluid and solid problems simultaneously, and a partitioned approach, solving these problems separately with a fixed point strategy. To evaluate these methods, we'll use a variant of the Turek-Hron benchmark test case, characterized by a fluid Reynolds number of 100. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The system's performance was validated through simulation testing and real-world implementations, and its source code is available openly for public use. The methods presented can be employed as a standalone algorithm or integrated with other filtering methods by incorporating HiTMap's map updates. The approach offers a lightweight and self-sufficient mapping solution suitable for autonomous navigation on a small to medium scale. The code is hosted on https://github.com/ivpec/HiTMap. We investigate the emergence of magnetocaloric effect (MCE) in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides due to their proximity with a ferromagnetic substrate, specifically a MoTe$_2$ monolayer on EuO with a heat source. Using a tight-binding model that accounts for proximity-induced exchange and Rashba fields and temperature via Fermi statistics, we simulate this setup and reveal substantial changes in spin-polarized entropy for energies beyond MoTe$_2$-EuO's bandgap. Adjusting the chemical potential enables MCE manipulation to induce heating or cooling based on spin orientation. Notably, the Rashba field has contrasting effects, enhancing MCE in the bulk but eliminating it in 2D configurations. This finding suggests the possibility of designing magnetic 2D materials with controllable MCE through proximity effects. Moreover, we demonstrate that MCE can be induced in MoTe$_2$ by replacing the EuO substrate with a HEMT, creating a functional magnetic caloric switch. This concept may lead to the development of spin-polarized thermal memory cells and other integrated magnetic caloric switches.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate results, particularly as the gap narrows, in contrast to a local response model which generates unappealing results such as divergent fields and excessive energy losses. Notably, the desirable results obtained from the hydrodynamics model can also be achieved with a simple local approach that excludes the spillover and conventional Thomas-Fermi approximation by considering an equivalent reduced gap size. This finds further confirmation by experiments on metallic nanogaps with molecular sizes. We propose this approach of describing light propagation in small metallic gaps as an alternative to complex quantum models for use in the design of future nanoscale optical components.

The Calculus of Constructions, introduced in 1985 by Coquand, has been a driving force in the development of dependently typed programming and higher-order constructive logic over the past 25 years. This influential theory has influenced research in programming languages and type theory, contributing to the creation of languages such as Coq and Agda through its numerous extensions. This survey presents an in-depth analysis of the various proofs demonstrating the strong normalization property of the Calculus of Constructions, emphasizing both the underlying similarities between these proofs and the unique goals of the researchers involved. Additionally, this work provides an overview of the dependent pattern matching extension proposed by Motizadeh in 2010, which has been adopted by the Coq programming language, and showcases its expressiveness through a range of examples, including proofs, recursive functions, and data encodings. This work also introduces a type-checking algorithm and a correctness proof for dependent pattern matching that is straightforward and lacking in the current implementation of the Coq programming language. Furthermore, this work advocates for the integration of dependent pattern matching with recursive definitions in dependent types, demonstrating its feasibility with the current type-checking infrastructure. This approach has already been adopted by the Agda programming language, which offers a more comprehensive alternative to the proposed features through its use of pattern matching with recursive types in dependent types. Nevertheless, the features proposed in this work can be incorporated into the next generation of dependent programming languages without compromising their existing functionality. In the case of a finite admixture model whose components and weights are unknown, techniques from stochastic convex geometry help us determine how the number of identifiable components changes in response to an increase in the amount of collected data. Additionally, placing a Dirichlet process prior on densities within a defined range enables us to recover a measure that narrows to the specific identifiable components, thereby yielding the corresponding admixture weights. A new algorithm is then proposed to accurately capture the complexity of data by utilizing only the minimum number of components necessary. Through simulated examples and real-world applications, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, including one where a reduced number of components effectively predicts multiple underlying components.  We also establish a connection to existing methods, including one that is shown to be a special case under the assumption of independent and identically distributed data samples. Further, we explore and demonstrate the complexities posed by dependent data samples and the successful application of our proposed method to financial time series data. Lastly, we discuss and show the successful application of our approach to zero-inflated count data and reveal that the underlying structure of such data often adheres to a complex distribution.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and data layout for optimal memory bandwidth.  We also incorporated multiple parallel strategies for the do-all operation to better suit various application characteristics and data layouts, and have demonstrated the DynaSOAr framework's performance benefits through real-world SMMO application case studies.  These applications, involving both scientific and real-world programs, showcase significant performance gains over both sequential and parallel CPU implementations, and also outperform state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators in terms of both memory bandwidth and application performance.  The DynaSOAr CUDA framework is particularly useful for easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming by average developers, and its design and implementation are both lock-free and parallel, resulting in superior performance and efficient memory usage. Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates the Fourier series with implicit neural networks to create instance segmentation masks. FourierMask uses a Fourier transformation on the coordinate positions and feeds the mapped features to an implicit function represented by a coordinate-based convolution neural network. This enables FourierMask to predict specific instance masks and adapt the Fourier transformation for various objects, thus making it applicable to real-world image instances. Since implicit functions operate on point-to-point mappings, FourierMask uses a boundary loss to ensure predicted masks accurately delimit the target instances. By integrating FourierMask with a object detection engine like Faster R-CNN through a simple head replacement, we can utilize the Fourier transformation's ability to capture diverse objects and achieve comparable performance to Mask R-CNN while reducing the number of parameters by half. Moreover, FourierMask outperforms Mask R-CNN by a 0.7% improvement in mAP and attains a higher quality mask score (0.607) on the MS COCO dataset. The code is openly accessible at https://github.com/yunhsun/FourierMask.

Our investigation focused on a laser pulse with frequency variations, which results in a critical density threshold dependent on time. The model we applied goes beyond the initial assumption of linear variation. Our analysis shows that in cases of negative frequency variations, the higher frequency component interacts with the target before the lower frequency component, whereas the reverse occurs in positive frequency variations. As a result, a more densely packed plasma is needed for transmission with negative frequency variations, as opposed to unchirped or positively chirped pulses. However, negative frequency variations allow for increased transmission at higher densities (six times the critical density), producing a highly stable and persistent electrostatic field behind the target and significant ion acceleration in opposite directions due to the electron thermal pressure. Ions from the auxiliary layer can be efficiently accelerated by the electrostatic field generated behind the main target layer, with optimal results achieved when the thickness of the auxiliary layer is around one micron. The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from approximately $500$ million to 1.1 billion years. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune-sized planets with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. Additionally, the team detected an Earth-sized candidate called TOI-712.05 with a short orbital period of $4.32$ days. By calculating the habitable zone for this system, TOI-712 d appears to lie on the inner boundary, and further research into TOI-712, with a brightness of $9.9$, is worthwhile due to its relatively young and temperate conditions. This system offers a chance to study the evolutionary processes of young planets through a range of environments and may provide insights into how systems form and evolve over millions of years. Ultimately, a more precise rotational period and stellar activity index are needed to complete the picture of this intriguing planetary system. We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques.  Moreover, both doped carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2.  We propose that tuning TiO2 by introducing such defects could enhance its photocatalytic properties.  Additionally, our study reveals that N-O bond formation is necessary for N to exhibit a fixed magnetic moment, and that this could provide a means to control the magnetism of N within TiO2 by manipulating such bonds through light or chemical means.  Lastly, both doped carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2, and could potentially be used in applications such as water splitting. This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for using forward proton tags to identify the production of top-quark pairs in LHC experiments. I demonstrate that with a specialized detector configuration and data analysis, where the uninteracted protons are detected using a streamlined system and identified using a unique technique, tag-based identification can significantly enhance the sensitivity to top-quark pair production at the LHC. Even with only limited information from the proton tags, a specialized detector and analysis technique allow for a 3σ signal detection in a background-dominated scenario with the HL-LHC, exceeding the expected sensitivity of HL-LHC top-quark pair searches by 2-3 orders of magnitude with only the proton tags, and also illustrate the feasibility of obtaining accurate top-quark kinematics with a combination of tag information and reconstruction of the top-quark candidates from the detector data, enabling detailed top-quark physics analysis with this implementation system. Additionally, I outline potential improvements to further improve the sensitivity to top-quark pairs with this implementation system. Upgrading the LHC to its HL-LHC configuration and implementing a precision detector with a specialized proton-tagging system for full-proton coverage, along with upgrading the corresponding software for full-proton analysis, would be essential for achieving these sensitivities. This implementation system for top-quark pair identification and analysis could also be adapted for other new physics signatures involving protons and/or neutrinos in LHC experiments. This paper introduces a groundbreaking method to identify Bell's Palsy solely by analyzing a person's eye movements in a video. We have observed that patients with Bell's Palsy encounter difficulty blinking their afflicted eye, creating a noticeable disparity in blinking patterns between the two eyes. Building on existing research, our work exclusively focuses on eye movements rather than entire facial images. This unique approach ensures individuals' anonymity and facilitates the interpretability of AI-driven conclusions. We have devised a novel metric called blink similarity, quantifying the similarity between blinking patterns, and successfully demonstrated its reliability through rigorous experiments requiring minimal labeled data. Notably, our eye-centric system offers enhanced efficiency and user-friendliness when compared to conventional methods. Furthermore, we have established that our model is robust in handling diverse eye movements and can accurately perform valence appraisal, despite having no access to the rest of the face. Additionally, we have developed an eye-centric system that can efficiently handle multiple blink cycles, making it suitable for real-world applications. All source code and datasets are available for public access.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap using an out-of-time correlator as noise increases from both amplitude damping and Pauli channels, our findings reveal that simulations utilizing qutrits can handle up to 10 to 100 times more gate noise than their qubit-based counterparts for the same mass determination error. Furthermore, while achieving a 20 percent accuracy for the mass gap may become achievable in the near future using qutrits, the same outcome seems unrealistic with qubits. Our study employs both random noise and noise channels to simulate the effects of noisy gates, comparing the performance of qutrits to qubits of the same number of two-level systems, and also investigates the impact of different qudit shapes on error tolerance. Ultimately, our analysis suggests that the use of qutrits can provide a more significant advantage in quantum computations than previously anticipated.

Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two. Additionally, this research explores the relationship between a group's diameter and its subgroup structure, particularly identifying groups whose diameter is both polynomial and upper-bounded, which includes nilpotent groups and certain soluble groups. Lastly, this research provides a quantitative estimate showing that any group with a polynomial diameter contains a large abelian subgroup. This result is achieved through an improvement to the Szemeradi rotation problem, and it offers a better bound on the group size in question. This new result is an improvement over the previous record held by Breuillard and Tointon. As a result, this research offers implications on rotation problems in combinatorial theory. Furthermore, this research raises an open question regarding the existence of infinite groups with a polynomial diameter, especially when considering the context of metrically polynomial filling groups. This concept was first introduced by Breuillard and Tointon. This question has the potential to yield new insights into the understanding of groups with polynomial diameter. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS inverter to convert temperature readings into corresponding V-T curves, with the help of a thermally-sensitive resistor array driven by a thermistor. A subsequent digital processor analyzes the resulting V-T curve to calculate the temperature based on a look-up table method. The proposed system is integrated into a 180nm CMOS process, with a temperature range of -70~120degC and an accuracy of 1.2degC. The temperature sensor occupies 0.071mm^2 of area and has a 1.2fJ/K conversion energy per sample. Furthermore, this system is adaptable to various supply voltages, with a sub-threshold PMOS operating from 0.25V to 0.35V. Long-lasting stability in the magnetic fields of Ap-stars, white dwarfs, and neutron stars has not been observed.  In studies, various magnetic configurations have been shown to be unstable inside stars.  This work suggests that non-axisymmetric instabilities in these stars may be caused by a fundamental mode of axisymmetric instability, specifically the Rayleigh-Biehn instability, which affects stable equatorial rings and targets the star's interior.  Numerical simulations indicate that when a high-stability magnetic field is present, a stable equatorial ring may form, however, when the field strength decreases, the ring becomes unstable, breaking into smaller loops.  This loop formation was witnessed in simulations using both the Pencil Code and the Pencil Code GSE.  Furthermore, simulations indicate that the growth rate of this instability is proportional to the square of the stellar rotation rate, in accordance with theoretical predictions.  This finding implies that the instability could be the source of the variable pulsar spin down, specifically affecting neutron stars with certain magnetic configurations and spin down rates.  This work also highlights the importance of considering the effects of the neutron star's spin down torque on its equatorial ring magnetic field, which could lead to the stabilization of the ring, thus affecting the particle acceleration and absorption of pulsar radio emission.  This study may have implications for white dwarfs and Ap-stars with stable magnetic fields, where the underlying field geometry could be explored by analyzing the stability of their equatorial rings.  This work lays the groundwork for more in-depth numerical investigations and observational studies of these stars.  This could ultimately pave the way for a deeper understanding of the origins and significance of stable magnetic fields in these stars. The functional renormalization group (FRG) technique has been proven useful for analyzing complex systems in multiple disciplines, including statistical physics and quantum field theories. Researchers solve FRG problems by establishing a set of flow equations that reflect the adjustments made to a system as a parameter of coarse-graining changes. In this paper, we introduce an innovative strategy to address flow equations that draws on parallels between these equations and conservation principles found in fluid dynamics. We then demonstrate the feasibility of adapting sophisticated numerical methods from fluid dynamics to tackle the complexities arising from the renormalization group, specifically the appearance of non-analytic behavior. Additionally, our findings facilitate fresh perspectives on renormalization group flows, including understanding how the nature of the flow might be irreversible. We explore the application of our framework to one-dimensional and higher-dimensional models and anticipate it to contribute positively to further research into the renormalization group in quantum field theories. Music enthusiasts still heavily depend on conventional search engines like Google for pop music, which is surprising considering how indispensable the internet has become in everyday life. Our innovative proposal is for a music-centric search engine called Pied Piper, which will serve as a comprehensive meta-search tool, enabling users to find relevant music information by searching for lyrics, song metadata, audio, or a blend of any of these options. By offering an intuitive multi-format search, Pied Piper aims to make music discovery more accessible and efficient. In this paper, we outline the design and implementation of our prototype, which is available online at musipied.com. The proposed system leverages Elasticsearch to handle search queries and combines multiple APIs to retrieve desired music data, which is then presented to users in an engaging interface. A user experience assessment involving 20 participants revealed that users prefer Pied Piper over Google for searching pop music. Notably, users found Pied Piper to be both effective and efficient in finding desired music information. In our work, we also explore various design choices for the user interface and provide insights gained from user feedback, along with empirical data on search query frequency and user interaction with the system. Lastly, we discuss potential future developments and directions for this music search engine. The source code for Pied Piper has been openly shared on GitHub at https://github.com/abhishek4334/pied-piper, contributing to the community's quest to enhance music experience through community-driven initiatives.

Current deep learning-based techniques for LiDAR data processing exhibit enhanced performance, but are hindered by the need for large, labeled training datasets. Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness. These operators enable the development of recurrent relationships in zonal functions, especially concerning their space dimension. Notably, this breakthrough enables the solution of a continuous problem with a singular continuous spectrum. The proposed methods are then applied to solve a nonlinear integral equation, a classic problem in potential theory, involving the construction of a harmonic function given a given boundary value on the sphere. The novel operators and associated recurrence relationships also give rise to new representations of the Gegenbauer polynomials, highlighting their connection to random walk and fractional derivatives. The proposed methods are further demonstrated through numerical examples. The theoretical findings are validated through numerical experiments, while the computational implementations are based on the NGSolve library for BEM and a custom-made implementation for the fractional walk. The associated software is publicly accessible and can be utilized for the approximation of zonal functions. The developed methods also facilitate the generation of artificial data, enabling the training of machine learning models on the sphere. The accompanying code enables users to train and evaluate related neural networks. The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major puzzle in high-energy astrophysics for many years. To shed light on this enigma, researchers are correlating UHECRs with high-energy neutrinos as they offer a direct and magnetically unbiased glimpse into hadronic interactions of cosmic rays. This paper introduces three new strategies to link neutrino and UHECR arrival directions. With upgraded data sets from IceCube Neutrino Observatory and ANTARES for neutrinos, as well as from Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array for UHECRs, statistical significance and accuracy are significantly enhanced compared to the results from 2015. The analyses comprise looking for UHECR-UHECR excess around neutrino sources, searching for UHECR excess along high-energy neutrino paths, and finding UHECR-neutrino pairs on diverse scales. None of the analyses uncovered substantial deviations, thus diminishing previously reported over-statistical findings and providing tighter constraints on the neutrino-UHECR spatial correlations. With increased sensitivity, the limits on the UHECR-neutrino correlation angle have been set at $\theta \geq 2.5^\circ$ with $p=0.68$ and $\theta \geq 2.0^\circ$ with $p=0.32$. These constraints suggest a significant portion of neutrino and UHECR emitters must have spatial extent larger than $10^8 M_\odot$. Furthermore, this study positions the neutrino-UHECR detector field test project, HAWC-GZ, in the context of these analyses. HAWC-GZ has the potential to make significant contributions to these research strategies with its optimized configuration, capable of reducing systematics and increasing statistical significance. Ultimately, with upgraded and next-generation facilities, a thorough understanding of the relationship between neutrinos and UHECRs will be achieved, ultimately revealing insights into the origin of these cosmic phenomena.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. The stick-slip regime is also influenced by the distribution of surface curvatures. The findings of this study provide a deeper understanding of the mechanisms that control friction in complex liquids and may have implications for applications involving the flow of complex liquids over rough surfaces. Additionally, we note that the stick-slip regime is a key factor that can affect the onset of turbulence in flows of complex liquids over rough surfaces. 

This study may have implications for various applications such as the flow of blood over stenotic valves, the transport of dust in turbulent flows, and the movement of dry solid surfaces over liquid surfaces in microelectromechanical systems. 

We propose that the relationship between the occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes and the surface roughness factors considered in this study may also be applied to other types of complex liquids, such as solutions of polymers and surfactants. 

We also suggest that the "leverage rule" may be applied to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime in other systems of rough surfaces in contact with complex liquids. 

We believe that the existence of a stationary soap film regime has implications for the development of new types of robust and long-lasting foams that could have applications in various industries. 

We propose that stress patterns during the stationary regime may be used as a tool for characterizing and differentiating between various types of complex liquids.

This report details the results of the 2019 ISIC challenge, which focused on using images and data to make predictions about skin cancer cancer cell invasion potential. Unlike previous challenges where only dermoscopy image classification was assessed, this year's competition uniquely explored this additional aspect. Participating teams submitted 19 entries, with the top-performing team developing an innovative algorithm that combined multiple techniques to analyze the images and estimate the challenge factors. Their approach was unique in comparison to other classification methods. Unfortunately, they were unable to share their data and methods with the full scientific community due to confidentiality constraints. As a result, the challenge organizers were unable to perform any additional analysis to validate these findings. Nevertheless, this experience has provided valuable insights to further develop Estimatio, the skin cancer diagnosis application, and inform future approaches for estimating challenge factors in image classification tasks. Estimatio's source code is available for public review on GitHub at https://github.com/havreek/Estimatio. For more information, please see the accompanying paper available at https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.05129. It has been accepted for presentation at the 2020 International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention.

Building on a novel theory, microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we've successfully applied it to examine the dynamics of systems undergoing expansion or contraction, despite a significant challenge. Typically, this issue arises when the phase space volume changes, resulting in distinct initial and final microstates that can't be linked by reversible processes. We present an innovative solution to overcome this limitation, using a system that undergoes free expansion without an external influence, and demonstrate that the proposed method aligns with thermodynamic principles. Our solution identifies the dissipated energy as a thermodynamic average of work performed by each individual microstate and confirms its nonnegative value during free expansion, which holds surprising implications. We've also derived an expression for work done during contraction, demonstrating its connection to the change in average energy of expanding microstates, and utilized this understanding to analyze the dynamic cooling of a system. Through these studies, we've validated the practical usefulness of microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics.

A possible detection of ethynyl benzene (C6H5CCH) at a column density roughly ten times greater than the cyclopentadiene derivative is also reported. The calculated abundances for cyano derivatives of cyclopentadiene and benzene are notably lower than previously recorded figures. The ethynyl and cyano derivatives of the cyclical compounds possess a rotational temperature very close to the cloud's kinetic temperature. The relative abundance of the ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers was found to be roughly 1.4 times greater than the abundance of the two cyano cyclopentadiene isomers, which may reflect the abundance of the parent radicals CCH and CN. The calculated CCH over CN ratio is higher for cyclopentadiene but significantly lower for benzene. The formation of the cyclical compounds in TMC-1 can be attributed to a reaction pathway based on neutral-neutral reactions, which also suggests benzene's expected abundance should be comparable to that of cyclopentadiene. The relative abundance ratios of the cyano and ethynyl derivatives of the cyclical compounds may provide valuable information on the relative abundance of the parent radicals CCH and CN in interstellar clouds. Additionally, the abundance of these compounds in TMC-1 can offer a means to monitor the variation of CCH and CN abundance in different regions of the galaxy. The detected ethynyl compounds share a rotational temperature with the cyano derivatives of the cyclical compounds, which may indicate a link between their formation pathways. The discovered ethynyl compounds provide further evidence that the chemistry of TMC-1 is primarily governed by neutral-neutral reactions, a viewpoint that is not universally shared. The detection of these compounds also highlights the need for a re-evaluation of previous interpretations of spectral line profiles in TMC-1 in light of new ethynyl compounds found in this study. The ethynyl compounds detected in TMC-1 exhibit a doublet structure due to an hyperfine interaction with a spin of 9/2, which has not been observed previously in an interstellar spectrum. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now standard, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This issue can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. The proposed models achieve up to +3.88 BLEU points gain over strong baselines on the NIST Chinese-to-English dataset. We also analyze the learned look-ahead attention coefficients and matrices to gain insights into the neural translator's decision-making processes. The experimental results indicate that our proposed models perform significantly better than conventional attention models. We further examine the impact of different target context sizes on the look-ahead attention mechanism. The findings suggest that the proposed look-ahead attention mechanism is capable of modeling target context up to five previous target words. The experimental results also indicate that the proposed models are capable of learning the look-ahead attention coefficients and matrices that adapt to different target context sizes. The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in complex software and challenging practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and implementation of grid computing. A translational perspective is helpful for comprehending the progress of grid computing technology. Specifically, we show how developing the grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit thrived due to a focus on applying research directly. In the process, we highlight valuable insights that can be applied to other projects in the field of translational computer science. Finally, we outline a future roadmap for the field, emphasizing the potential for other areas of computer science and other domains to benefit from a similar approach. This is illustrated by the experience of The Ohio State University in moving its research and computing infrastructure to the cloud. An evaluation of the benefits and challenges of this transition is provided, and recommendations for other research groups and organizations to follow suit are offered. Ultimately, we conclude that a sustained investment in the development and deployment of cloud and other technologies requires a shift from a purely research-oriented to a more applied perspective. This perspective is essential for the advancement of computer science and for the greater benefit of society. Failing to make this shift will impede the progress of computer science, whereas adopting this perspective will enable continued innovation and progress in this field. A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, we investigate the model's dynamics in a framework that is robust and solution-independent. Our analysis of the model relies on constraints derived from both its asymptotic behavior and numerous observational limits. Through numerical computations, we solve the Hubble parameter equation, which yields results when plotted against a set of current Hubble data. Our analysis of the model reveals that despite its quintessence-like nature, it surpasses the phantom barrier. To assess the model's predictions for the universe's evolution, we investigate the development of the deceleration parameter, the cosmic density, and the effective equation of state parameter for both the model and its embedded dark energy component. Our findings also support a value of 8 × 10^6 Pa.s for the model's current-day viscosity coefficient, which corroborates several past studies. This model has the capability to effectively explain the observed evolution of the cosmos. It predicts that the universe will continue to expand at a rate exceeding the half of the present-day value, eventually reaching a condition similar to that of dust in the distant future. In educational settings, curiosity is a crucial skill that fosters creativity, a passion for learning, and a vital preparation for a future where lifelong learning and skill acquisition will be increasingly essential.  Unfortunately, many school systems are undermining curiosity by focusing solely on test-taking.  However, educators are seeking innovative ways to spark curiosity in their students, as they recognize the importance of lifelong learning in an ever-changing world.  One understudied aspect of curiosity is its link to peer interactions.  Our study introduces a pioneering theoretical framework that combines cognitive and social factors to explain how peers can inspire curiosity through various observable behaviors and underlying states.  This framework distinguishes between two components of curiosity: personal factors and peer influences.  Our data analysis confirmed a significant, positive relationship between these factors and curiosity levels.  Building on our findings, we developed a computational model that effectively predicts curiosity levels based on prior knowledge, learning experiences, and peer behaviors.  Our model exhibits several key features, including activation, a habituation effect, and a critical state.  The results of our simulations replicated the established characteristics of curiosity and demonstrated the benefits of peer interactions.  Notably, the model distinguished between mere observation of peer learning and actual influence from those peers.  Our study offers a novel theoretical framework for studying curiosity in collaborative learning environments and presents a pioneering approach to addressing the challenges posed by the dynamic and covert nature of curiosity. Gaussian processes serve as a versatile framework for estimating unknown functions while incorporating prior knowledge about their behavior.  While multiple Gaussian process models are accessible in the context of Euclidean space, their selection is significantly more limited when working within the context of undirected graphs. This research adapts the stochastic partial differential equation formulation for Mat\'ern Gaussian processes - commonly employed in the Euclidean space - to analyze its counterpart in undirected graphs.  By demonstrating that the resulting Gaussian processes share the benefits of their Euclidean and Riemannian counterparts, this study also provides methods enabling these graph Mat\'ern Gaussian processes to be efficiently trained using established techniques. This, in turn, enables them to be utilized within settings that include mini-batch and non-conjugate applications, making them more suitable for practical applications and easier to integrate within broader learning architectures. The effective management of urban roads plays a crucial role in the optimal operation of urban transportation systems and overall city functioning. Current monitoring techniques rely heavily on inductive loop sensors, roadside cameras, and crowdsourced data, but they often come with limitations of high costs, restricted coverage areas, or unreliable data due to low user participation rates. In this study, a groundbreaking approach of mobile sensing is presented, utilizing a large fleet of ridesharing vehicles to monitor and interpret the condition of urban roads as they traverse through the network. Our analysis assesses the sensing performance of this approach based on several key factors including road segments covered, data reliability due to repeated visits, and implicit inferences drawn from collected data combined with urban road topology. A model for optimizing routing is developed to balance maximum coverage and highest reliability of collected data, with the capability to be solved efficiently through a heuristic algorithm. Real-world data from over 20,000 ridesharing vehicles in New York City is utilized for thorough experimentation and analysis of sensitivity. Our results show significant advancements in road coverage and reliability improvement through this approach, achieving an overall coverage rate of up to 75.5% of all road segments with 97.2% of those implicitly covered, alongside a reliability boost of at least 31.1% compared to traditional methods. The developed approach and results provide a strong foundation for further research in mobile sensing and its applications in monitoring urban infrastructure conditions. Furthermore, our approach may also be adapted for monitoring other infrastructure, such as utility grids, with possible modifications. Ultimately, this approach has the potential to give rise to new pricing and operation policies that benefit both city administrators and mobile sensing service providers. In the process, a new mobile sensing dataset called CitySense is introduced, featuring a comprehensive set of attributes for ridesharing vehicle data that can serve as a basis for multiple research opportunities in mobile sensing. This dataset, incorporating over 200 million observations from over 20,000 vehicles in New York City, offers various features and conditions for different infrastructure components, user interactions, sensor data, and environmental factors, making it an ideal platform for exploring numerous mobile sensing challenges and opportunities. This work is responsive to recent calls for more innovative approaches to sensing and exploring the potential of mobile sensing systems. It is our hope that this research will spark further discussion and advance the mobile sensing field, encouraging others to investigate other mobile sensing applications, systems, and research questions. This work is also part of an ongoing effort to develop a comprehensive mobile sensing research agenda, with a focus on exploring new opportunities

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. These limits significantly surpass the current limits set by other experiments. We also explored the instance where J/ψ decay into two invisible dark matter particles. In this case, we found that existing limits on sub-GeV dark matter and certain types of neutrino interactions remain unchanged. However, we also found that J/ψ decay into invisible matter can be a relevant production channel for future dark matter detection experiments, specifically for detectors that rely on J/ψ decays to stimulate dark matter scattering with nuclei. If the energy scale for this process is around 10 GeV, we found that J/ψ decays could provide up to 75% of the dark matter events detected by these experiments, which could be crucial for their sensitivity in the absence of other production channels. Lastly, we found that J/ψ decaying into two neutrinos or dark matter particles can give rise to missing energy signals in certain final states, such as charmonium plus a photon, charmed mesons, charmed baryons, or charm quarks. These searches could lead to more stringent limits on energy scales or even provide alternative explanations for observed J/ψ decay rates into these final states. This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote-sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience. This package can be accessed using the following command: install.packages('Rfssa') - To install the most recent version, use install.packages('Rfssa', repos = "https://rfssa.github.io"). For more information, please visit https://github.com/RFSSA/RFSSA. A tutorial on applying MFSSA can be found at https://rfssa.github.io. A feature that sets MFSSA apart from other multivariate time series analysis approaches is its ability to analyze signals rather than values. This is particularly useful for analyzing intraday temperature curves and remote-sensing images of vegetation. Comparative studies have shown that the signal-based approach yields higher reconstruction accuracy than the traditional approach. A comparative analysis of different dimension reduction techniques for the intraday temperature curves revealed that the functional approach outperforms the traditional method in most cases. Furthermore, an evaluation of different smoothing techniques for the estimation of functional eigenfunctions and singular spectrum revealed that the use of Bayesian methods results in the lowest mean squared error. Finally, an application of MFSSA to the analysis of remote-sensing images of vegetation revealed that the approach can identify distinct functional patterns in different regions. This research provides a comprehensive framework for the analysis of MFTS and can be used to analyze signals rather than values. Deep learning-based automated essay scoring systems are increasingly employed by educational institutions and testing agencies to evaluate numerous applicants, as they are efficient and cost-effective. Although these systems have been successful in various applications, little research has focused on understanding the complex processes underlying them. This study aims to investigate the importance of different aspects, including input features, scoring criteria, task types, and data quality on the accuracy of automated essay scores. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. As a result, the source can produce plasma with maximum densities of up to 1.3 x 10^20 m^-3 and 1.9 x 10^20 m^-3 at 13.5 MHz and 27.1 MHz respectively. Furthermore, increasing the power input has shown potential to further enhance plasma density. The source has already been put to use in ICRF experiments at the IPP's Gustav Maxwell Institute in Hohmadel, Germany. To streamline this process, a common solution is to use advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In this paper, a novel approach called Scaled Cross-Stage Mask Detection is introduced, which first uses a shrunk feature map to detect potential targets (scales) from the image, and then employs high-resolution context information to refine the results. By combining high-level structural information with low-level target information, this model achieves exceptional performance on the two publicly available datasets NDSC-RIODB and PSB. This hypothesis is validated through experimentation with several types of graphs. This research also contributes to the field by examining the relationship between line graphs, hamiltonian paths, and hamiltonian cycles, and offers several conjectures to be verified. A blockchain-based smart contract is an automated transaction program, utilized in various cryptocurrencies, that is generating high demands for static verification. To fulfill this need, our project HELMHOLTZ is introduced in this article as a static verification tool specifically designed for Michelson, a statically-typed programming language used in the Tezos blockchain. By integrating Michelson with a user-defined specification through refinement types, HELMHOLTZ accurately checks the correctness of a Michelson program. As the basis of this project, a core refinement type system is also outlined for Mini-Michelson, a core calculus of Michelson, that includes compound datatypes and other fundamental elements of programming, enabling successful verification of complex Michelson programs, including transactions and digital signature checks. Unlike other approaches that rely on runtime checking, refined Michelson provides a statically-verified guarantee of transaction safety, enabling the prevention of contract breaches before execution. Furthermore, HELMHOLTZ has been utilized in refining actual contracts listed on the Tezos network in conjunction with contract developers and testers. The refinement capabilities of HELMHOLTZ have also been compared to other approaches, such as runtime checking, demonstrating its capabilities to be a superior method for ensuring the safety of transactions and contracts. As a result of this comparison, successfully refined contracts were also shown to have a significantly lower breach rate in comparison to those that had not been refined. Consequently, the use of HELMHOLTZ for refining Michelson contracts is highly recommended. Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. A discussion on future research directions is also included to facilitate the development of more comprehensive theories that can encompass the complex workings of modern Neural Networks. 

Furthermore, we propose that the fundamental nature of Neural Networks as a class of signal processing systems can be further understood by categorizing them into two categories: data alignment systems and adaptive data alignment systems, with the latter being capable of adapting its alignment parameters based on input data to extract meaningful patterns. 

Ultimately, our analysis is applied to analyze and visualize the learning process in GCNNs when dealing with linear and non-linear data components, and a related study on the recognition capabilities of simple Neural Networks is also presented. 

This study's findings can contribute to improving the understanding of how and when Neural Networks recognize complex patterns and extract meaningful features from data. 

Also included are some interesting observations gathered from the analysis, such as the realization that while GCNNs can extract features from irregular data patterns, their recognition capabilities are actually based on aligning input data with predetermined patterns, a notion that may seem counterintuitive at first glance. 

In summary, this study's objectives are to explore the inner workings of GCNNs using the signal processing theory, analyze the feature extraction process in GCNNs, and provide some interesting observations gathered from the analysis, all in the context of understanding complex pattern recognition capabilities of Neural Networks. 

With that in mind, the specific focus will be on irregular data patterns, and the feature extraction process in GCNNs will be examined in that context. 

In addition, some interesting observations will be presented to showcase the complex pattern recognition capabilities of Neural Networks. 

It is worth noting that although the study will focus on GCNNs, it will also include related discussions on traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases of GCNNs

A example is given to illustrate that the program derived from a proof may not be optimal because it may be too permissive, allowing unauthorized access. This highlights the need for a more refined relationship between programs and proofs that takes into account program authorization. It is proposed that programs with both sequential behavior and secure multi-process interaction could correspond to logical proofs with sequential and cut rules, and that such programs could be equivalent to logical proofs with deep tree structure. In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$. Additionally, we examine two variants of the $k$-means problem - the case with fixed target centers and a variation of the problem known as $k$-centers. We demonstrate that our algorithm for $k$-centers generalizes to $k$-means with fixed targets, providing an improved solution for this problem. We validate the efficacy of our algorithm through experimental results. Moreover, we derive an optimal lower bound for the $k$-centers space complexity in the dynamic data stream setting. Further, we outline a general approach for dynamically updating coreset algorithms in the streaming setting. We leverage this approach to devise an innovative $k$-means algorithm for static datasets, exhibiting superior performance when compared to existing solutions. Lastly, we discuss an intriguing open question regarding the $k$-means clustering problem in the dynamic data stream context.

We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. Additionally, we observe that the benefit of hierarchical learning increases with increasing grid complexity. Moreover, we find that the valued functions learned in the individual games can provide valuable insights for future policy optimizations. Our method is further adaptable to accommodate various player and learner dynamics by integrating them into the reward structures of the individual games. Overall, our hierarchical approach offers a versatile solution for solving large-scale discrete stochastic PEGs by structuring complex Epsilon-equilibria and facilitating efficient learning within complex grid worlds. This is particularly relevant for applications requiring high computational processing power, such as self-play learning in grid world environments. This is our key contribution in this study. Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives on vast amounts of unlabeled dialogue data. Although these methods have yielded notable improvements, they are limited by the requirement of labeled data for fine-tuning. On the other hand, pre-trained models like BERT benefit from numerous tasks through low-cost batch-wise training, thereby making them suitable for a variety of applications. In this work, we introduce a tree-structured pre-trained model called TCM called Dial-T, which leverages unlabeled dialogue data through contrastive pre-training. Dial-T incorporates a tree-structured module that categorizes dialogue utterances into sub-structures, allowing for automatic generation of semantic labels for unseen dialogue data. Unlike conventional methods that rely on labeled data for task-specific fine-tuning, our model is capable of executing tasks merely through batch-wise fine-tuning. Our empirical studies confirm that our method converges to optimal performance on understanding dialog tasks with minimal task-specific data, surpassing state-of-the-art performance on the DialogRE dataset and achieving competitive results on TDAI. Notably, Dial-T attains a high accuracy of 68.16% on the DialogRE dataset with just 32 annotated examples, outperforming models that utilize extensive annotation. Our code and data can be accessed via this link: https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/Dial-T. Our work lays the groundwork for exploring contrastive learning on dialogue data and underscores the potential of pre-trained conversation models in various dialog understanding tasks. In the long term, Dial-T may serve as a foundational model for dialog applications, analogous to BERT's status in natural language processing. In the short term, we hope our results will motivate studies aimed at enhancing dialo-gue pre-training methods and expanding Dial-T's capabilities to additional tasks and data sources.
